subtopic_detail: Baseline metabolic screen before SGA initiation
stem:
A 23-year-old woman is being admitted informally for a first episode of psychosis and the consultant plans to commence a second-generation antipsychotic tomorrow. She has no known chronic illness, takes only the combined oral contraceptive pill, and denies illicit substance use on urine drug screen. Her mother has type 2 diabetes diagnosed at 52.

On examination she is settled. Vital signs are within normal limits. She has never had blood tests through this service and the intern is asked to organise the baseline metabolic panel per the RANZCP monitoring schedule before the first dose is given tomorrow morning.

data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 62 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 22.8 kg/m2, waist not yet measured.
data_table.Bloods: None on file for this admission.

lead_in: Which set of baseline investigations best matches the recommended pre-initiation metabolic panel?

options.text: Waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, and 12-lead ECG
Fasting glucose, fasting lipids, blood pressure, and prolactin as the mandatory pre-initiation panel
Oral glucose tolerance test, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, blood pressure, and echocardiogram
Weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, urea and electrolytes, and thyroid function tests only
Weight, blood pressure and urinalysis alone, deferring all bloods until the six-month review

subtopic_detail: Prolactin monitoring on risperidone
stem:
A 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been on risperidone 4 mg daily for six months with excellent symptom control. At her routine review she reports that her periods have stopped over the last three cycles and she has developed a small amount of milky discharge from both nipples on gentle expression.

She has no headache, no visual change and no galactorrhoea spontaneously. She is not sexually active, uses no hormonal contraception and a urine beta hCG done today is negative. TSH is within normal limits. Her weight, BP, fasting glucose and fasting lipids have all been stable since baseline.

data_table.Observations: Weight 64 kg, BMI 23.5 kg/m2, BP 118/74 mmHg.
data_table.Bloods today: Urine beta hCG negative; TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to assess for primary ovarian or uterine pathology
MRI pituitary with contrast to exclude a prolactinoma before any bloods
Repeat TSH, free T4, morning cortisol and LH/FSH as a broad endocrine screen
Fasting serum prolactin level with a repeat sample if elevated
Bone mineral density DEXA scan of lumbar spine and both hips

subtopic_detail: SGA choice with metabolic risk factors
stem:
A 42-year-old man with a new diagnosis of schizophrenia has been reviewed by the community team for antipsychotic initiation. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes eight months ago, is on metformin 1 g twice daily with the most recent HbA1c 58 mmol/mol, and has a BMI of 34 with waist 118 cm. His father died from a myocardial infarction at 54.

He has never taken an antipsychotic before, has a normal ECG with QTc 410 ms, and has no known allergy. He tells you he is very worried about further weight gain because he lost his last job partly because of fatigue from his diabetes.

data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 104 kg, BMI 34.0 kg/m2, waist 118 cm.
data_table.Bloods: HbA1c 58 mmol/mol (target under 53), fasting lipids: LDL 3.4 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which antipsychotic is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg orally at night, titrated to response
Quetiapine 300 mg orally at night, titrated to response
Aripiprazole 10 mg orally daily, titrated to response
Risperidone 3 mg orally daily, titrated to response
Clozapine 12.5 mg orally at night, titrated per protocol

subtopic_detail: Diabetes screening cadence on olanzapine
stem:
A 31-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has been on olanzapine 15 mg at night for four months since discharge from his index admission. He has gained 6 kg over that period (weight now 92 kg, BMI 28.8, waist 100 cm) despite dietitian input arranged through the community team. His baseline HbA1c was 34 mmol/mol and today it is 43 mmol/mol; fasting glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. Fasting lipids are borderline (LDL 3.2, HDL 1.0, triglycerides 1.9).

He has no symptoms of hyperglycaemia, no personal history of diabetes and no Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander heritage. His father was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at 60. He is due for his scheduled 12-week metabolic review today and asks how often his diabetes bloods should be checked from now on.

data_table.Trend: Baseline HbA1c 34, week 12 HbA1c 43 mmol/mol; fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4).
data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 92 kg (+6 kg), BMI 28.8 kg/m2, waist 100 cm.
data_table.Lipids: LDL 3.2 mmol/L, HDL 1.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.9 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diabetes-screening cadence from this review onward?

options.text: Repeat HbA1c and fasting glucose in 12 months as part of the annual metabolic review
Repeat HbA1c and fasting glucose within three months with reassessment of weight and lifestyle
Proceed straight to a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test today and repeat annually
Screen with fasting glucose only every six months and drop HbA1c from the panel to reduce cost
Screen only when he develops symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia or unexplained weight loss

subtopic_detail: Statin threshold in serious mental illness
stem:
A 52-year-old woman with schizophrenia on quetiapine 400 mg at night attends the community clinic for her annual metabolic review. She is a lifelong non-smoker, has a BP of 138/86 mmHg, and her fasting lipid panel today shows total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L, LDL 3.9 mmol/L, HDL 1.1 mmol/L and triglycerides 1.6 mmol/L. HbA1c is 41 mmol/mol and she has no diagnosis of diabetes or chronic kidney disease.

She has never had a cardiovascular event. She has no Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander heritage. Her Australian absolute cardiovascular disease risk calculator score today is 9 percent over five years. She is currently on no lipid-lowering therapy and asks whether she needs to start one.

data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 78 kg, BMI 28.6 kg/m2, waist 96 cm.
data_table.Bloods: TC 6.1 mmol/L, LDL 3.9 mmol/L, HDL 1.1 mmol/L, TG 1.6 mmol/L, HbA1c 41 mmol/mol, eGFR over 90 mL/min/1.73 m2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate lipid management step?

options.text: Repeat lifestyle counselling only and reassess absolute CVD risk in 12 months
Commence fenofibrate 145 mg daily as first-line lipid-lowering therapy
Add ezetimibe 10 mg daily as monotherapy alongside lifestyle counselling
Switch quetiapine to aripiprazole and defer any lipid therapy decision until after the switch
Commence a moderate-intensity statin such as atorvastatin 20 mg daily plus lifestyle counselling

subtopic_detail: Metformin for antipsychotic-induced weight gain
stem:
A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia has responded well to olanzapine 15 mg at night after two prior antipsychotics were stopped for extrapyramidal effects (haloperidol) and akathisia (risperidone). Over eight months on olanzapine he has gained 12 kg (baseline 78 kg, now 90 kg, BMI 29.4, waist 103 cm) despite four months of engagement with a dietitian and a supervised gym program.

Today his HbA1c is 44 mmol/mol (baseline 33) and fasting lipids show LDL 3.6 mmol/L and triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L. He is psychiatrically stable and adamantly does not want to change antipsychotic because 'nothing else has worked for me'. eGFR is over 90 mL/min/1.73 m2 and LFTs are normal.

data_table.Trend: Weight +12 kg over 8 months, waist 103 cm, BMI 29.4 kg/m2.
data_table.Bloods: HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (baseline 33), LDL 3.6 mmol/L, TG 2.4 mmol/L, eGFR over 90, LFTs normal.
data_table.History: Failed haloperidol (EPS) and risperidone (akathisia).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step, in addition to continuing lifestyle input?

options.text: Halve the olanzapine dose to 7.5 mg at night to reduce metabolic load
Commence orlistat 120 mg with each main meal as first-line adjunct
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily with meals and titrate as tolerated
Refer for bariatric surgery consideration as the next weight intervention
Add topiramate 25 mg twice daily as an appetite suppressant

subtopic_detail: Interpreting elevated prolactin on amisulpride
stem:
A 37-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been on amisulpride 600 mg daily for two years with good symptom control after failed trials of quetiapine and olanzapine. She has developed amenorrhoea over the past six months. Her fasting serum prolactin today is 2400 mIU/L (reference under 500 in females). Repeat sample confirms 2280 mIU/L. Urine beta hCG is negative, TSH is 1.6 mIU/L and creatinine is 62 micromol/L.

She has no headache, no visual field disturbance and no galactorrhoea. She weighs 68 kg with BMI 24 and waist 82 cm. HbA1c is 34 mmol/mol and fasting lipids are within range. She has no personal or family history of pituitary tumour, has never taken opioids, metoclopramide or a proton pump inhibitor, and asks how you plan to sort out her elevated prolactin.

data_table.Bloods: Prolactin 2400 mIU/L then 2280 mIU/L (under 500 in females), beta hCG negative, TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), creatinine 62 micromol/L.
data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 68 kg, BMI 24 kg/m2, waist 82 cm.
data_table.Other: HbA1c 34 mmol/mol, fasting lipids within range.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent MRI pituitary with contrast to exclude a macroadenoma before any medication change
Add cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly to lower prolactin while continuing amisulpride unchanged
Switch amisulpride to aripiprazole, monitor mental state closely, and repeat prolactin in 6 to 8 weeks
Continue amisulpride unchanged and start a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore withdrawal bleeds
Refer directly to endocrinology and defer any antipsychotic change to the endocrinologist

subtopic_detail: Clozapine 12-week review with new metabolic derangement
stem:
A 33-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine for 12 weeks, currently 350 mg at night, with PANSS reduction from 98 to 66 and a return to part-time work he had lost during his last relapse. He had failed adequate trials of olanzapine and risperidone in the preceding two years. He attends the community clozapine clinic for his scheduled 12-week metabolic review with his case manager.

Baseline values were weight 80 kg, BMI 26.1, waist 94 cm, BP 122/76 mmHg, fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, HbA1c 34 mmol/mol, LDL 2.7 mmol/L, HDL 1.2 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.3 mmol/L. Today he weighs 89 kg (BMI 29.1, +11.3%), waist 104 cm, BP 132/84 mmHg, fasting glucose 6.0 mmol/L, HbA1c 40 mmol/mol, LDL 3.5 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L. He denies chest pain or dyspnoea. Today's ANC is 3.6 x 10^9/L (green zone).

data_table.Baseline (week 0): Weight 80 kg, BMI 26.1, waist 94 cm, FG 5.0, HbA1c 34, LDL 2.7, HDL 1.2, TG 1.3.
data_table.Week 12: Weight 89 kg (+11.3%), BMI 29.1, waist 104 cm, BP 132/84, FG 6.0, HbA1c 40, LDL 3.5, HDL 0.9, TG 2.6.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop clozapine now and cross-titrate to aripiprazole monotherapy over the next four weeks
Continue clozapine, add lifestyle intervention plus metformin, repeat metabolic panel in 4 to 6 weeks
Continue clozapine unchanged and defer the next metabolic review to the 12-month anniversary
Halve the clozapine dose to 175 mg at night to lower his overall metabolic burden
Add low-dose aripiprazole 5 mg daily as prolactin-sparing augmentation to reduce clozapine dose

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD DSM-5 diagnostic criteria
stem:
A 29-year-old software developer presents to her GP requesting assessment for ADHD after her 7-year-old son was recently diagnosed. She describes lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, losing keys and wallets, being easily distracted in meetings, and starting many projects without completing them. She recalls being told at school she was bright but disorganised, though her Year 6 report card describes her as an average student without significant behavioural concerns. Her current symptoms cause her to miss deadlines at work and she has been passed over for promotion twice. She has no history of head injury and no current substance use. Screening for depression and anxiety is negative. Mental state examination reveals restlessness but no thought disorder.

She asks whether she meets criteria for adult ADHD.

data_table.History: Symptoms present since primary school; no clear teacher-reported concerns before age 12
data_table.Occupational impact: Missed deadlines; passed over for promotion twice
data_table.Screening: K10 within normal range; AUDIT-C negative

lead_in: Which feature is most important to establish before confirming the diagnosis?

options.text: That she meets at least six inattention symptoms on an adult self-report scale
That her symptoms respond to a methylphenidate trial over four weeks
That several symptoms causing impairment were present before age 12
That her symptoms are present and impairing in two or more settings
That functional MRI or QEEG shows evidence of executive dysfunction

subtopic_detail: Pre-stimulant cardiac screening
stem:
A 34-year-old man has confirmed adult ADHD combined presentation. You are considering starting lisdexamfetamine. He plays social soccer without symptoms, has never had chest pain, palpitations, or syncope, and does not use recreational stimulants. He takes no regular medications. His father had coronary stenting at age 62. On examination his pulse is 74 bpm regular, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, BMI 26 kg/m2, and cardiovascular examination is unremarkable with normal heart sounds and no murmurs.

He asks what cardiac workup is required before you can prescribe.

data_table.Family history: Father CAD at 62; no premature (<50) cardiac death or inherited arrhythmia
data_table.Vital signs: HR 74, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Normal heart sounds, no murmurs, no signs of Marfan features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pre-treatment cardiac assessment?

options.text: Baseline troponin and NT-proBNP with 24-hour Holter monitoring for arrhythmia surveillance
Baseline 12-lead ECG for all adults before commencing any stimulant medication
Transthoracic echocardiogram and exercise stress test given family history of coronary disease
Referral to cardiology for exclusion of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy before commencement
Baseline heart rate and blood pressure with targeted ECG if cardiac risk is identified

subtopic_detail: ADHD with comorbid substance use disorder
stem:
A 27-year-old man is referred for management of ADHD. He was diagnosed at age 9 and treated with methylphenidate until age 16 with good response. He now reports daily cannabis use for the last three years and weekly binge drinking (10 standard drinks per session). He denies methamphetamine or non-prescribed stimulant use, and a urine drug screen confirms cannabis only. He wants to reduce his cannabis intake but has not yet done so. His inattention and disorganisation are markedly impairing his apprenticeship.

Cardiovascular examination is normal and he has no family history of premature cardiac death.

data_table.Substance use: Cannabis daily; alcohol 10 standard drinks weekly; no stimulant misuse
data_table.Urine drug screen: THC positive; amphetamines negative; opioids negative
data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 126/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temp 36.5

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for ADHD?

options.text: Immediate-release dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily titrated to symptom response
Immediate-release methylphenidate 10 mg three times daily titrated to effect
Atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated toward a target of 80 mg over four weeks
Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for concurrent ADHD and cannabis dependence
Deferral of pharmacotherapy until at least six months of documented cannabis abstinence

subtopic_detail: Stimulant response monitoring and switch
stem:
A 38-year-old woman with ADHD combined presentation has been on osmotic-release methylphenidate 54 mg once daily for eight weeks. She has been titrated up from 18 mg using a weekly protocol. Her inattention and disorganisation are only modestly improved on the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, and her partner also reports minimal change at home. She reports mild dry mouth but no palpitations, no weight loss beyond 1 kg, no sleep disturbance, and no mood change. Her resting pulse is 82 bpm and blood pressure 122/78 mmHg. She takes the medication reliably every morning with breakfast.

She asks what should happen next.

data_table.Current medication: Methylphenidate osmotic-release 54 mg mane, taken with food, adherent
data_table.Response: Modest improvement only on ASRS and partner-report after 8 weeks at target dose
data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 122/78 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add clonidine 100 mcg at night to augment the methylphenidate response
Continue methylphenidate 54 mg and add cognitive behavioural therapy for ADHD in adults
Switch to lisdexamfetamine 30 mg once daily and titrate to response
Increase methylphenidate to 72 mg daily and reassess after four further weeks
Cease stimulant medication and start atomoxetine as a non-stimulant alternative

subtopic_detail: Bush-Francis recognition and lorazepam challenge
stem:
A 26-year-old woman with a known history of bipolar I disorder is brought to the emergency department by her family. Over three days she has become progressively withdrawn, is not eating or drinking, and now barely speaks. On examination she is alert with eyes open but does not answer questions, resists passive movement of her limbs, holds an arm in whatever position it is placed, and stares vacantly. There is no fever, no tremor, and no muscle rigidity beyond the postural holding. She takes no antipsychotic medications and has not commenced any new medications recently. Bloods including creatine kinase, thyroid function, sodium, and calcium are within normal limits.

A CT brain is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Mute; negativism; waxy flexibility; posturing on formal testing
data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temp 36.8
data_table.Investigations: CK within normal limits; TSH within normal limits; sodium within normal limits; calcium within normal limits; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous fluid resuscitation and observe overnight before further intervention
Commence olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly for the withdrawn presentation
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy within the next 24 hours
Administer lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly and reassess response after 10 minutes
Administer dantrolene 1 mg/kg intravenously for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome

subtopic_detail: NMS versus malignant catatonia discrimination
stem:
A 41-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia was recently switched from olanzapine to haloperidol depot four weeks ago. He now presents to the emergency department after 48 hours of confusion, muteness, and diaphoresis. His examination shows generalised lead-pipe rigidity, temperature 39.2, pulse 132 bpm, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, and reduced conscious state. He is not moving spontaneously, does not follow commands, and there is no posturing or waxy flexibility. Creatine kinase is 6800 U/L, white cell count 14.2, and urine dipstick shows myoglobin. Prior to the depot switch he was fully independent and euthymic.

Ambulance staff report no seizure activity was witnessed.

data_table.Recent medications: Switched from olanzapine to haloperidol depot 4 weeks ago
data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 168/104 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96%, temp 39.2
data_table.Examination: Lead-pipe rigidity; mute; reduced conscious state; no waxy flexibility; no posturing
data_table.Investigations: CK 6800 U/L (<200); WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (4-11); myoglobinuria on dipstick

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial intervention after cessation of the offending agent?

options.text: Intramuscular lorazepam 2 mg with rapid reassessment for a diagnostic response
Intravenous fluid resuscitation and active cooling with consideration of dantrolene
Urgent electroconvulsive therapy within the next 12 hours as definitive treatment
Restart olanzapine at 5 mg orally to reverse the withdrawal-related presentation
Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g with lumbar puncture to exclude bacterial meningitis

subtopic_detail: Medical workup for new-onset catatonia
stem:
A 62-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is admitted after her family found her staring, mute, and refusing to eat for two days. On examination she resists movement, holds imposed limb positions, and does not respond verbally. She has become incontinent of urine. Her temperature is 37.4, pulse 96 bpm, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg. On admission bloods, her sodium is 133 mmol/L, calcium 2.32 mmol/L, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, creatine kinase 180 U/L, C-reactive protein 12 mg/L, and urinalysis is negative. A CT brain is reported as normal. She has been on stable citalopram 20 mg for two years and takes no other medications.

Her family reports she had a mild viral upper respiratory illness three weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 138/84 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 97%, temp 37.4
data_table.Examination: Mute; negativism; waxy flexibility; new urinary incontinence
data_table.Investigations: Na 133 mmol/L (135-145); Ca 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.55); TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); CK 180 U/L (<200); CRP 12 mg/L (<5); urinalysis negative; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat MSU with culture and start empirical trimethoprim for occult urinary tract infection
MRI brain and lumbar puncture including NMDA receptor antibodies and viral PCR
Serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper for Wilson disease exclusion
EEG for non-convulsive status epilepticus without cross-sectional imaging first
Serotonin syndrome workup and immediate withdrawal of citalopram 20 mg daily

subtopic_detail: ECT for benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia
stem:
A 34-year-old man with major depressive disorder has been in hospital for six days with catatonia (Bush-Francis score 18). He received an initial diagnostic dose of lorazepam 2 mg IM with partial response and has been on scheduled lorazepam 4 mg orally every 6 hours for four days. He remains mute, minimally oral, and has now lost 3 kg. He has no active medical illness on repeat examination, his metabolic and infective workup is unremarkable, and he consents through his substitute decision-maker under the state Mental Health Act after formal capacity assessment.

The treating team is planning next-line treatment.

data_table.Current treatment: Lorazepam 4 mg orally 6-hourly for 4 days after initial 2 mg IM challenge
data_table.Response: Partial only; Bush-Francis remains 18; ongoing mutism and poor intake
data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temp 36.9
data_table.Consent: Substitute decision-maker consent per state Mental Health Act after capacity assessment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer to intensive care unit for propofol sedation and mechanical ventilation cover
Increase lorazepam to a total daily dose of 24 mg and reassess after 48 hours
Add olanzapine 10 mg daily for the underlying depressive episode with psychotic features
Add memantine 5 mg daily for glutamatergic augmentation of the catatonia response
Proceed to bilateral electroconvulsive therapy as the recommended next-line treatment

subtopic_detail: HEEADSSS assessment - sensitive-topic phrasing with parent present
stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a suburban general practice with her mother for a follow-up after 3 months of headaches, poor sleep and declining school marks. Her mother has done most of the talking so far and has stayed in the room. Basic history, examination and neurological assessment are unremarkable, and you have decided to complete a HEEADSSS psychosocial assessment before the visit ends.

When you gently signal a shift toward more personal questions, the mother says she would prefer to stay because "we do not have secrets". The girl looks at her feet and says nothing. There is no acute safety concern in the room and the appointment has time available.

data_table.Presentation: 3 months of headaches, poor sleep, declining marks
data_table.Examination: General and neurological examination within normal limits
data_table.Consultation dynamic: Mother has led the history; adolescent quiet and avoiding eye contact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to begin the HEEADSSS interview?

options.text: Explain that adolescent care works best when the young person is seen alone for part of the visit, invite the mother to the waiting room for the next ten minutes, and describe the limits of confidentiality before starting HEEADSSS

Proceed with HEEADSSS in the mother's presence but soften the wording of every sensitive item so the adolescent is not embarrassed and can nod or shake her head instead of answering aloud in full sentences

Defer HEEADSSS to a follow-up appointment booked without the mother in one week, and use today only for the physical complaint of headaches so the young person does not feel put on the spot in front of her parent

Ask the mother directly what she believes is happening at home and at school first, using her account as the framework for HEEADSSS, then ask the adolescent to confirm or clarify each domain in her mother's presence

Hand the adolescent a printed HEEADSSS questionnaire to complete silently in the room while you continue to speak with her mother about school performance and family stressors over the same ten-minute period

subtopic_detail: CRAFFT screen interpretation and motivational interviewing entry point
stem:
A 16-year-old boy is reviewed alone in a regional headspace centre after his GP referred him for "partying too much". You have already explained the confidentiality limits and he has consented to a CRAFFT-based substance-use screen.

He reports drinking alcohol at parties on most weekends, occasional cannabis with friends, no other substances, no injecting drug use, and no acute intoxication today. He scores 3 on the CRAFFT (yes to Car, Forget, Friends; no to Relax, Alone, Trouble). Vital signs are within normal limits and his mental state is euthymic with no suicidal ideation. He tells you he does not think his use is a problem but is happy to keep talking.

data_table.Setting: 16-year-old male, alone, headspace consultation with confidentiality discussed
data_table.Substance history: Weekend alcohol, occasional cannabis, no other substances, no injecting
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, no intoxication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly to a residential adolescent alcohol and other drug rehabilitation unit for a structured 4-week withdrawal and relapse-prevention program including supervised abstinence and weekly urine drug screens

Commission a urine drug screen and full biochemistry today as the primary intervention, deferring any counselling or brief intervention until the objective substance results and liver function tests are back at the follow-up visit

Reassure him that weekend alcohol and occasional cannabis are normative for his age, take no further substance-related action today, and review only if he re-presents with a specific new alcohol or other drug related concern

Notify his parents of the CRAFFT results at the end of the visit without his consent because his substance use meets a threshold that overrides adolescent confidentiality under mandatory-reporting duties in this jurisdiction

Provide brief motivational interviewing today - explore importance and confidence to change, offer information on cannabis and alcohol harms, and agree a follow-up appointment within 2-4 weeks with brief-intervention documentation

subtopic_detail: School refusal - anxiety-driven vs conduct-driven differentiation
stem:
A 13-year-old girl is brought by her father to the GP because she has attended school on only 4 of the last 20 school days. On the mornings she stays home she complains of stomach aches and headaches, is tearful, and asks to be with her mother. She spends the day at home doing schoolwork online, does not seek out peers or games, and returns to bed. Weekends and school holidays are unremarkable.

She describes worry that "something bad will happen" to her mother if she is at school, denies being bullied, and denies substance use. There is no history of conduct problems, running away, or lying. Physical examination and basic bloods are within normal limits. Her father is exhausted and wants "a note keeping her home until she is ready".

data_table.Attendance: 4/20 school days over the last month
data_table.Somatic complaints: Morning stomach aches and headaches; resolve by afternoon
data_table.Behaviour at home: Stays in bed or does schoolwork; not with peers; no antisocial acts
data_table.Examination: Within normal limits; basic bloods within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Provide a medical certificate for extended home-based learning until the adolescent independently reports she feels ready to return, with GP review in 8 weeks and no active return-to-school plan in the interim

Refer to child protection services on grounds of educational neglect because school attendance has fallen below the state-mandated compulsory-attendance threshold and the father is not enforcing daily attendance at the school gate

Formulate this as anxiety-driven school refusal and coordinate a graded return-to-school plan with parents and school welfare, refer for CBT-based psychology, and treat somatic complaints without further investigation

Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily today as first-line intervention for presumed separation anxiety disorder, arrange fortnightly GP review for dose escalation to 50 mg, and defer psychological therapy until medication is titrated

Undertake extensive gastrointestinal investigation including coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin, abdominal ultrasound and outpatient paediatric gastroenterology referral for recurrent abdominal pain before addressing school attendance

subtopic_detail: Cyberbullying with self-harm ideation - safety planning priority
stem:
A 14-year-old girl is seen alone in a headspace outreach clinic after her school counsellor referred her. Over 6 weeks a group of former friends have posted altered images of her on a public social-media account and sent group-chat messages calling her worthless. She has become withdrawn, sleeps 4-5 hours, and marks have fallen.

Today she discloses that on two occasions in the past week she has thought "it would be easier not to be here" while lying in bed at night, but has no plan, has not accessed means, and finds the thoughts frightening. She has never self-harmed. She has a supportive mother who is aware of some but not all of the online content and lives in the family home. Vital signs are within normal limits and she has consented to your involvement of her mother.

data_table.Cyberbullying: 6 weeks; altered images publicly posted; group-chat harassment
data_table.Suicidality: Passive ideation twice in past week; no plan, no means, no prior self-harm; ideation is ego-dystonic
data_table.Family: Supportive mother, lives at home; adolescent consents to mother involvement
data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Complete a collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping strategies and adult supports, engage her mother today, report the material to the eSafety Commissioner and the platform, and arrange psychology review within 1 week

Arrange same-day involuntary transfer to a paediatric emergency department under the Mental Health Act for assessment and consideration of admission to an adolescent psychiatric inpatient unit for suicide risk observation

Commence fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily today as first-line pharmacotherapy for presumed adolescent major depression, arrange GP review in 2 weeks for dose review, and defer psychological therapy until the SSRI has had time to work

Reassure her that ignoring the messages, blocking the accounts and giving the situation time is the most effective strategy, without any external reporting or safety plan today, and review at the next scheduled headspace visit

Advise the mother to contact the parents of the alleged perpetrators directly to seek an apology and voluntary removal of the material, and defer any professional or regulatory reporting until that private approach has been attempted

subtopic_detail: Conduct disorder vs oppositional defiant disorder - pathway to antisocial personality disorder
stem:
A 14-year-old boy is brought by his mother to the GP after being suspended from school for the third time this year. Over 18 months he has repeatedly bullied a smaller classmate, damaged a neighbour's fence, been caught shoplifting from a supermarket twice, and been aggressive to a family dog. He has been out overnight without telling his mother on two occasions in the past 3 months and has been truant from school on more than 20 days.

He shows no remorse when asked directly. He denies substance use and hallucinations, and mental state is otherwise unremarkable with normal affect and no psychotic features. There is no head injury history. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Behaviours (18 months): Bullying, property destruction, shoplifting x2, cruelty to animals, truancy >20 days, running away x2
data_table.Mental state: No remorse, no psychosis, no depressive features, no substance use
data_table.Medical: No head injury; vital signs within normal limits

lead_in: Which of the following best characterises this presentation and its long-term risk?

options.text: Oppositional defiant disorder with a low probability of progression, best managed with parent management training and school-based behavioural supports and unlikely to require any specialist mental-health follow-up beyond adolescence

Early-onset schizophreniform disorder with negative symptoms, requiring urgent referral to the early intervention psychosis service for ultra-high-risk assessment and consideration of low-dose atypical antipsychotic pharmacotherapy

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder combined presentation with untreated comorbid learning disorder, best managed by trial of methylphenidate immediate release and educational assessment for a formal learning-support plan at school

Adolescent-onset conduct disorder with limited pro-social emotions specifier, associated with substantially increased risk of adult antisocial personality disorder, warranting parent management training and multi-systemic therapy referral

Antisocial personality disorder with paediatric-onset criteria met early, warranting immediate diagnostic disclosure, personality-focused psychotherapy referral, and documentation of the personality-disorder diagnosis in the medical record

subtopic_detail: ARFID vs picky eating - thresholds for concern
stem:
A 13-year-old boy is brought to a paediatric outpatient clinic because he eats only 6 foods (white bread, plain pasta, chicken nuggets, apples, cheese, and milk) and refuses all others due to texture and smell. This pattern has been present since age 4 and has narrowed further in the past year.

He is on the 3rd centile for weight, has fallen from the 25th to the 3rd centile over 2 years, is fatigued, and has iron deficiency (ferritin 6 micrograms/L, reference 20-300) with mild microcytic anaemia. There is no fear of weight gain, no body-image distress, no purging, no exercise-driving, and he wants to eat more variety but cannot tolerate it. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Diet: 6-food repertoire since age 4, narrowing further; texture/smell-driven
data_table.Growth: Weight 3rd centile; fallen from 25th centile over 2 years
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 6 micrograms/L (20-300), microcytic anaemia; UEC/LFT within normal limits
data_table.Psychopathology: No fear of weight gain, no body-image distress, no purging, no compulsive exercise
data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits

lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Atypical anorexia nervosa presenting with fear of texture rather than weight, with a similar treatment pathway and prognosis and requiring family-based therapy directed at weight restoration and reintroduction of feared foods

Longstanding picky eating within normal developmental variation, with no specific mental-health intervention needed beyond parental reassurance, gradual exposure at family meals, and routine child-health surveillance at annual checks

Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder driven by sensory sensitivity, meeting DSM-5 criteria via faltering growth and nutritional deficiency, requiring a multidisciplinary eating disorder pathway including dietitian and psychology

Autism spectrum disorder with associated food selectivity, best managed by autism-specific behavioural intervention alone without formal eating-disorder pathway involvement, and referral to a developmental paediatrician as the primary service

Coeliac disease with secondary food avoidance from post-prandial symptoms, requiring urgent coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy before any psychological or dietetic diagnosis is considered, and gluten-free trial deferred until confirmed

subtopic_detail: Adolescent major depression - first-line SSRI and monitoring
stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a Melbourne GP with her mother, referred by the school counsellor for 4 months of low mood, anhedonia, initial insomnia, poor concentration, and marked functional decline. She meets DSM-5 criteria for a moderate-to-severe major depressive episode. She has had 10 sessions of individual CBT over 3 months at headspace with a certified therapist without meaningful benefit and the therapist has recommended stepping up.

She denies psychotic symptoms, denies past mania or hypomania, and denies substance use. She has current passive suicidal ideation with no plan or means; she has agreed to a safety plan and her mother has consented to involvement and means restriction. Weight, growth, LFTs, TSH and glucose are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder.

data_table.Prior treatment: 10 sessions CBT at headspace with recommendation to step up
data_table.Suicidality: Passive ideation, no plan/means, safety plan documented, means restricted
data_table.Bipolar screen: Negative personal and family history; no psychosis
data_table.Investigations: Weight/growth, TSH, LFTs, glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily as first-line SSRI for adolescent depression, continue CBT concurrently, and review at 1 week for tolerability and emergent suicidality per the black-box early-treatment warning

Commence mirtazapine 15 mg orally at night as first-line antidepressant to address depressive insomnia and poor appetite, continue CBT concurrently, and review at 2 weeks for weight, sedation and mood response

Commence venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg orally daily as first-line antidepressant, arrange fortnightly review for tolerability, and continue CBT concurrently while dose is escalated to a target of 75 to 150 mg daily

Commence fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily as first-line, continue CBT concurrently, and review at 1 week then 2-weekly for the first 4 weeks for tolerability and emergent suicidality per the black-box early-treatment warning

Continue CBT alone for a further 8 weeks at higher intensity without any pharmacological step-up because SSRIs in adolescents carry unacceptable early-treatment suicidality risk that outweighs the potential efficacy benefit at any dose

subtopic_detail: NSSI vs suicide attempt - function and DBT-A indication
stem:
A 16-year-old girl is seen in a community mental-health clinic after her mother found superficial linear cuts on her forearms. Over the past 8 months she has cut herself with a pencil sharpener blade 2-3 times per week, always superficially, only when overwhelmed by strong emotions (anger, shame after arguments with her mother), and the cutting reliably reduces the intensity of the feeling within minutes.

She does not want to die and has never intended to die when cutting. She has no plan or intent for suicide today and denies past suicide attempts. She has emotion-regulation difficulties, an unstable sense of self, and chronic emptiness. There is a strong family history of anxiety. Vital signs are within normal limits and cuts are superficial with no deep-tissue involvement.

data_table.Self-harm pattern: 8 months, 2-3 x/week, superficial cuts to forearms, emotion-regulation function
data_table.Suicidal intent: Absent, both historically and today; no past attempts
data_table.Personality features: Emotion dysregulation, unstable self, chronic emptiness
data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management pathway?

options.text: Categorise this as suicidal behaviour and arrange same-day admission to an adolescent inpatient unit under the Mental Health Act with 24-hour observation, means restriction, and structured risk assessment on discharge planning

Reassure her that self-harm without suicidal intent carries no long-term risk and does not require psychological therapy beyond routine GP mental-health care, and provide sterile dressings and general wound-care advice today

Formulate as non-suicidal self-injury with emerging borderline traits, refer for adolescent-modified dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT-A), and support the family with skills coaching alongside a documented individual safety plan

Commence quetiapine 25 mg orally at night as first-line pharmacological treatment for emotion dysregulation and superficial self-harm, with review in 4 weeks for sedation, weight change and reduction in cutting frequency

Refer for standard supportive counselling only, avoid any specific structured therapy, and defer a personality-focused formulation until age 18 in case a formal borderline personality disorder diagnosis becomes clinically appropriate

subtopic_detail: Gillick / Mature Minor mental-health consent + confidentiality limits
stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a Sydney general practice alone. She has 3 months of low mood, initial insomnia and anhedonia meeting criteria for a moderate major depressive episode, has completed 8 sessions of CBT at headspace without benefit, and after informed discussion wants to start fluoxetine.

She demonstrates understanding of the diagnosis, the black-box early-treatment suicidality warning, the need for weekly monitoring, potential sexual side effects and discontinuation issues, and she can explain her reasoning coherently. She lives with both parents. Her mother knows she has been at headspace but has not been told about today's visit; the young person is worried her father would react badly and asks that neither parent be informed today. There is passive suicidal ideation without plan or means and she has agreed to a safety plan. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Diagnosis and prior care: Moderate MDD; 8 sessions CBT without benefit
data_table.Capacity assessment: Understands diagnosis, risks/benefits, monitoring, alternatives; coherent reasoning
data_table.Family: Lives with both parents; mother partially informed; adolescent requests no disclosure today
data_table.Safety: Passive ideation, no plan/means, safety plan agreed
data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding consent and confidentiality?

options.text: Decline to prescribe today on the basis that a mental-health medication in an adolescent requires written parental consent in New South Wales, regardless of the young person's demonstrated capacity to consent to her own treatment
Prescribe today on her demonstrated mature-minor capacity, document the capacity assessment and confidentiality limits, and encourage but do not compel parental disclosure with review at next visit

Telephone the mother today without the adolescent's consent because SSRI initiation in a minor overrides the confidentiality expectation and requires parental awareness of the black-box early-treatment suicidality warning at all times

Refer directly to the child and adolescent mental health service (CAMHS) and refuse to prescribe fluoxetine in general practice for anyone under 16 in New South Wales because of local-jurisdictional prescribing restrictions on adolescent SSRI use

Provide a limited script for one week only and use the constraint to compel the adolescent to bring a parent to the next visit for continuation, framing it as a safety-monitoring requirement rather than as a confidentiality override

subtopic_detail: Anorexia MARSIPAN-AU admission criteria and refeeding risk
stem:
A 15-year-old girl is reviewed in an emergency department after her GP referred her with restrictive eating and rapid weight loss over 4 months. She weighs 38 kg (height 165 cm, BMI 14.0), has lost 18 percent of her body weight, and has been drinking water only for the last 48 hours.

Seated pulse rate is 38/min, supine BP 88/54 with a postural drop to 68/40, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 percent, temperature 35.4 degrees Celsius. Investigations: potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), magnesium 0.65 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), glucose 3.1 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 490 ms. She denies suicidal ideation, has a supportive family, and wants to get better.

data_table.Anthropometry: 38 kg, 165 cm, BMI 14.0; 18% weight loss over 4 months
data_table.Vital signs: PR 38, supine BP 88/54, postural drop to 68/40, RR 16, SpO2 98%, T 35.4°C
data_table.Biochemistry: K 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.5); Mg 0.65 mmol/L (0.7-1.0); glucose 3.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home with same-day dietitian and family-based treatment referral, arrange GP review in 48 hours for repeat electrolytes, and agree an outpatient meal plan targeting slow weight gain and progressive oral refeeding

Admit to a paediatric medical ward for cardiac monitoring, cautious refeeding under MARSIPAN-AU with electrolyte replacement and thiamine before caloric load, and involve the specialist eating-disorder service from day 1

Transfer to an adolescent psychiatric unit for weight restoration and family-based treatment initiation because her medical status is stable enough for a purely psychiatric admission and behavioural containment is the priority

Commence high-caloric nasogastric refeeding at 2000 kcal/day from day 1 in the emergency department to correct starvation rapidly and reduce the length of the medical admission and total inpatient stay for the family

Give a 20 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid bolus for postural hypotension and reassess disposition in 4 hours based on repeat vital signs before deciding whether medical admission or outpatient management is more appropriate

subtopic_detail: Bulimia nervosa - FBT-BN vs CBT-E choice in an adolescent
stem:
A 16-year-old girl attends an eating-disorder outpatient clinic after a headspace referral. Over 6 months she has had 3-4 objective binge episodes per week followed by self-induced vomiting, with intense guilt and shape/weight over-evaluation. Her weight is on the 50th centile.

Biochemistry, ECG and dental review are within normal limits and she is medically stable. She lives at home with two engaged parents who want to be involved in her treatment, has no comorbid substance use, no active suicidal ideation, and no history of childhood trauma that would preclude family-based work. She has never had structured eating-disorder therapy. She has consented to family involvement in whatever plan is chosen and is motivated to change.

data_table.Diagnosis: Bulimia nervosa; 3-4 binge/purge episodes weekly for 6 months
data_table.Weight and medical: 50th centile; biochemistry, ECG, dental review within normal limits
data_table.Family: Two engaged parents, consenting to involvement, no trauma contraindication
data_table.Comorbidity: No substance use; no active suicidality; no prior structured ED therapy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line psychological therapy?

options.text: Family-based treatment for bulimia (FBT-BN) as first-line, with the family taking initial control of eating and interruption of binge and purge cycles, transitioning to adolescent autonomy in phases 2 and 3

Enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-E) as first-line individual therapy, with the family involved only for meal-time monitoring at home and no formal family therapy sessions across the 20-week treatment protocol

Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) as a stand-alone first-line intervention targeting interpersonal difficulties driving binge-purge cycles, with 16-20 weekly sessions and no direct behavioural work on eating patterns or purging

Fluoxetine 60 mg orally daily as first-line monotherapy without psychological therapy, using the recognised anti-bulimic dose to reduce binge and purge frequency across a 12 week trial before any therapy is considered

Admission to an adolescent inpatient eating-disorder unit for behavioural interruption of the binge-purge cycle under supervised meals, with structured meal exposure and post-meal supervision as the primary treatment modality

subtopic_detail: ADHD - stimulant class choice and formulation for driving
stem:
A 17-year-old boy has been diagnosed with ADHD (combined presentation) after multi-source assessment by a paediatrician, with symptoms since primary school and functional impairment across school and home. Baseline cardiac history and family history for sudden cardiac death are negative, resting ECG is normal, and he has no history of psychosis, substance use disorder, or tics.

He recently obtained his learner driver permit and drives with a supervising parent daily. He needs sustained afternoon concentration for his final school year and part-time evening work, and his previous trial of a short-acting stimulant (2 weeks of dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily) produced afternoon rebound irritability and inconsistent evening symptom control despite good tolerability during school hours. His parents are engaged in shared decision-making.

data_table.Diagnosis: ADHD combined presentation; multi-source assessment; longstanding impairment
data_table.Cardiac screen: Negative personal + family history; resting ECG within normal limits
data_table.Prior trial: Dexamfetamine 5 mg BD x 2 weeks; afternoon rebound; poor evening cover
data_table.Comorbidity: No psychosis, no SUD, no tics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological choice?

options.text: Switch to atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily as a non-stimulant first-line agent to avoid any driving impairment risk from stimulants, titrating over 4-6 weeks to a target of 1.2 mg/kg per day for symptom control
Continue immediate-release dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily and add a third afternoon dose of 5 mg at 3 pm to extend cover through evening driving and part-time work, with review of rebound at 4 weeks
Switch to methylphenidate osmotic-release 18 mg orally in the morning, titrated fortnightly against symptom control and tolerability, giving 10-12 hours of cover for school, driving and evening work

Withhold pharmacotherapy for the remainder of the driving-permit year and rely on behavioural strategies, executive-function coaching and school accommodations alone until he holds a full unrestricted driver licence

Refer for cardiology review with echocardiogram and Holter monitor as a mandatory pre-requisite before any modified-release stimulant is started in an adolescent with a learner permit and evening work commitments

subtopic_detail: Late-diagnosis autism spectrum disorder in adolescent girls - masking + comorbid anxiety
stem:
A 15-year-old girl is referred by her GP with 12 months of escalating anxiety, exhaustion after school, selective mutism at school but normal speech at home, and self-reported burn-out after masking her difficulties socially. Her mother describes lifelong subtle social differences (scripted phrases, intense interests in horses and Japanese language, sensory sensitivities to clothing tags and fluorescent light).

She has one long-term female best friend, presents as socially motivated but exhausted, and school reports have historically described her as "quiet but doing well". Two previous CBT courses at headspace addressed anxiety symptoms without lasting benefit. There is no intellectual disability, no history of trauma, and no psychotic features. Vital signs and physical examination are within normal limits.

data_table.Presenting features: 12 months escalating anxiety, post-school exhaustion, selective mutism at school only
data_table.Lifelong features: Scripted phrases, intense narrow interests, sensory sensitivities (tags, fluorescent light)
data_table.Social: One long-term best friend; socially motivated but exhausted from masking
data_table.Prior treatment: Two CBT courses at headspace without lasting benefit
data_table.Investigations: No ID, no trauma history, no psychosis; examination within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in assessment and formulation?

options.text: Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder with school-refusal features and start sertraline 25 mg orally daily as first-line with weekly review for 4 weeks and a further CBT course focused on social exposure at school

Formulate as burnout secondary to academic overload and recommend a reduced school-attendance plan, weekly wellness check-ins with the school nurse, and no further mental-health assessment or diagnostic investigation at this stage

Diagnose selective mutism as a discrete anxiety disorder and refer for speech pathology and behavioural exposure therapy focused on gradual verbal responses in the school setting with weekly progress monitoring

Diagnose social anxiety disorder with avoidant features and refer for group-based social skills training with peers, providing psychoeducation to parents about social exposure and homework practice between sessions

Refer for a multidisciplinary autism assessment using the Autism CRC national guideline, incorporating a female-presentation-sensitive tool (ADOS-2 module 4 or MIGDAS-2), and formulate anxiety as an ASD comorbidity

subtopic_detail: Adolescent suicide - demographic patterns and means-restriction priority
stem:
A 17-year-old boy is brought by his mother to a rural Queensland ED after she found a written suicide note in his room. He has 6 months of low mood after his father's death and 6 weeks of active suicidal ideation with a specific plan to shoot himself with his late father's licensed rifle, currently stored at home in a locked safe. He has recently purchased ammunition online.

He scores 22 on the PHQ-A. Access to alcohol has increased at family gatherings since the bereavement. He denies psychosis and has no prior suicide attempts. He has agreed to admission today. On formal assessment there is active intent, a specific plan with available means, no protective factors mitigating the plan, and a recent behavioural rehearsal step. His mother is present, distressed, but supportive and willing to act on any plan you make.

data_table.Bereavement: Father died 6 months ago; escalating family alcohol use
data_table.Suicidality: 6 weeks active ideation, specific plan (firearm), means available (rifle in home safe), recent ammunition purchase
data_table.Risk factors: Male, rural, firearm access, bereavement, alcohol
data_table.Consent: Agreed to admission; mother present and willing to act

lead_in: In addition to psychiatric admission for stabilisation, what is the single highest-priority intervention today?

options.text: Arrange immediate removal of the firearm and ammunition from the home today with the mother's consent, coordinated with Queensland Police weapons licensing to secure the rifle off-site before any discharge is considered

Commence fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily today with 1 week review for tolerability and emergent suicidality per the black-box warning, alongside psychology follow-up within 72 hours of discharge from the admission

Complete a structured suicide-risk assessment tool such as the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale to categorise him as high risk and use the numerical score to determine level of observation and length of admission stay

Have him sign a written no-suicide contract with explicit undertakings not to act on suicidal thoughts for 30 days as a discharge criterion, with copies retained in his medical record and provided to his mother

Restrict his access to social media and internet platforms for the first two weeks post-discharge to reduce exposure to potentially triggering content, coordinated by his mother with parental-control filters on all his devices

subtopic_detail: Early psychosis - ultra-high-risk criteria and EPPIC referral
stem:
A 16-year-old girl is reviewed at headspace with 8 weeks of a new belief that her classmates are subtly whispering about her when she walks past; she recognises the belief may not be true and finds it distressing. She has withdrawn socially, marks have dropped, and she now scores in the borderline range on the SOFAS with a 30-point drop from her prior baseline over 12 months.

Her mother has a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder. She has no positive family history of any other psychiatric condition, no substance use on collateral, and no head injury. There are no frank hallucinations, no clear delusions held with full conviction, and no formal thought disorder. Vital signs and neurological examination are within normal limits. Basic metabolic and thyroid screens are within normal limits.

data_table.Attenuated psychotic symptoms: 8 weeks of paranoid ideation with retained insight; distressing; subthreshold conviction
data_table.Function: SOFAS in borderline range; 30-point drop over 12 months
data_table.Substance and neurological: No substance use on collateral; no head injury; neurological examination within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Metabolic and thyroid screen within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence risperidone 1 mg orally daily today as first-line pharmacological intervention on the basis of a first-degree family history plus attenuated psychotic symptoms with functional decline in the ultra-high-risk pattern

Refer to the early intervention psychosis service (or equivalent local EIS) for structured ultra-high-risk assessment and CAARMS interview, and offer evidence-based CBT for UHR states while monitoring for frank transition

Diagnose brief psychotic disorder based on 8 weeks of persecutory beliefs with functional decline in an adolescent, and arrange same-day acute inpatient adolescent mental-health admission for observation and diagnostic clarification

Formulate this as social anxiety disorder with paranoid features driven by peer-comparison stress, and refer for group-based social-skills training combined with GP-delivered supportive counselling and school liaison over 6 weeks

Discharge from headspace to primary-care GP follow-up in 3 months given retained insight and absence of frank psychosis, with GP-led escalation only if new hallucinations or delusions with full conviction subsequently develop

subtopic_detail: Adolescent bipolar recognition and mood-stabiliser selection
stem:
A 17-year-old girl is reviewed 4 weeks after being started on fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily for what her GP diagnosed as major depressive disorder. Since starting she has slept 3 hours per night, become elated with pressured speech, spent her entire term-time savings on online purchases in one afternoon, and had unprotected sex with two new partners in the past week.

Collateral from her mother identifies a maternal aunt with lithium-treated bipolar I disorder. Reviewing history reveals a self-limited 4-day episode of decreased sleep, increased energy and impulsive spending at age 15 that resolved spontaneously and was not disclosed at the original assessment. Vital signs are within normal limits. Urine drug screen is negative and TSH, LFTs and calcium are within normal limits.

data_table.Presenting episode: 4 weeks post-fluoxetine start: sleep 3 h, elated, pressured speech, hypersexuality, impulsive spending
data_table.Prior episode (age 15): 4 days decreased sleep + increased energy + impulsivity, self-limited, not previously disclosed
data_table.Family history: Maternal aunt with lithium-treated bipolar I
data_table.Substances and metabolic: UDS negative; TSH, LFTs, corrected Ca within normal limits
data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Continue fluoxetine at the current dose, add quetiapine 25 mg orally at night as an adjunct for agitation and impaired sleep, and review the working diagnosis of major depression with mixed features at 2 weeks

Cease fluoxetine and commence lamotrigine 25 mg orally daily as first-line mood stabiliser to cover bipolar depression prophylaxis, titrating slowly over 6 weeks to reduce risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome

Cease fluoxetine and commence sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily as first-line mood stabiliser for acute mania, provide contraception counselling, and arrange fortnightly LFT and drug-level review

Cease fluoxetine, admit for stabilisation, and start lithium as first-line mood stabiliser for acute mania given the family lithium-response predictor, targeting a serum level 0.8-1.0 mmol/L after baseline workup

Cease fluoxetine and initiate olanzapine 10 mg orally daily as first-line acute-mania monotherapy, arrange baseline weight and metabolic screen, and review at 2 weeks with a plan to add lithium if response is inadequate

subtopic_detail: Panic attack presenting to ED - workup and immediate management
stem:
A 28-year-old woman self-presents to a metropolitan emergency department at 2200 hours with a 40-minute history of chest tightness, palpitations, breathlessness and a sense that she is about to die. This is her fourth similar attack in six weeks. Each attack has begun suddenly, peaked within about 10 minutes and settled within an hour. Between attacks she has become preoccupied with when the next one will occur and now avoids the local shopping centre where the second attack happened.

She has no personal history of asthma, cardiac disease or thyroid disease, takes only the combined oral contraceptive pill, drinks 2 standard drinks per week and does not use illicit substances. Her mother died suddenly at 61 of a myocardial infarction last year. On arrival she is anxious and tearful; on your review 30 minutes later she is settled and her symptoms have almost fully resolved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 128/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7.
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, heart sounds dual with no added sounds, calves soft, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG sinus rhythm rate 90 with no ischaemic changes, high-sensitivity troponin at 0 hours below the assay limit, venous blood gas with normal pH and lactate, TSH within reference from her GP two weeks ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her ED management?

options.text: Explain that her symptoms are consistent with a panic attack, discharge with written information and refer for a Mental Health Treatment Plan and CBT within one to two weeks
Repeat high-sensitivity troponin at 3 hours and arrange inpatient stress echocardiogram before any consideration of discharge from ED
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for two weeks as a scheduled course and arrange routine GP follow-up review within a fortnight
Commence propranolol 40 mg orally twice daily and arrange a 24-hour Holter monitor as an outpatient before any mental health referral is made
Admit for overnight cardiology observation and outpatient exercise stress test in the coming week before any mental health follow-up

subtopic_detail: Generalised social anxiety pharmacotherapy - SSRI vs propranolol
stem:
A 24-year-old graduate lawyer attends her GP after her firm rotated her onto a client-facing team. She reports that since university she has avoided any situation involving being observed by others: eating in the tearoom, speaking up in meetings, using public toilets and making phone calls. She feels intense fear of humiliation and has always managed by declining or delegating. Since the rotation four weeks ago she has had daily anticipatory nausea and has taken 12 sick days, and her partner has noticed she now avoids their local supermarket.

She drinks no alcohol, uses no substances, and has no cardiac or respiratory history. Her mother has treated social anxiety. She has never trialled psychological therapy or medication. She asks about propranolol because a friend takes it before job interviews and finds it works well.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Anxious, reduced eye contact, no depressive or psychotic features, insight preserved.
data_table.Investigations: TSH within reference from screening three months ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological recommendation?

options.text: Propranolol 20 mg orally 30 minutes before any anticipated stressful social situation, taken as needed up to three times daily
Diazepam 2 mg orally daily as a short-term measure until formal psychological therapy is available in three months
Moclobemide 300 mg orally twice daily as the recommended first-line pharmacotherapy for social anxiety disorder in Australia
Escitalopram 10 mg orally daily alongside referral for CBT with graded in-vivo exposure to feared social situations
Mirtazapine 15 mg orally at night with GP review at four weeks and no formal psychology referral in the interim

subtopic_detail: OCD - clomipramine trial after failed SSRI trials
stem:
A 36-year-old man with an 11-year history of contamination-themed OCD returns to your community mental health clinic. He has completed 20 sessions of exposure and response prevention with a psychologist over 18 months with partial response. His symptoms remain moderate with a Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) score of 22 despite two adequate SSRI trials: fluoxetine at 80 mg orally daily for 14 weeks and sertraline at 200 mg orally daily for 12 weeks, each escalated in accordance with Australian OCD dosing.

He has no history of bipolar disorder, no cardiac disease, no epilepsy and no urinary retention. His most recent 12-lead ECG shows a QTc of 415 ms in sinus rhythm. He is otherwise well and highly motivated to keep trying pharmacotherapy before augmentation. He asks whether a different class of medication is worth attempting.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: MSE unremarkable other than resistance to contamination obsessions and hand-washing rituals.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within reference from last month. 12-lead ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 415 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Add risperidone 1 mg orally at night as the first augmentation step before trialling any further serotonergic monotherapy
Swap to venlafaxine XR 225 mg orally daily as the preferred evidence-based next serotonergic monotherapy for OCD in Australia
Commence clomipramine 25 mg orally at night and titrate towards 150 to 250 mg daily with periodic ECG review of QTc
Combine sertraline 200 mg orally daily with fluoxetine 40 mg orally daily to increase overall serotonergic effect at receptor level
Refer for deep brain stimulation of the ventral capsule as the appropriate next pharmacological step for his refractory OCD

subtopic_detail: OCD SSRI target dose distinct from depression target dose
stem:
A 19-year-old university student is diagnosed with OCD after 12 months of contamination obsessions and 3 to 4 hours of daily hand-washing and shower rituals. Her Y-BOCS score is 24 and she is functionally impaired. She has been referred for ERP and you agree with the psychiatry registrar to commence fluvoxamine at the same time.

She has no cardiac, hepatic or renal disease. She takes no other medications and has no allergies. She asks how long it will take to know if the medication is working and what dose she should expect to reach.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Chapped hands with dermatitis; MSE otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within reference.

lead_in: Which dose target and trial duration best matches the recommended OCD-specific regimen?

options.text: Fluvoxamine 100 mg orally daily reviewed at 4 weeks with switch to a different SSRI if no meaningful response is seen
Fluvoxamine 50 mg orally daily indefinitely with no planned dose titration or scheduled treatment review appointment
Fluvoxamine 400 mg orally daily reviewed at 6 weeks as a maximum-effect strategy given her marked functional impairment
Fluvoxamine 100 mg orally daily plus lorazepam 1 mg orally three times daily to accelerate anxiolytic response early on
Fluvoxamine 200 to 300 mg orally daily reviewed at a minimum of 10 to 12 weeks after target dose is reached

subtopic_detail: PTSD - benzodiazepine avoidance rationale
stem:
A 41-year-old paramedic presents to his GP nine months after a mass-casualty road traffic incident. He describes vivid intrusive memories of the scene, nightly nightmares, hypervigilance while driving, avoidance of the section of highway involved and marked emotional numbing towards his wife and children. His alcohol use has doubled to 6 standard drinks per night as a way of getting to sleep. He has taken 14 sick days in the last three months.

He asks specifically for diazepam because a colleague has been given it and reports feeling better on it. He has no history of substance dependence prior to this year, no bipolar disorder and no psychotic symptoms. He accepts referral for trauma-focused therapy but says he needs something for the meantime.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Anxious, avoidant eye contact, hypervigilant to background noise; no thought disorder or psychosis.
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 58. AUDIT-C 8. LFTs mildly raised (GGT 78 U/L, RR under 60). TSH within reference.

lead_in: Which is the best justification for declining his request for diazepam?

options.text: Benzodiazepines interact directly with SSRIs to cause serotonin syndrome and therefore cannot be safely co-prescribed in his case
Diazepam causes rebound flashbacks on cessation and is teratogenic in any male-partner co-prescription in the household
Diazepam is contraindicated in men over 40 years of age due to a well-documented falls risk and cognitive impairment profile
Benzodiazepines impair extinction learning central to trauma-focused therapy and add dependence risk on his escalating alcohol use
Benzodiazepines are only unhelpful here because of PBS restrictions on their long-term supply for anxiety indications in general practice

subtopic_detail: PTSD SSRI selection - sertraline vs paroxetine
stem:
A 29-year-old woman meets DSM-5 criteria for PTSD 8 months after a serious sexual assault. She has completed initial psychoeducation with her GP and is on a 6-month waiting list for a trauma-focused CBT program at her local community mental health service. She and her GP agree to commence an SSRI while she waits.

She hopes to conceive within the next 12 months and has stopped hormonal contraception. She has no cardiac, hepatic or renal disease and no drug allergies. She takes no other regular medication and asks which SSRI is the best first choice given her plans.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Intrusive memories, hyperarousal, avoidance and negative cognitions consistent with PTSD.
data_table.Investigations: TSH, FBC, UEC, LFTs within reference.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line SSRI?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily titrated to 60 mg as the preferred agent for PTSD in reproductive-age women
Paroxetine 20 mg orally daily titrated to 40 mg as the preferred agent given TGA registration for PTSD in Australia
Sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrated to a target of 100 to 200 mg over four to six weeks with regular review
Mirtazapine 30 mg orally at night as an evidence-based first-line PTSD monotherapy in Australian primary care
Diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily as a short-term measure until trauma-focused therapy commences at 6 months

subtopic_detail: EMDR vs trauma-focused CBT - patient factors
stem:
A 34-year-old refugee man from Iran meets DSM-5 criteria for PTSD following torture in detention two years ago. He is fluent in Farsi but has limited English and speaks with the aid of a Farsi interpreter through your community clinic. He has no comorbid substance use disorder, no active psychosis and no acute suicidality. He finds writing distressing and disclosed that in his cultural context talking at length about the trauma feels shameful.

He is willing to engage with a psychological therapy but has previously stopped a group program that involved writing an account of his trauma. His psychologist offers a choice between trauma-focused CBT with imaginal exposure and written narrative, and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR).

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: MSE unremarkable other than PTSD features.
data_table.Investigations: Nil relevant.

lead_in: Which factor most supports EMDR as the preferred first-line psychological therapy for this patient?

options.text: EMDR requires less verbal disclosure and no written narrative, aligning with his cultural context and prior drop-out from a written program
EMDR is more effective than trauma-focused CBT for all adult PTSD patients according to current Australian guideline recommendations
EMDR is the only trauma-focused therapy that does not require an interpreter in his refugee context and Farsi language pairing
Trauma-focused CBT is explicitly contraindicated in all survivors of torture in the Australian refugee mental health model of care
EMDR does not require any verbal or non-verbal recall of the trauma during any phase of the treatment protocol

subtopic_detail: Adjustment disorder vs PTSD - Criterion A stressor threshold
stem:
A 46-year-old accountant presents to his GP three months after being made redundant from a role he had held for 18 years. He describes persistent low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep with early morning waking and reduced appetite. He ruminates about lost identity and worries constantly about the family mortgage. He denies intrusive re-experiencing, flashbacks, nightmares or hypervigilance. He has not avoided any specific reminders of work; he still meets colleagues socially and drives past his old office without distress.

He has no personal or family history of mood disorder. He drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, does not use other substances and has no active suicidal ideation. His symptoms have caused him to withdraw from his weekly football team and he has been unable to update his CV or apply for new roles.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Tearful, low mood, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features. K-10 score 26.
data_table.Investigations: TSH, FBC, UEC within reference.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Persistent complex bereavement disorder secondary to identity loss
Post-traumatic stress disorder secondary to job loss
Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood
Major depressive disorder single episode, moderate severity
Generalised anxiety disorder with depressive features

subtopic_detail: Complex PTSD (ICD-11) - disturbances in self-organisation triad
stem:
A 33-year-old woman presents to a community mental health clinic with a history of chronic sexual and physical abuse by a family member between ages 6 and 15. She describes persistent intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of anything connected to the perpetrator and generalised hyperarousal. In addition she describes lifelong difficulty regulating emotions with frequent explosive anger and sustained periods of shutdown, a deeply negative self-view (she describes herself as fundamentally broken and shameful), and pervasive difficulty maintaining any close relationship, including with her current partner and her two adult children.

She has not previously been diagnosed with a mental illness. She has no history of psychosis or mania. She uses alcohol occasionally but not to problematic levels, and she takes no regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: MSE reveals PTSD phenomena as above with additional pervasive affect dysregulation and interpersonal impairment.
data_table.Investigations: TSH, FBC, UEC within reference.

lead_in: Which is the single most accurate ICD-11 diagnosis?

options.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder in the absence of any personality-level disturbance
Borderline personality disorder without concurrent trauma-related disorder recognised
Dissociative identity disorder with trauma-related re-experiencing as the leading presentation
Complex post-traumatic stress disorder with disturbances in self-organisation
Persistent depressive disorder as the primary trauma-related diagnostic category

subtopic_detail: Illness anxiety disorder - test-negative but preoccupation persists
stem:
A 39-year-old accountant has attended your practice on 14 occasions in the past 12 months, each visit motivated by a new fear of a serious illness. Over the past 8 months he has been convinced at different times he had bowel cancer, motor neuron disease, a brain tumour and thyroid cancer. Each concern has been triggered by minor bodily sensations such as passing normal-textured stool of variable colour, a leg twitch after exercise or a fleeting sensation of neck swelling.

Despite two normal colonoscopies, an MRI brain, thyroid ultrasound and repeated bloods including TFTs and creatine kinase, his fears settle briefly then reappear with the next symptom. He spends 3 to 4 hours daily searching the internet for illness information. He does not describe any prominent physical symptom that dominates his day - his distress centres on the fear of having or acquiring a serious illness.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable. No focal neurological signs, no palpable thyroid nodule.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, CK within reference. Colonoscopy x2 normal. MRI brain normal. Thyroid ultrasound normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
