options.text: Delusional disorder, somatic subtype, persistent presentation
Somatic symptom disorder, persistent care-seeking type
Obsessive-compulsive disorder, contamination and checking subtype
Factitious disorder imposed on self, chronic recurrent type
Illness anxiety disorder, care-seeking predominant type

subtopic_detail: Body dysmorphic disorder - muscle dysmorphia subtype
stem:
A 22-year-old male gym instructor presents at the urging of his mother. He weighs 96 kg at 178 cm tall (BMI 30 kg/m2, with visibly increased muscle mass and low body fat). He spends 4 hours daily at the gym, mirrors constantly to check his shoulders and chest, weighs and photographs his physique twice daily, and describes himself as too small and skinny. He has withdrawn from a serious relationship and left an accounting cadetship to work in a gym where he feels less exposed.

He volunteers that he has been injecting testosterone enanthate 500 mg intramuscularly weekly for the last 6 months, sourced online, and takes clenbuterol during cuts. He has no other psychiatric history and denies eating disorder pathology in the classic sense - his intake is high in protein, not restricted overall. He has no insight into how others perceive his appearance and is highly distressed when unable to train.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 148/94, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.6.
data_table.Examination: Heavily muscled, acne over back and shoulders, mild gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy on examination.
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.54 (RR 0.40-0.50), LFTs mildly deranged, LH and FSH suppressed.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anabolic androgenic steroid use disorder as the primary and sole diagnosis
Anorexia nervosa, atypical subtype without a low body weight criterion
Body dysmorphic disorder, muscle dysmorphia subtype presentation
Obsessive-compulsive disorder, ordering and symmetry subtype
Narcissistic personality disorder with grandiose subtype presentation

subtopic_detail: Selective mutism - discrimination from autism spectrum
stem:
You are a GP registrar seeing a 6-year-old girl brought by her mother because she has never spoken at school since starting reception two years ago. Her teacher reports that she plays alongside other children, follows instructions and completes tasks, but never speaks and communicates by pointing and nodding. Her mother reports that at home she is chatty, tells long stories, argues with her older brother, sings, and has age-appropriate vocabulary and grammar. She also speaks freely at her grandparents' house and to her one close friend on play-dates at home.

She has no history of developmental delay. She reached all milestones on time, makes eye contact with familiar people, engages in imaginative play, shares interests and has no restricted or repetitive behaviours. She is otherwise healthy.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits for age.
data_table.Examination: Cooperative with mother, watchful with you, does not speak. Age-appropriate play. Normal hearing screen documented.
data_table.Investigations: Nil relevant.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Selective mutism, situationally-restricted subtype
Autism spectrum disorder, level 1 subtype
Reactive attachment disorder, inhibited subtype
Expressive language disorder, developmental type
Social anxiety disorder alone as a standalone diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Adult separation anxiety disorder - DSM-5 recognition in adulthood
stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to her GP with 3 years of increasing distress around any separation from her partner. She experiences intense worry that harm will come to him whenever they are apart, checks on him by text every 15 minutes when he is away, and has twice left work early because of fear that he had been in a car accident when he did not answer immediately. She has nightmares of losing him. Physical complaints of nausea and stomach ache occur when he goes on interstate work trips.

She has no history of a childhood anxiety disorder and functioned well through university and her twenties in previous relationships. Her partner is well, works in an office role and has never had a serious accident or illness. She has no personal history of trauma, no substance use and no other current psychiatric symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Anxious; no low mood, no psychotic features.
data_table.Investigations: TSH, FBC within reference.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Panic disorder with agoraphobia specifier as the primary diagnosis
Dependent personality disorder in adult onset form
Obsessive-compulsive disorder, checking and reassurance subtype
Generalised anxiety disorder, single-domain presentation
Separation anxiety disorder, adult-onset attachment-figure form

subtopic_detail: Panic disorder with agoraphobia - interoceptive exposure rationale
stem:
A 37-year-old woman with 4 years of panic disorder attends for CBT with a clinical psychologist. She has now developed marked agoraphobia and only leaves the house when accompanied. She has taken 6 weeks off her administrative role. She has been on sertraline 100 mg orally daily for 8 weeks with partial reduction in panic frequency. Her psychologist plans to begin exposure work.

She has learned to identify her early panic symptoms (palpitations, breathlessness, depersonalisation) and reports that these bodily sensations are what she most fears. She has been managing panic by immediately sitting down, sipping cold water, and using slow breathing to abort the sensations before they build. She has no cardiac history and a recent 12-lead ECG was normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Anxious but composed in the clinic room.
data_table.Investigations: TSH, FBC, UEC within reference. ECG normal.

lead_in: Which exposure component is the most important target for her CBT?

options.text: Interoceptive exposure to feared bodily sensations with concurrent response prevention of safety behaviours during the exercise
Cognitive restructuring of catastrophic thoughts without any accompanying behavioural exposure component in the treatment plan
Situational exposure with continued slow-breathing safety behaviour to abort panic during each exposure attempt
Progressive muscle relaxation training as the primary standalone intervention with agoraphobia work deferred to later sessions
Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) as the primary intervention for her established panic and agoraphobia

subtopic_detail: Postpartum OCD - intrusive harm thoughts distinct from postpartum psychosis
stem:
You are called by the child and family health nurse about a 31-year-old woman she has just visited at home. The patient is 6 weeks postpartum after an uncomplicated first pregnancy. Over the last 3 weeks she has developed distressing intrusive images of harming her baby - specifically, of dropping her over the balcony rail or in the bath. She describes the thoughts as horrifying, alien and unwanted, and she is deeply ashamed. She has responded by refusing to bathe her baby alone, avoiding the balcony entirely, and asking her partner to check on the baby repeatedly during the night.

She denies wanting to harm her baby, has no plan or intent, and is not hearing voices telling her to act. She has no confusion, elated mood, grandiose beliefs or paranoid ideas. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder or postpartum psychosis. She is breastfeeding exclusively and there is no history of substance use. EPDS is 18. Her interaction with the baby during the visit was warm and appropriate.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Tearful, anxious, insight preserved, no thought disorder, no psychotic features. MSE reveals ego-dystonic intrusive imagery.
data_table.Investigations: TSH within reference at 4 weeks postpartum. FBC within reference.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Report to child protection as a mandatory notification of imminent risk of harm from a mother describing thoughts of dropping her baby
Offer CBT with response prevention plus sertraline commenced at 25 mg titrated to 100 mg with breastfeeding maintained
Commence olanzapine 5 mg orally at night as first-line pharmacotherapy for postpartum intrusive thoughts of harming the baby
Arrange urgent involuntary admission to a mother-baby unit for suspected postpartum psychosis with mandatory temporary separation from the baby
Recommend she cease breastfeeding immediately today before any SSRI is prescribed or CBT referral is initiated

subtopic_detail: Acute stress reaction ICD-11 vs acute stress disorder DSM-5
stem:
You are the resident on the trauma ward reviewing a 27-year-old cyclist 3 days after a high-speed collision with a car. He sustained a fractured tibia now internally fixed and multiple minor abrasions. He is otherwise medically stable. Over the last 72 hours he has been tearful, has vivid intrusive memories of the impact, has slept poorly with nightmares, feels emotionally detached from his family visiting, and startles at loud noises on the ward. He is very distressed but is oriented, cooperative with rehabilitation, engaging with his physiotherapist and is able to describe the events coherently.

He has no personal or family history of psychiatric illness, no substance use disorder, no prior trauma exposure and no premorbid anxiety condition. The trauma social worker asks whether this warrants a formal psychiatric diagnosis and referral to a trauma-focused therapy service, and whether he should be prescribed anything today.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Distressed but engaged; MSE consistent with acute stress phenomena.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs within reference. TSH not indicated.

lead_in: Which is the most accurate description of his condition and the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Diagnose acute stress disorder now under DSM-5 and start sertraline 50 mg orally daily today to prevent progression to PTSD
Provide single-session critical incident stress debriefing today at the bedside to prevent the development of subsequent PTSD
Provide psychological first aid with watchful waiting and review at 2 to 4 weeks, referring only if symptoms persist or worsen
Commence diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for the first two weeks post-injury to prevent the development of PTSD
Diagnose PTSD now on the strength of his intrusive memories and start prazosin overnight to treat the nightmares he is experiencing

subtopic: Mental Health Act - certificate vs involuntary patient order
subtopic_detail: Which NSW instrument authorises initial detention for examination
stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to a NSW emergency department by police after neighbours reported him shouting from his windows. He says strangers are pumping gas into his flat and that he has not slept for four nights. He declines admission and asks to leave. There is no previous psychiatric contact and no collateral. You cannot yet establish a diagnosis or a treatment plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 148/92, RR 20, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Vigilant, pressured speech, persecutory content

lead_in: Which step under the NSW Mental Health Act is most appropriate?

options.text: Complete a mental health certificate authorising detention and further examination
Make an involuntary patient order to start antipsychotic medication tonight
Make a community treatment order requiring depot medication after discharge
Rely on common law necessity to hold him without any statutory certificate
Discharge him and ask police to return him if he deteriorates overnight

subtopic_detail: Least restrictive care under the NSW Act
stem: A 27-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder stopped her aripiprazole depot 6 weeks ago. She believes her neighbour is monitoring her but is not distressed and not acting on it. She agrees to restart the depot today and to a case manager home visit tomorrow. Her mother, with whom she lives, is present and offering support. She has no suicidal ideation and no history of acting on such beliefs.

data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged, mildly guarded, no thought disorder, no command hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, recent bloods normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Complete a mental health certificate and admit her involuntarily today
Restart the depot, arrange the home visit, continue voluntary care
Apply for a community treatment order compelling her depot medication
Defer the depot until psychiatrist review, with family observation only
Notify police of a threat to the neighbour and discharge her

subtopic_detail: Four-limb functional framework
stem:
A 78-year-old man is admitted with a wet gangrenous right forefoot on a background of type 2 diabetes and peripheral vascular disease. The vascular team recommends a below-knee amputation given failed revascularisation. He tells you he understands he could die of infection if he refuses, describes the operation as 'cutting my leg off below the knee', but insists that he would rather die intact than live as an amputee. His daughter says he has always felt this way.

He has a mild vascular cognitive impairment (MoCA 24/30) but is oriented, not delirious, and consistent across two conversations 24 hours apart. The surgical team asks you to determine whether he has decision-making capacity to refuse surgery.

data_table.Examination: Alert, coherent, no fluctuating attention.
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs within normal limits; CRP 180; delirium screen negative on both reviews.

lead_in: Which finding most strongly supports the conclusion that he has capacity to refuse the amputation?

options.text: The presence of a mildly abnormal MoCA score above the standard impairment cut-off used for cognitive screening
His daughter confirms this refusal is consistent with his lifelong values around bodily integrity and disability
He can weigh the risks of death from sepsis against his own valuation of body integrity and communicate a stable choice
He describes the proposed operation accurately in lay terms and can restate the surgical plan on repeat questioning
He is oriented to time, place and person and shows no signs of delirium on repeat bedside cognitive screening

subtopic_detail: Consent for admission does not equal consent for medication
stem:
A 45-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder is admitted voluntarily to a mental health unit for a manic episode after discussion with her outpatient psychiatrist. She signs the voluntary admission form and settles on the ward overnight. The next morning the treating team wants to commence olanzapine 10 mg orally. She reads the medication information sheet, tells the team she does not want any medication and would prefer to try to sleep more and 'ride it out', and reiterates that she is happy to remain on the ward for observation.

She describes the risks of untreated mania, recognises she is unwell, and is coherent. She has capacity assessed to be intact for this decision.

data_table.Examination: Elevated mood, mildly pressured speech, no psychotic features, sleeping 3 hours per night.
data_table.Investigations: Bloods within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Administer the olanzapine now because her voluntary admission implies broader consent to routine inpatient ward treatment
Convert her to involuntary status under the state Mental Health Act so that oral medication can be commenced today
Discharge her from the ward this morning given that she has declined the specific medication that was proposed
Withhold the olanzapine and continue observation, with a documented plan to reassess if her mental state or capacity changes
Administer the olanzapine covertly in her breakfast to prevent further clinical deterioration while she remains on the ward

subtopic_detail: Criteria for a NSW community treatment order
stem: A 32-year-old man with a 10-year history of schizophrenia has had three admissions in 18 months, each after he stopped oral risperidone, became paranoid and was brought in by police. Each admission improved his symptoms. He works part-time when well, and says he does not believe he has an illness and will stop treatment on discharge. He is now settled on paliperidone depot and nearing discharge.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no active psychotic symptoms, insight into illness limited
data_table.Investigations: Nil acute

lead_in: Which features most strongly support a community treatment order?

options.text: The team's shared concern that he will disengage from services after discharge
His family's request that his medication be legally enforced at home
His limited insight into having a chronic illness during this admission
His involuntary inpatient status carrying over automatically into the community
Past refusal, relapse and deterioration, with hospital care producing improvement

subtopic_detail: Presser criteria
stem:
You are asked to see a 41-year-old man in custody who has been charged with a serious assault. His solicitor has raised concerns about his ability to participate in proceedings. He has a background of chronic schizophrenia with residual negative symptoms, is currently stable on clozapine, and denies acute psychotic symptoms. On interview he can name his solicitor, states the charge against him accurately, and describes what happened at the alleged incident coherently.

However, when you explore his understanding of court process he tells you he thinks the magistrate is 'like a referee' who will 'decide who wins the argument', and that if he pleads not guilty the jury will vote about whether they believe him or the victim, without being able to describe the role of evidence, cross-examination or the meaning of a guilty plea.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no thought disorder, no active hallucinations or delusions.
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine level within therapeutic range.

lead_in: Which is the most accurate conclusion regarding his fitness to stand trial under Australian common-law criteria?

options.text: He is likely unfit because he cannot follow proceedings or grasp the substantial effect of evidence given against him
He is fit because he can state the charge accurately and gives a coherent factual account of the alleged incident
He is fit because he is not currently floridly psychotic and is clinically stable on his maintenance clozapine treatment
He is fit because the defence of insanity applies only to the accused's mental state at the time of the offence
The fitness question is for the treating psychiatrist alone to determine at the next multidisciplinary team meeting

subtopic_detail: Structured professional judgment vs actuarial
stem:
A 39-year-old man with a diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder, chronic methamphetamine use, and one prior conviction for assault is being reviewed after admission for suicidal ideation. Before discharge you are asked to document a violence-risk assessment. You have access to his full history, the collateral from partner and probation, an actuarial risk instrument scored by the on-call registrar, and a structured professional-judgement schedule (HCR-20 v3).

The registrar is asking which framework should carry most weight when you formulate risk and communicate it to the treating team.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no active psychotic symptoms; irritable affect.
data_table.Investigations: UDS positive for methamphetamine; bloods within normal limits.

lead_in: Which approach is most appropriate to guide clinical decision-making here?

options.text: Rely on the actuarial score alone because it yields a numerical probability that is easily communicated to the team
Use structured professional judgement (HCR-20 v3) integrating historical, clinical and risk-management items, and formulate
Use unstructured clinical judgement based on your overall impression of the patient after your interview with him today
Assign him to a categorical low, medium or high risk band as the primary output for the discharge documentation
Decline to produce a risk assessment because violence prediction has poor accuracy at the level of the individual patient

subtopic_detail: Chemical vs mechanical decision
stem:
A 24-year-old man on a state Mental Health Act assessment order in the ED has become acutely agitated. Verbal de-escalation over 20 minutes and offered oral olanzapine have both failed. He is pacing, punching walls and has now threatened staff. He has not eaten today. The clinical team must act to prevent injury to himself and others.

He has no known cardiac history, no relevant drug allergies, and a code black team has arrived.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, tachycardic, no evidence of head injury or intoxication other than clinical impression.
data_table.Investigations: Nil obtainable.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step consistent with least-restrictive-practice principles?

options.text: Apply mechanical restraint for the rest of the shift so that the team can safely monitor him from a distance in seclusion
Continue verbal de-escalation without further medication as escalation is a nursing rather than a medical issue tonight
Administer parenteral sedation as chemical restraint with the smallest safe team, monitoring vitals and airway continuously
Call police to remove him from the department under public-order offences and transfer him into the local watch-house
Give a large stat oral benzodiazepine dose despite prior oral refusal to try to achieve chemical control non-parenterally

subtopic_detail: Monitoring and review requirements
stem: A 30-year-old woman on an inpatient psychiatric unit has been placed in seclusion after a serious assault on a nurse. She is under a state Mental Health Act treatment order. The consultant psychiatrist has authorised the seclusion order and documented the indication. You are the medical registrar covering the ward that evening.

data_table.Examination: Post-medication, drowsy but rousable, breathing normally.
data_table.Investigations: Vitals recorded pre-seclusion within normal limits.

lead_in: Which set of monitoring requirements is most consistent with Australian standards for a seclusion episode?

options.text: Check on the patient at the start of the shift and again at the end of the shift with a documented mental state note
Use continuous CCTV monitoring without in-person checks in order to minimise staff exposure during the seclusion event
Have medical review only at the next scheduled ward round on the following morning, with nursing observations overnight
Continuous visual observation with regular physical and mental-state checks, timely medical review, and release considered each review
Release the patient at the end of the standard four-hour block regardless of ongoing clinical need or risk to staff

subtopic_detail: Child protection
stem:
A 34-year-old woman brings her 3-year-old son to your GP clinic for review of a rash. During the consultation she becomes tearful and discloses that her partner has been drinking heavily, has been hitting her, and last week grabbed the child roughly and left a bruise on his upper arm. She does not want to involve authorities, and asks you to keep the disclosure confidential.

On examination the child has an oval bruise on the medial upper arm consistent with a grip mark. She agrees to a domestic violence phone service referral.

data_table.Examination: Child alert, well-grown, oval bruise medial right upper arm; no other injuries noted.
data_table.Investigations: Nil required at this visit.

lead_in: What is your obligation regarding the child?

options.text: Respect her stated request for confidentiality and document a plan to reassess the situation at the next scheduled clinic visit
Report only if she consents to disclosure after further counselling in a dedicated follow-up appointment later this week
Refer to the paediatrician you know at the local hospital and ask them to make the report on your behalf next week
Report the partner directly to police for assault instead of contacting the state child protection agency about the child
Make a mandatory report to the state child protection agency given a reasonable belief of significant harm to the child

subtopic_detail: Australian equivalent of Tarasoff
stem:
A 46-year-old man attends his second session with you in a community mental health clinic. He has depression and long-standing conflict with a specific former business partner. He tells you today that he has bought a specific firearm, has looked up his former partner's address, and describes a detailed plan to shoot him next weekend when the former partner is expected to be at his home. He says he is only telling you because he wanted 'someone to know'.

He explicitly asks that this remain confidential and threatens to end therapy if you break confidence. He has capacity for this discussion.

data_table.Examination: Mood low, affect constricted, no psychotic features.
data_table.Investigations: Nil relevant.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Breach confidentiality by warning police and the intended victim, then arrange urgent psychiatric assessment for detention
Maintain confidentiality on the basis that no such duty to warn a third party exists in current Australian medical practice
Ask him to sign a written no-harm contract and continue outpatient treatment with weekly review by yourself at the clinic
Warn only the intended victim and not the police in order to preserve as much of the therapeutic confidentiality as possible
Formally terminate the therapy relationship today so that you no longer have a treating clinician's duty to act on the disclosure

subtopic_detail: Adolescent decision-making
stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends your GP clinic alone requesting a prescription for the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has been in a sexual relationship for 4 months with her 16-year-old partner. On assessment she can describe how the pill works, the main side-effect profile including VTE risk, the requirement for daily dosing, and the option of condoms for STI protection. She has thought about whether to tell her parents and prefers not to.

She has no medical contraindications and safeguarding screening (HEADSSS) does not raise any concerns about the relationship being non-consensual.

data_table.Examination: Age-appropriate, engaged, no concerning features.
data_table.Investigations: BP within normal limits; BMI 22.

lead_in: Which principle most correctly guides your decision on whether to prescribe?

options.text: Refuse to prescribe without parental consent because she is under 16 years of age and cannot lawfully consent alone
Assess her Gillick competence for this decision, including understanding of the treatment and implications, and prescribe if competent
Contact her parents against her stated wishes today to obtain parental consent for the combined oral contraceptive pill
Report the sexual relationship to police because she is a minor engaged in a sexual relationship with a peer of similar age
Defer prescribing until she returns to the clinic with a parent for a joint follow-up consultation to discuss contraception

subtopic_detail: Aged care setting
stem:
You are the GP for an 82-year-old woman living in a Commonwealth-funded residential aged care facility. She has moderate Alzheimer disease and periodically loses capacity for complex decisions. Her son (financial enduring power of attorney) has been observed by staff shouting at her repeatedly during visits, and a bruise pattern on her forearm was noted at last week's shower. She tells you today, when he is not present, that she is 'scared when he visits'. She does not want you to do anything.

Her capacity for this specific decision (about reporting) is impaired; she cannot describe options for action, or weigh the implications of reporting or not reporting.

data_table.Examination: Frail, resolving bruise linear pattern medial left forearm; MoCA previously 14/30.
data_table.Investigations: FBC and coags within normal limits.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Respect her stated wish that no action be taken and document the conversation, arranging closer nursing observation and review
Confront the son directly and demand that he stop the behaviour before contemplating any formal safeguarding or agency report
Report through the Serious Incident Response Scheme via the facility and consider notifying the Public Advocate given impaired capacity
Report the son directly to police as the only channel available for adult abuse in a Commonwealth-funded aged-care setting
Ask the facility to restrict his visits informally without any formal report to a safeguarding agency or state authority

subtopic_detail: Advance care directives and compulsory treatment in NSW
stem: A 38-year-old woman with bipolar disorder wrote an advance care directive while well, recording that during manic relapse she prefers oral quetiapine and refuses lithium, which she found intolerable. She also nominated her sister as her designated carer. She now presents in an acute manic episode, lacks capacity, and is detained in a NSW declared mental health facility. Quetiapine and lithium are both clinically reasonable.

data_table.Examination: Elevated mood, pressured speech, mildly disorganised
data_table.Investigations: Bloods sent, results pending

lead_in: How should her recorded preferences most appropriately be handled?

options.text: Disregard the directive, because she now lacks capacity to reaffirm it
Follow it only if her sister agrees with every element it records
Prefer lithium, because guidelines list it first line in bipolar disorder
Prescribe quetiapine, notify her designated carer, and document any departure
Withhold medication until she regains capacity and can consent afresh

subtopic_detail: Delirium and consent to procedure
stem:
An 84-year-old woman is admitted with a displaced intracapsular hip fracture. The orthopaedic team recommends hip hemiarthroplasty within 48 hours. When you assess her at 09:00 she is oriented, understands the operation and the risks of anaesthesia, and agrees to proceed. At 17:00 the ward calls: she is now confused, pulling at her drip, telling nurses she wants to go home to feed her cat (she has no cat), and is refusing surgery loudly. She has fluctuating attention, is easily distracted, and cannot follow a three-step command. Nothing is documented about her earlier capacity assessment beyond a brief operative consent form she signed at 09:00.

She has no formal enduring guardian. Her daughter (next of kin) is contactable and was not present for either conversation. Surgery within the next 24 hours reduces her mortality risk substantially.

data_table.Examination: At 09:00 alert, oriented; at 17:00 4AT score 8, inattentive, mildly hyperactive delirium.
data_table.Investigations: UEC and inflammatory markers pending; UA leukocytes and nitrites positive.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to consent for surgery now?

options.text: Accept the current refusal as valid because it is the most recent expressed preference recorded from the patient this admission
Apply urgently to the state Guardianship Tribunal for an emergency guardian to consent to surgery before proceeding with the operation
Proceed under the emergency common-law doctrine of necessity, ignoring the earlier capacitous consent that was signed at 09:00 today
Wait until she is fully lucid and no longer delirious before proceeding with surgery, regardless of how long the recovery takes
Rely on the earlier capacitous consent as it was given for this operation while she had capacity, and consult daughter as person responsible

subtopic_detail: McNaghten rules and Australian equivalents
stem:
You are asked to write an expert report on a 33-year-old man charged with the serious assault of his neighbour. At the time of the offence he had untreated schizophrenia with a fixed delusion that the neighbour was a government operative sent to kill his family. He believed he was defending his children pre-emptively. Interviews after treatment reveal that he had a coherent understanding of the physical nature of the act (that punching would cause injury), and knew that ordinarily punching a person would be legally wrong, but believed at the time that his specific act was morally right because it was necessary to save his family from imminent harm.

His chronic schizophrenia is well documented, contemporaneous ambulance and police records describe florid psychosis at the scene, and there is no evidence of intoxication.

data_table.Examination: Now stabilised on clozapine, insight into past psychosis intact.
data_table.Investigations: Historical records confirm chronic schizophrenia.

lead_in: Which formulation most correctly applies the mental impairment defence in this case?

options.text: The defence fails because he knew that punching a person is generally illegal and this satisfies the legal wrongness limb entirely
The defence succeeds automatically because he was documented as psychotic at the time of the alleged assault on the neighbour
He may satisfy the wrongness limb because a delusion making him believe the act was morally right can defeat knowledge of wrongness
The defence turns on his current mental state on clozapine rather than his mental state at the time of the alleged offence itself
The defence is exclusively a matter for the treating psychiatrist and cannot be independently evaluated by an expert court reporter

subtopic_detail: 4AT interpretation in ED
stem:
An 82-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a fall at home. Her daughter reports that her mother has been "not quite right" for two days, sometimes drowsy in the afternoons and then wide awake and confused about who her visitors are at night. She has a background of osteoarthritis and hypertension. She usually manages her own medications and does her own shopping with a taxi.

On assessment she is alert but slow. She names her daughter but says the year is 1998 and cannot name the current Prime Minister or the one before. Asked to state the months of the year backwards from December, she gets to October, then loses the sequence and starts listing days of the week instead. Her daughter confirms she has never been like this at baseline.

data_table.Observations: Pulse 88, BP 142/84 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius.
data_table.Bedside cognition: Alertness: mildly abnormal (drowsy but rousable in prior hour per triage). AMT4: age correct, year 1998 (incorrect), place "the hospital" (correct), DOB correct. Months backwards: 2 errors and abandonment.
data_table.Collateral: Baseline independent, no prior cognitive concerns per GP letter.

lead_in: Which single interpretation of the 4AT screen is correct?

options.text: Score 0 to 3, cognitive impairment unlikely and no further delirium workup indicated today
Score 1 to 3, possible cognitive impairment only, arrange outpatient memory clinic referral
Score 4 or above with abnormal alertness, indicating possible delirium and precipitant search
Score 4 or above but attributable to dementia alone given her age, so no acute precipitant search needed
Score is uninterpretable without a formal MMSE or MoCA and delirium diagnosis should be deferred

subtopic_detail: Differentiating delirium, dementia, depression
stem:
A 79-year-old man attends the general practice with his wife, who has taken time off work to come with him. Over the last four months he has become withdrawn and stopped attending his weekly bowls club. He complains that his memory is failing and he cannot concentrate on the newspaper. He denies any recent illness, hospital admission, medication change or alcohol use above his usual two beers a week.

On examination he is oriented to person, place and date. He answers questions with "I don't know" repeatedly but on encouragement can register three items and recall two after five minutes. His MoCA score is 22 out of 30. His wife notes that his sleep is fragmented with 3 am wakening and his appetite is poor. Physical examination and screening bloods (FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, calcium) are within normal limits.

data_table.Cognition: Oriented x3. MoCA 22/30 with effort-limited errors in attention and delayed recall.
data_table.Mood/sleep: Fragmented sleep with early morning wakening, appetite reduced, anhedonia and social withdrawal for 4 months.
data_table.Bloods: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, corrected calcium all within normal limits.

lead_in: Which pattern best fits this presentation?

options.text: Acute confusional state with fluctuating attention consistent with hypoactive delirium
Late-life depression with cognitive slowing, formerly termed depressive pseudo-dementia
Early Alzheimer's dementia with anosognosia and preserved insight into daily function
Vascular cognitive impairment based on the stepwise decline and vascular risk profile
Frontotemporal dementia behavioural variant given social withdrawal and reduced engagement

subtopic_detail: Medication review in delirium precipitants
stem:
An 84-year-old woman on the general medical ward has developed a hypoactive delirium 48 hours after admission for a lower respiratory tract infection now improving on oral amoxicillin. Nursing staff report she is drowsy through the day, minimally engaged at meals, and disoriented to place overnight. She has no fever and vital signs are within normal limits today. Chest X-ray shows improving consolidation.

Her regular medications are shown below. Bloods today: sodium 136 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, calcium and TSH within normal limits, urinalysis clear. She had a normal cognitive assessment on admission and there was no evidence of cerebrovascular event on non-contrast CT head this morning.

data_table.Medications: Oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily (urge incontinence), amitriptyline 25 mg nocte (chronic low back pain), diazepam 5 mg PRN (recently "regular" per nursing observation chart, three doses in 24 h), amoxicillin 500 mg tds, paracetamol 1 g qid, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte.
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 136 mmol/L (135 to 145), urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, corrected calcium and TSH within normal limits.
data_table.Imaging: CT head: no acute intracranial pathology. CXR: improving consolidation.

lead_in: Which single medication change is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and reassess cognition in 48 hours as a common contributor to delirium in older adults
Switch amoxicillin to intravenous ceftriaxone to treat presumed occult meningitis contributing to delirium
Add risperidone 0.5 mg at night with structured behavioural charting to manage the hypoactive delirium symptoms
Cease amoxicillin now for suspected antibiotic-induced encephalopathy given the temporal association with admission
Cease oxybutynin, amitriptyline and PRN diazepam and use non-pharmacological measures for symptom control

subtopic_detail: Hyperactive delirium acute management
stem:
An 86-year-old man on the geriatric medicine ward has been agitated overnight, pulling at his intravenous cannula and attempting to climb over the cot sides despite one-to-one nursing. He was admitted 48 hours ago with a urinary tract infection and is on ceftriaxone. His delirium workup has identified the UTI as the precipitant; a repeat CT head this morning showed no new pathology. Non-pharmacological measures (reorientation, family at bedside, quiet single room, hearing aids in) have not settled him.

He now poses a risk of falling and of self-extubating the cannula. He is haemodynamically stable. His medications include cefriaxone, paracetamol, and a home dose of atenolol 25 mg daily. He has no known allergies, no history of Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, and a normal QTc of 420 ms on today's ECG.

data_table.Observations: Pulse 92, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius.
data_table.Behaviour: RASS +3, pulling at cannula, attempting to climb, non-verbally responsive to redirection for less than 30 seconds.

lead_in: Which single pharmacological agent and dose is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally, repeated in 30 minutes if agitation not settled
Haloperidol 0.5 mg orally with a 60-minute review before any repeat dose
Olanzapine 10 mg orally as a single sedating dose overnight
Zopiclone 7.5 mg orally to enforce sleep and end the agitation cycle
Midazolam 5 mg intramuscularly to achieve rapid tranquillisation

subtopic_detail: Non-pharmacological first-line for BPSD
stem:
An 81-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer's disease living in a residential aged care facility has become verbally aggressive and physically resistive during personal care over the past three weeks. Staff report he shouts and pushes carers away when they try to shower him in the morning. He is otherwise settled at meals, during activities, and in the evening. The facility GP has been asked to review.

His behaviour chart shows escalation only during morning showers (never at bedtime or during meals). There is no fever, urinalysis is clear, chest is clear, bowels are opening daily, he denies pain on movement and paracetamol given empirically for two days did not change the pattern. His medications are donepezil 10 mg mane and perindopril 4 mg mane. Nursing staff ask you to "prescribe something" for the agitation.

data_table.ABC chart pattern: Antecedent = morning shower initiated by unfamiliar carer. Behaviour = shouting and pushing away, resolved within 5 minutes of stopping. Consequence = shower postponed.
data_table.Screen for reversibles: Afebrile, urinalysis clear, chest clear, bowels regular, empirical paracetamol trial x 48 h with no effect.
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg mane, perindopril 4 mg mane.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Prescribe risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily as first-line pharmacological management and review in six weeks
Prescribe lorazepam 0.5 mg orally 30 minutes before each morning shower as pre-emptive sedation
Implement a person-centred care plan tailored to the shower task and review in two weeks
Prescribe quetiapine 25 mg at night to cover both nocturnal agitation risk and residual morning behaviours
Cease donepezil as a suspected contributor to the recent behavioural escalation and reassess in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Risperidone initiation and review interval
stem:
An 83-year-old woman with moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease has escalating aggression over eight weeks in her residential aged care facility, with three incidents of striking staff during personal care and one incident of hitting another resident. A structured non-pharmacological care plan has been in place for six weeks including trigger-avoidance, one-to-one carer during high-risk times, music therapy and pain review. Reversible causes have been excluded (afebrile, urinalysis clear, no constipation, no undiagnosed pain, medications rationalised).

Her daughter, who is the substitute decision maker, has given informed consent to a trial of an antipsychotic after a discussion of risks including stroke, mortality and sedation. She weighs 58 kg, has an eGFR of 62 mL/min/1.73 m2, has no history of Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia, no diabetes, and a QTc of 430 ms on ECG this week.

data_table.Behaviour: Aggression during personal care and one peer-directed episode. Structured non-pharmacological plan for 6 weeks, insufficient effect.
data_table.Investigations: Afebrile, urinalysis clear, bowels regular, structured pain assessment negative. ECG QTc 430 ms.
data_table.Baseline: Weight 58 kg, eGFR 62, no diabetes, no PD or DLB.

lead_in: Which prescribing plan best matches Australian guidance?

options.text: Haloperidol 1 mg twice daily orally for the aggression, review at 12 weeks
Risperidone 2 mg twice daily to achieve rapid effect and review at 6 months
Olanzapine 10 mg at night for the same indication, review at 12 weeks
Risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily with formal review at 6 to 12 weeks
Diazepam 5 mg at night as a lower-risk alternative, review at 6 weeks

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic sensitivity
stem:
A 78-year-old man is referred to the emergency department by his GP with escalating visual hallucinations of small animals and children in his lounge room for four weeks, unchanged by reassurance. His wife reports fluctuating cognition day to day, with periods of clarity and periods of "staring into space" for several minutes. She has also noticed a recent tremor and small shuffling steps.

On examination he is oriented but slow, has a symmetric rest tremor in both hands, mild cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, and a shuffling gait with reduced arm swing. There is no fever, no infection screen positive, medications reconciled with no new agents, and imaging shows generalised atrophy without acute pathology. The ED registrar plans to write up an antipsychotic for the hallucinations before discharge to the geriatric medicine ward.

data_table.Motor exam: Symmetric rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity both wrists, shuffling gait, reduced arm swing, expressionless face.
data_table.Cognition: Fluctuating, MoCA 22/30 today with prior GP MoCA 27/30 two weeks ago.
data_table.Precipitant screen: Afebrile, MSU negative, chest clear, no new medications, CT head atrophy only.

lead_in: Which single management step is most appropriate?

options.text: Prescribe haloperidol 0.5 mg orally at night for the hallucinations
Prescribe risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily as the PBS-listed BPSD antipsychotic
Withhold antipsychotics and commence rivastigmine for the neuropsychiatric symptoms
Prescribe olanzapine 5 mg at night to cover both hallucinations and sleep
Start levodopa/carbidopa to treat the parkinsonism as first priority

subtopic_detail: Behavioural variant recognition and cholinesterase eligibility
stem:
A 62-year-old man is brought to the memory clinic by his wife of 30 years. Over 18 months he has become disinhibited, making inappropriate sexual comments at his adult daughter's workplace Christmas party and repeatedly walking out of a restaurant without paying. His wife says he has become "flat" and no longer greets her or the grandchildren. He eats large quantities of sweet food and has gained 8 kg.

On cognitive testing his short-term recall is preserved (three items at five minutes). His MoCA is 25 out of 30 with losses on abstraction and verbal fluency. Neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable. MRI brain shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, greater on the right. His son asks whether donepezil, which helped his aunt, might help his father.

data_table.Behavioural change: Disinhibition, apathy, stereotyped eating (sweet foods), loss of empathy, over 18 months.
data_table.Cognition: 3-item recall preserved. MoCA 25/30. Losses on abstraction and verbal fluency.
data_table.MRI brain: Bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, right greater than left.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding cholinesterase inhibitor therapy?

options.text: Commence donepezil as the presentation and imaging support behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia
Do not commence cholinesterase inhibitors as the picture supports behavioural-variant FTD
Commence memantine as the first-line agent because it is licensed for all types of dementia
Refer directly to neurosurgery for consideration of decompressive surgery
Commence risperidone for the behavioural changes without further assessment

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in the elderly
stem:
A 77-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2), hypertension on perindopril, osteoarthritis and mild urge incontinence presents with a 12-week history of low mood, anhedonia, early morning wakening at 4 am, poor appetite with 4 kg weight loss and passive suicidal ideation without plan. Her PHQ-9 score is 18. She has never taken an antidepressant.

A structured assessment excludes bipolar history, substance use, hypothyroidism (TSH normal), B12 deficiency and abnormal calcium. She lives alone but has daily contact with her daughter. She is worried about "tablets clashing" with her other medications and dislikes side effects. Her current medications are perindopril, atorvastatin, alendronate weekly, and paracetamol PRN.

data_table.Bloods: eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2, sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), TSH within normal limits, B12 within normal limits, corrected calcium within normal limits.
data_table.Screening: PHQ-9 18/27, MoCA 27/30, no history of mania or hypomania.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line antidepressant?

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg daily titrated slowly with early sodium check
Amitriptyline 25 mg at night, titrated for mood and sleep
Paroxetine 20 mg daily, chosen for its short elimination half-life
Fluoxetine 20 mg daily, chosen for its once-weekly formulation option
Venlafaxine 75 mg daily as an SNRI with dual serotonergic action

subtopic_detail: SIADH from SSRI
stem:
A 76-year-old man was started on sertraline 25 mg daily for major depressive disorder three weeks ago, titrated to 50 mg after one week. He now presents to the GP with two days of headache, nausea and unsteadiness. His daughter says he has been slower and has been repeating himself over the last 48 hours. He is on perindopril 5 mg daily for hypertension and has no history of heart failure, cirrhosis or thiazide use.

On examination he is euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, JVP not raised, no oedema, and no postural change in blood pressure. Bloods today: sodium 124 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, cortisol and TSH within normal limits. Urine sodium is 62 mmol/L and urine osmolality is 480 mosmol/kg.

data_table.Serum: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1, urea 4.8, creatinine 82 micromol/L, glucose 5.2, cortisol and TSH within normal limits.
data_table.Volume status: Euvolaemic, no oedema, no postural BP change.
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 50 mg daily (started 3 weeks ago), perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Continue sertraline unchanged, add fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily to raise sodium
Cease sertraline and admit for cautious fluid restriction with serial sodium checks
Continue sertraline and give 3% hypertonic saline 500 mL over one hour for rapid correction
Cease perindopril as the most likely offending cause and continue sertraline
Give 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over one hour and reassess

subtopic_detail: ECT indication in the elderly
stem:
An 80-year-old woman with severe major depressive disorder has lost 9 kg over three months and is now refusing to eat or drink. She has developed nihilistic delusions that her internal organs are rotting. She has already had adequate 6-week trials of sertraline (titrated to 200 mg) and mirtazapine (titrated to 45 mg) with negligible response, and augmentation with aripiprazole was ceased at 10 days for akathisia. She is now on the inpatient psychiatry ward under an involuntary treatment order.

Her PHQ-9 was 24 on admission and remains 22 today. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and postural hypotension. Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L (SSRI-related), urea 9.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, and albumin 28 g/L. She has no pacemaker, no recent stroke, no unstable ischaemic heart disease and her most recent ECG showed sinus rhythm with QTc 440 ms.

data_table.Illness: Severe MDD with psychotic features (nihilistic), 3 months, food and fluid refusal, 9 kg weight loss.
data_table.Trials to date: Sertraline 200 mg 6 weeks minimal response; mirtazapine 45 mg 6 weeks minimal response; aripiprazole ceased for akathisia at day 10.
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 128 mmol/L, urea 9.6, creatinine 92, albumin 28 g/L.
data_table.Cardiac: No pacemaker, no recent stroke, ECG sinus rhythm, QTc 440 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Continue current pharmacotherapy for a further 4 to 6 weeks to allow full response
Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (phenelzine) after a two-week washout
Add lithium augmentation to mirtazapine targeting a level of 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L
Add nortriptyline to mirtazapine as a combination antidepressant strategy
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy as the treatment of choice in this presentation

subtopic_detail: Highest-risk demographic
stem:
A 74-year-old man attends his GP two weeks after his wife of 48 years died. He lives alone in the family home, is retired, and has adult children interstate. He has hypertension, hearing loss, chronic back pain and a background of harmful alcohol use with 40 g of alcohol per day. He states his mood is "about what you'd expect" and denies suicidal ideation on direct questioning.

During the consultation you notice he has lost 3 kg since his last visit, has cancelled his upcoming knee surgery consultation and mentions in passing that he has given his fishing gear to his son "because I don't need it any more". His PHQ-9 is 14 with item 9 (thoughts of being better off dead) answered as "nearly every day". He has a licensed firearm at home.

data_table.Risk factors: Male, 74, recent bereavement, socially isolated, harmful alcohol use, chronic pain, hearing loss, firearm at home, giving away possessions, PHQ-9 item 9 positive daily.
data_table.Physical: Weight loss 3 kg since prior visit, cancelled elective surgery.
data_table.Denial: Denies active suicidal ideation on direct questioning.

lead_in: Which single statement about his suicide risk is correct?

options.text: Older men have the lowest completed suicide rate of any Australian age-sex group
Direct denial of suicidal ideation reliably excludes suicide risk in the elderly
Older Australian men have the highest completed suicide rate and this patient warrants urgent psychiatric input
Attempt-to-completion ratio in older men is similar to that of adolescent females
A firearm at home does not modify suicide risk in an older man because access does not equate to use

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal over 65
stem:
A 71-year-old man is admitted with a fractured neck of femur after a mechanical fall at home. On day 2 post-op he becomes tremulous, sweating, and mildly confused. His wife discloses that he has consumed a bottle of red wine each evening for the last 20 years and has not had a drink since admission 40 hours ago. His CIWA-Ar score is 14. He has hypertension on amlodipine, mild CKD (eGFR 54 mL/min/1.73 m2), and no cirrhosis on prior imaging.

He is haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and his post-operative pain is well controlled on paracetamol and low-dose oxycodone. Bloods show normal LFTs, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.9, glucose 6.0 mmol/L. He has no history of complicated withdrawal or seizures. The intern asks about the appropriate benzodiazepine choice given his age and renal function.

data_table.Withdrawal: CIWA-Ar 14 (tremor, sweating, mild confusion) at 40 h post last drink.
data_table.Bloods: LFTs within normal limits, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.9, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, eGFR 54 mL/min/1.73 m2.
data_table.History: Bottle of wine daily for 20 years, no prior seizures or DTs, no cirrhosis on prior imaging.

lead_in: Which benzodiazepine and dosing approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Diazepam 20 mg every hour by symptom-triggered dosing until CIWA-Ar below 10
Phenobarbital 130 mg intramuscularly as first-line treatment for withdrawal
Chlordiazepoxide 50 mg four times daily for 5 days on a fixed schedule
Oxazepam 15 to 30 mg symptom-triggered on CIWA-Ar with regular review
Withhold benzodiazepines and manage with hydration and clonidine to avoid delirium risk

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine deprescribing
stem:
A 78-year-old woman has been on temazepam 20 mg at night for 12 years, first prescribed after her husband died. She lives alone, mobilises with a four-wheel walker and had a fall three weeks ago requiring six stitches to her forehead. Her cognitive assessment today is MoCA 25 out of 30. She tells you she "needs" the temazepam to sleep and has been reluctant to change it. She has no formal diagnosis of insomnia disorder and denies mood or anxiety symptoms today.

Her medications are perindopril 5 mg mane, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte and temazepam 20 mg nocte. Her renal function is normal, LFTs are within normal limits and she has no known contraindication to sleep hygiene measures or short-term CBT-I. She has attended one bereavement counselling session in the past.

data_table.History: Temazepam 20 mg nocte for 12 years, recent fall with stitches, lives alone, MoCA 25/30.
data_table.Screen: No current mood or anxiety diagnosis; sleep-hygiene measures not previously trialled.
data_table.Bloods: eGFR over 60, LFTs within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to deprescribing?

options.text: Cease temazepam abruptly at the next appointment to avoid further fall risk
Switch to zopiclone 7.5 mg at night as a safer alternative for chronic use
Continue temazepam indefinitely because 12 years of use makes deprescribing unsafe
Negotiate a gradual dose reduction of 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks with CBT-I
Add mirtazapine 30 mg at night to cover sleep and then cease temazepam within one week

subtopic_detail: Recognition and response
stem:
An 82-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 24 out of 30, retains capacity for financial and care decisions on formal assessment last month) attends the general practice with her son. He answers most of your questions on her behalf. She has come in for a repeat prescription and to "sort out the pension". You notice bruising in various stages of healing on her upper arms and a small circular burn on her forearm which she attributes to "being clumsy".

When you ask to see her alone, her son says "she gets confused, I need to stay". Her Medicare card and bank card are held by the son. She lives with him after selling her own home last year, with the proceeds transferred into his name to "help pay the bills". On direct questioning alone, she says she is "fine" but avoids eye contact and asks whether her son is going to be told what she says.

data_table.Cognitive status: MoCA 24/30, retains decision-making capacity on formal assessment 4 weeks ago.
data_table.Injuries: Bruising of upper arms in various stages of healing, small circular burn on forearm.
data_table.Financial: Sold own home in past year, proceeds transferred to son's name. Medicare and bank cards held by son.
data_table.Interaction: Son answers on her behalf, resists private interview.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Confront the son directly in the consultation about the injuries and financial concerns
Report to the police today as mandatory reporting of elder abuse applies in all Australian states
Refer directly to the public guardian for financial substitute decision-making today
Complete the repeat prescription and address her concerns at the next annual review
Interview her alone and, with her consent, contact the state elder abuse helpline

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic risk decision in vascular dementia with recent stroke
stem:
An 84-year-old man with vascular dementia (MMSE 16) is admitted from a residential aged care facility with escalating aggression: he has struck two staff and another resident in the last week, and non-pharmacological measures over four weeks (structured routine, one-to-one, redirection, tailored music) have failed. A full reversible-cause workup is negative. His MRI three months ago showed multiple bilateral small-vessel infarcts and one small right middle cerebral artery cortical infarct sustained six weeks ago from which he has largely recovered motor function.

He is on aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg and no antipsychotic. His current QTc is 460 ms. His son (substitute decision maker) asks for a plan. He has no history of Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies. He weighs 62 kg and eGFR is 55 mL/min/1.73 m2.

data_table.Behaviour: Aggression with harm to staff and resident, 4 weeks of failed non-pharmacological plan, reversible-cause workup negative.
data_table.Cerebrovascular: Multiple bilateral small-vessel infarcts; right MCA cortical infarct 6 weeks ago.
data_table.Cardiac/renal: QTc 460 ms, eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m2, weight 62 kg.
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily with informed consent covering stroke and mortality risk
Prescribe olanzapine 5 mg orally at night as the safest antipsychotic option given the recent stroke
Prescribe haloperidol 1 mg twice daily as a non-atypical option that carries no cerebrovascular signal
Prescribe diazepam 2 mg twice daily as an antipsychotic alternative to avoid cerebrovascular risk
Continue non-pharmacological measures for another 12 weeks without any medication change

subtopic_detail: EPDS interpretation and next step
stem:
A 31-year-old woman attends her general practice in suburban Adelaide for a 6-week postnatal check. Her first baby was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth at 40 weeks and is exclusively breastfed and growing well. The practice nurse has administered the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) in the waiting room and the total score is 15. On item 10 (self-harm) she scored 0.

She tells you the last three weeks have felt "grey", she cries most days, sleep is broken beyond what the baby demands, and she finds no pleasure in things that previously interested her. She denies suicidal or infanticidal ideas, has no psychotic features, and eats reasonably. Her partner is supportive and she has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder. Basic postnatal examination and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.History: 6 weeks postpartum, breastfeeding, no bipolar history, no psychosis, no suicidal/infanticidal ideas
data_table.Examination: Postnatal examination within normal limits; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that this represents normal baby blues resolving spontaneously and arrange telephone review with the practice nurse in 2 weeks
Repeat the EPDS in 2 weeks before making any diagnostic decision or committing to psychological or pharmacological management
Undertake structured clinical assessment for perinatal depression and commence psychological therapy, with sertraline added if moderate or worse
Refer urgently to the acute mental health team for same-day psychiatric review and consideration of inpatient admission to a mother-baby unit
Commence paroxetine 20 mg orally daily as first-line pharmacotherapy and continue breastfeeding without further specialist monitoring

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis - urgent disposition
stem:
A 28-year-old primipara is brought to a metropolitan emergency department 9 days postpartum by her mother. Her pregnancy and vaginal birth were uncomplicated. Over the last 48 hours she has slept less than 3 hours per night, become progressively agitated, and now insists that her baby's cry contains coded messages from her deceased grandmother telling her the baby must be "purified by water". She is fluctuating between elated and tearful within minutes.

She has a personal history of bipolar I disorder (last episode 4 years ago on lithium, ceased 8 months preconception with psychiatric agreement) and a maternal history of postpartum psychosis. On examination she is oriented but distractible with pressured speech; the baby is with her partner and appears well and feeding. Vital signs are within normal limits. Routine bloods including urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs, calcium, TSH, glucose and CRP are within normal limits and urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Timeline: Day 9 postpartum; 48 h agitation, insomnia, delusions, mood lability
data_table.Psychiatric history: Bipolar I, last episode 4 years ago; mother had postpartum psychosis
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, corrected Ca, TSH, glucose, CRP within normal limits; UDS negative
data_table.Infant: With partner, feeding, no injuries reported

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home on olanzapine 10 mg orally nightly, provide a written safety plan, and arrange acute community mental health team review the following morning
Admit as a psychiatric emergency (Mother-Baby Unit preferred where available), commence olanzapine, and reintroduce lithium after baseline bloods
Perform lumbar puncture and MRI brain to exclude autoimmune or viral encephalitis before initiating any psychiatric admission or antipsychotic therapy
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily, refer to community psychology for postnatal depression, and arrange partner-supervised follow-up in three days
Advise the partner and grandmother to supervise her at home for 24 hours, remove access to means, and represent immediately if symptoms worsen at all

subtopic_detail: Bipolar in pregnancy - lithium in the first trimester
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder that has been stable for 5 years on lithium modified-release 900 mg orally nightly (steady-state serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L) attends her GP at 6 weeks gestation after a positive home pregnancy test. Her last three episodes off lithium were severe manias, one requiring involuntary admission; two prior trials of valproate and lamotrigine each failed to prevent relapse within 4 months. She is otherwise well, plans to continue the pregnancy, and asks what to do about her medication.

She tells you she has read that lithium causes heart defects and wants to stop today. Renal function, thyroid function, and corrected calcium are within normal limits. Fetal ultrasound and dating are booked.

data_table.Psychiatric history: Bipolar I, stable 5 y on lithium; two prior alternative mood stabilisers ineffective
data_table.Current medication: Lithium MR 900 mg nocte, steady-state level 0.7 mmol/L
data_table.Investigations: UEC, TSH, corrected calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her lithium in the first trimester?

options.text: Continue lithium, arrange fetal cardiac ultrasound at 18-22 weeks, monitor serum lithium every 4 weeks with dose adjustment as pregnancy progresses
Stop lithium abruptly today because of the risk of Ebstein anomaly, switch to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily, and rely on obstetric monitoring alone
Cross-taper lithium to lamotrigine 200 mg orally daily over 4 weeks with weekly review and no additional fetal cardiac imaging beyond the routine anatomy scan
Continue lithium but empirically reduce the dose to 450 mg nocte to lower fetal exposure, without a maternal serum lithium level to guide the change
Stop lithium and rely on close psychiatric monitoring alone for the first trimester, restarting after 12 weeks only if she remains well and asymptomatic

subtopic_detail: Lithium in breastfeeding
stem:
A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is 3 weeks postpartum after a healthy term birth. She restarted lithium modified-release 900 mg nocte on day 2 postpartum on your advice and is currently well, with a maternal serum lithium of 0.7 mmol/L. Her infant is breastfeeding well, growing along the 50th percentile, and appears alert and hydrated.

Her partner has read online that lithium is "absolutely contraindicated" in breastfeeding and is anxious. She would strongly prefer to continue breastfeeding. The infant has no dysmorphism, no jitteriness, and no poor feeding; a paediatric review the previous day was unremarkable.

data_table.Maternal medication: Lithium MR 900 mg nocte; maternal serum Li 0.7 mmol/L
data_table.Infant: Term, 3 weeks old, feeding well, growing along 50th percentile, no jitteriness or lethargy
data_table.Family concern: Partner concerned about breastfeeding on lithium

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise she must stop breastfeeding immediately and switch to formula because lithium is absolutely contraindicated in lactation regardless of maternal preference
Continue breastfeeding but empirically reduce her maternal lithium dose to 450 mg nocte to reduce infant exposure and repeat maternal levels in a fortnight
Cross-taper her from lithium to olanzapine 15 mg nocte over 4 weeks so she can breastfeed safely, and cease all lithium once olanzapine is established
Continue breastfeeding with informed consent, monitor infant serum lithium, UEC, and TSH at 2-4 weeks, and educate parents on signs of infant toxicity
Recommend she express and discard breast milk for 4 hours after each lithium dose and then feed the infant to reduce peak lithium exposure through milk

subtopic_detail: SSRI selection in pregnancy
stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 7 weeks gestation attends her GP with an escalating major depressive episode. This is a planned first pregnancy. She has a 4-year history of recurrent moderate to severe depression previously stabilised on paroxetine 20 mg orally daily, which she stopped 3 months before conception on her own initiative. She now reports 3 weeks of low mood, early morning waking, poor appetite, and thoughts that life is "not worth it" without a specific plan. She is not psychotic and has no bipolar history. Basic bloods and thyroid function are within normal limits.

She is willing to restart medication but has read that antidepressants "cause heart defects" in the first trimester and asks what is safest.

data_table.History: Recurrent MDD, 4 y; stopped paroxetine 3 months preconception
data_table.Current episode: 3 weeks moderate-severe depression, passive suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart paroxetine 20 mg orally daily because she previously responded to it, and refer for structured psychological therapy in parallel over 6 weeks
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily and refer for structured psychological therapy such as CBT or interpersonal therapy
Withhold pharmacotherapy for the first trimester and reassess mood, appetite, and suicidal ideation at 13 weeks with a repeat EPDS at that visit
Commence venlafaxine 75 mg extended release orally daily as first-line perinatal antidepressant therapy with a plan to titrate up in 2 weeks if needed
Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy as the safest treatment in pregnancy given her passive suicidal ideation and prior antidepressant responsiveness

subtopic_detail: ECT in pregnancy - severe depression with suicidality
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 24 weeks gestation is admitted involuntarily under the Mental Health Act to a tertiary maternal mental health unit with severe depression. She has psychomotor retardation, has stopped eating and drinking for the past 3 days requiring intravenous fluids, believes her fetus "is already dead" despite normal cardiotocograph tracings, and has begun to endorse a specific plan of self-strangulation. Adequate trials of sertraline (200 mg) and mirtazapine (45 mg) for 6 and 8 weeks respectively during this pregnancy have failed. Obstetric assessment shows a well fetus of appropriate size for gestational age. Bloods including urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs and TSH are within normal limits.

data_table.Presentation: Severe MDD with psychotic features, active suicidal plan, food refusal 3 days
data_table.Prior treatment: Sertraline 200 mg 6 wks; mirtazapine 45 mg 8 wks - both ineffective
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Add olanzapine 10 mg orally nightly to her current sertraline and mirtazapine, continue involuntary care, and reassess mood, suicidality, and oral intake in 4 weeks
Add lithium 750 mg nocte as augmentation, continue current antidepressants at maximum tolerated doses, and reassess her mood and suicidality over the next 2 weeks
Proceed with electroconvulsive therapy after joint obstetric-anaesthetic assessment, with left lateral tilt, airway protection, and pre- and post-treatment fetal monitoring
Commence intranasal esketamine 84 mg twice weekly as a rapid-acting antidepressant, continue current antidepressants, and monitor blood pressure after each dose
Defer any definitive treatment change until after delivery, maintain her current sertraline and mirtazapine regimen, and continue one-to-one nursing observation

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management in ED
stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police under mental health apprehension powers after 5 days of progressively pressured speech, minimal sleep, spending $12 000 on cryptocurrency, and grandiose delusions of being a "chosen prophet". He has a known diagnosis of bipolar I disorder and admits to stopping his lithium 3 weeks ago. He is not on any other regular medication.

He is oriented but distractible with flight of ideas and paces the interview room. He denies suicidal or homicidal ideation and has no active plan of harm. He accepts oral medication. Vital signs: pulse 108 bpm, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 C. Urea, electrolytes, creatinine, LFTs, TSH, and urine drug screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Presentation: 5 days manic symptoms; pressured speech, grandiose delusions, no suicidal or homicidal intent
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, TSH, UDS within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Recommence lithium modified release 750 mg orally nocte as monotherapy, offer oral lorazepam 1 mg for sleep, and reassess mania severity clinically in 48 hours
Give a single intramuscular droperidol 10 mg immediately for tranquillisation, physically restrain until sedated, and admit to a psychiatric intensive care unit
Commence sodium valproate 1000 mg orally daily as monotherapy and discharge with community mental health follow-up in 3 days, with a partner-supervised safety plan
Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg or quetiapine 400 mg, reintroduce lithium once renal function is confirmed, and offer oral lorazepam 1-2 mg for agitation
Commence carbamazepine 400 mg orally twice daily with diazepam 10 mg orally three times daily and discharge with community psychiatric follow-up in one week

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus NMS versus anticholinergic
stem:
A 42-year-old man presents to a regional emergency department 6 hours after being started on tramadol 50 mg orally four times daily by his GP for acute back pain. His regular medications include venlafaxine 150 mg extended release daily (for depression, stable 2 years) and selegiline that was recently prescribed by a neurologist. He is agitated, sweating profusely, and complaining of jaw clenching.

On examination he is diaphoretic, has spontaneous bilateral lower limb clonus on ankle dorsiflexion (right greater than left), brisk reflexes throughout, hyperactive bowel sounds, and dilated but reactive pupils. Vital signs: pulse 128 bpm, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.2 C. He is oriented but restless.

data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, spontaneous lower limb clonus R>L, hyperreflexia, hyperactive bowel sounds, dilated reactive pupils, jaw clenching
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine 150 mg XR, selegiline (recent), tramadol 50 mg qid (started 6 h ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, stop the offending antipsychotic, provide aggressive cooling, and admit to intensive care for supportive care
Anticholinergic toxicity; give IV physostigmine 1 mg with cardiac monitoring, provide aggressive cooling and IV fluids, and admit for continued observation overnight
Sympathomimetic toxicity from occult stimulant use; obtain a urine drug screen, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation, and manage supportively with cooling and fluids
Panic attack with concurrent fever from a viral illness; give oral lorazepam 1 mg, provide paracetamol for the fever, reassess in an hour, and discharge if settled
Serotonin syndrome; cease all serotonergic agents, provide aggressive cooling and IV fluids, give benzodiazepines for agitation, consider cyproheptadine if severe

subtopic_detail: Rapid tranquillisation choice in ED
stem: A 38-year-old man with a known diagnosis of schizophrenia is brought to a large metropolitan emergency department by police under mental health apprehension powers after threatening staff at a supported accommodation service. In the ED he is pacing, shouting at unseen figures, refusing to speak with staff, and has just struck a chair against the wall. Verbal de-escalation by a psychiatric nurse and a security officer for 10 minutes has been unsuccessful, and he refuses all oral medication. His weight is estimated at 90 kg, he has no known allergies, and there is no clear history of QT prolongation. Point-of-care ECG is not immediately available. He has not taken alcohol or benzodiazepines in the past 24 hours per accompanying support worker.

data_table.Presentation: Acute severe behavioural disturbance, active aggression, refusing oral medication
data_table.Relevant history: Schizophrenia, no known QT prolongation, no recent alcohol or benzodiazepine

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg, with strict avoidance of concurrent parenteral benzodiazepines and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with intramuscular promethazine 50 mg, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and a baseline 12-lead ECG once feasible
Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg as monotherapy, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and airway equipment ready at the bedside for the next 2 hours
Physical restraint alone until behaviour settles, with continuous nursing observation and reassessment for pharmacological therapy after 30 minutes if not settled
Oral quetiapine 200 mg with continuous observation on a secure ward, and a further dose in 30 minutes if he remains agitated and continues to accept oral therapy

subtopic: Suicide risk and Mental Health Act
subtopic_detail: Severe depression with active suicidality
stem:
A 52-year-old man is brought to a NSW emergency department by his sister after she found a suicide note on his kitchen table and a coiled rope in his shed. He has an 18-month history of severe major depressive disorder that has not responded to adequate trials of sertraline 200 mg then venlafaxine 300 mg. In interview he is guarded, describes his suicide plan in detail, states he still intends to act if discharged, and refuses admission because he believes he "deserves" to die.
