He has no known psychiatric admission history and has capacity to understand the information you provide, but his depressive beliefs prevent him from choosing consistent with survival. He has no comorbid substance use and vital signs, basic bloods, and ECG are within normal limits.

data_table.Presentation: 18 months severe MDD, current plan and intent, refusal of voluntary admission
data_table.Prior treatment: Sertraline 200 mg, venlafaxine 300 mg - both ineffective
data_table.Assessment: Guarded, understands information, cognitive distortions dominate decision
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits; ECG within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Discharge with an urgent GP appointment in 24 hours, a written safety plan, and a follow-up phone call from the community mental health team the following day
Admit involuntarily under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007, arrange expedited psychiatric review for ECT consideration, and remove access to means
Ask his sister to remove all sharps and the rope from home, provide constant one-to-one supervision at home for 72 hours, and represent immediately if any change
Commence lithium augmentation 500 mg orally nocte, discharge with community mental health follow-up in 5 days, and a written safety plan with removal of means
Because he has capacity, respect his refusal of admission, provide a Wellness Recovery Action Plan, and arrange community mental health follow-up in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: ED assessment sequence after intoxicated self-poisoning
stem:
A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 90 minutes after ingesting 30 tablets of quetiapine 100 mg and drinking about 750 mL of wine following an argument with her partner. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, tearful, and asking to be discharged so she can go home. Vital signs: pulse 108 bpm, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 C. Fingerstick glucose is 5.6 mmol/L, blood alcohol is 0.18 g/100 mL, and ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QTc 468 ms.

The on-call psychiatry registrar has been paged and asks whether she can be assessed for discharge planning now, as the department is very busy.

data_table.Ingestion: Quetiapine 30 x 100 mg tablets + ~750 mL wine, 90 min ago
data_table.Investigations: BSL 5.6 mmol/L, blood alcohol 0.18 g/100 mL, ECG sinus tachy QTc 468 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit to a monitored bed, provide cardiorespiratory monitoring and serial ECGs, and defer formal psychiatric risk assessment until she is medically cleared and clinically sober
Allow the psychiatry registrar to complete the mental state examination and structured risk assessment now to expedite disposition and free up the emergency department bed
Discharge with her partner because she is rousable and asking to leave, with a general practice appointment in 48 hours and a safety plan given to her partner
Administer oral activated charcoal 50 g now to reduce quetiapine absorption, obtain airway protection with intubation if necessary, and repeat ECG in 2 hours
Apply an involuntary treatment order under the Mental Health Act to compel psychiatric admission today, without further medical work-up or observation of sobriety

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge and ECT if refractory
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of bipolar I disorder is brought to the emergency department by her family after 4 days of progressive withdrawal, mutism, and refusal of food and fluids. On examination she stares fixedly, does not respond to questions, holds her left arm in an awkward flexed position for several minutes when placed there by the examiner, and echoes fragments of the examiner's speech when she does speak. Her Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 14. Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 C. Creatine kinase is 380 U/L (normal upper limit 200). Bloods, urine drug screen, TSH and CT brain are within normal limits.

The on-call psychiatry registrar administers 2 mg IV lorazepam under monitoring. Within 20 minutes she engages briefly, drinks a small volume of water, but returns to mutism after 90 minutes.

data_table.Presentation: 4 days progressive catatonic features (mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, echolalia); BFCRS 14
data_table.Investigations: CK 380 U/L; FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, UDS, CT brain within normal limits
data_table.Response to 2 mg IV lorazepam: Brief 20-min engagement then mutism returns at 90 min

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg to treat presumed underlying psychotic disorder, continue supportive care, and reassess her Bush-Francis score in 24 hours
Discharge her from the emergency department with community psychiatric follow-up in 48 hours, encouragement of oral intake at home, and family observation overnight
Commence scheduled lorazepam 2 mg orally or IM three times daily, ensure hydration and DVT prophylaxis, and refer for ECT if catatonia persists over 48-72 hours
Commence dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome, admit to intensive care for cooling and monitoring, and stop all psychotropic agents
Give a further single dose of lorazepam 4 mg IV as an escalated challenge, observe her for 24 hours in the emergency short-stay unit, and reassess before further action

subtopic_detail: Baby blues versus postnatal depression
stem:
A 29-year-old primipara presents to her general practice on day 5 postpartum for a routine newborn check. She had a normal vaginal birth of a healthy term baby. She reports tearfulness that comes and goes over the past 3 days, mild irritability, difficulty sleeping when the baby is settled, and rapid mood swings but denies pervasive low mood or loss of interest. She has no suicidal or infanticidal thoughts, no psychotic features, and no history of psychiatric illness. She is breastfeeding and the baby is feeding and growing well. EPDS today is 9.

On examination she looks tired but engaged, cries briefly when describing the birth, then laughs when discussing the baby. Postnatal observations and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Symptoms: Transient tearfulness, mood lability, no anhedonia, no suicidal or psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order urgent thyroid antibodies, morning cortisol, and repeat TSH given that the most likely cause of this presentation is early postpartum thyroiditis and adrenal insufficiency
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily now to prevent progression to postnatal depression, continue breastfeeding, and arrange community midwife review in 1 week
Refer urgently for perinatal psychiatry review today with a follow-up EPDS in 1 week and a plan to consider inpatient admission if any symptoms worsen or persist
Recommend she stop breastfeeding to improve her sleep and mood, transition to formula feeding gradually over 1 week, and arrange lactation consultant support
Reassure her that these symptoms are consistent with baby blues, provide psychoeducation and family support, and arrange EPDS repeat in 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: Neonatal adaptation syndrome after third-trimester SSRI
stem:
A 32-year-old woman was maintained on sertraline 100 mg orally daily through pregnancy for recurrent major depressive disorder. Her baby was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth and Apgars were 8 and 9. At 6 hours of age the baby, who is otherwise term and vigorous, has developed mild tremor, hypertonia, jitteriness with handling, feeding difficulties, and is grunting intermittently. Axillary temperature is 36.9 C, heart rate 168, respiratory rate 68, and SpO2 96% in air. Bedside glucose is 3.4 mmol/L. There is no maternal history of chorioamnionitis or Group B streptococcus colonisation and there was no prolonged rupture of membranes.

The midwifery team asks whether sertraline should be stopped in the mother and formula introduced.

data_table.Infant at 6 h: Jitteriness, hypertonia, tremor, tachypnoea 68, feeding difficulty; T 36.9, HR 168, SpO2 96% RA, BSL 3.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit the baby to a neonatal intensive care unit for phenobarbital treatment of presumed neonatal drug withdrawal and monitor the neonatal abstinence score every 4 hours
Full septic workup including blood culture, lumbar puncture, urine culture, and empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending cultures at 48 hours
Stop maternal sertraline immediately, switch the infant to exclusive formula feeding, and monitor maternal mood daily with EPDS by the community midwife
Neonatal observation on the postnatal ward with regular vital signs, feeding support, and glucose monitoring; continue maternal sertraline and encourage breastfeeding
Order an urgent echocardiogram to exclude persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, obtain a pre- and post-ductal SpO2, and consider transfer to a tertiary neonatal unit

subtopic_detail: Antenatal SSRI - continue versus stop before delivery
stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation attends her antenatal clinic. She has been on sertraline 100 mg orally daily for recurrent major depressive disorder for 3 years and remained well throughout this pregnancy. She had a severe postpartum relapse after her first pregnancy 4 years ago when she was persuaded to stop her SSRI at 36 weeks. Fetal growth, dopplers, and CTG today are reassuring. Her partner and community midwife are supportive and a joint plan for postpartum care is in place.

Her obstetrician has asked whether her sertraline should be tapered before delivery to "reduce neonatal withdrawal".

data_table.History: Recurrent MDD, on sertraline 100 mg 3 y, well through pregnancy
data_table.Obstetric: 34 weeks; growth, dopplers, CTG reassuring; postpartum relapse in first pregnancy after 36-week SSRI cessation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her sertraline?

options.text: Recommend an elective caesarean at 38 weeks to control the timing of SSRI exposure at delivery and to allow the neonate to be admitted directly for observation
Taper sertraline by 25 mg per week to zero by 38 weeks gestation to reduce neonatal adaptation syndrome, and restart sertraline in the immediate postpartum period
Switch her from sertraline to fluoxetine 20 mg daily, as fluoxetine has a longer half-life and a smoother neonatal course than sertraline in the postpartum period
Reduce her sertraline dose to 50 mg daily until delivery, then increase again postpartum once the infant is established with feeding and is being monitored by paediatrics
Continue sertraline 100 mg daily through delivery and the postpartum period, plan neonatal observation for adaptation, and maintain postnatal mental health follow-up

subtopic_detail: Prophylaxis after delivery in bipolar I disorder
stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida with bipolar I disorder is seen at 36 weeks in a joint perinatal psychiatry and obstetric clinic. She has been well through pregnancy off medication after psychiatric advice to stop lithium preconception. Her most recent manic episode was 5 years ago and required inpatient care. Her mother had a postpartum psychosis. Fetal growth and welfare are reassuring and vaginal birth is planned.

She strongly wishes to breastfeed. She and her partner are engaged with the perinatal team, and the paediatric team is willing to co-manage.

data_table.Psychiatric history: Bipolar I; last mania 5 y ago; mother had postpartum psychosis
data_table.Gestation: 36 weeks; fetal welfare reassuring; vaginal birth planned

lead_in: What is the most appropriate postpartum plan to reduce her risk of postpartum psychosis and mania?

options.text: Start sertraline 100 mg orally daily as prophylaxis against postnatal depression, and reassess her mood, sleep, and function fortnightly for the first 3 months postpartum
Watchful waiting alone with weekly EPDS monitoring by the community midwife for the first 3 months, and rapid access to acute psychiatry review if any symptoms develop
Advise her to formula-feed and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily immediately postpartum as the mood stabiliser of choice for postpartum bipolar prophylaxis
Introduce prophylactic lithium immediately after delivery with baseline UEC and TSH, lithium level day 5, and paediatric infant monitoring alongside supported breastfeeding
Defer any pharmacological intervention until symptoms of mania or psychosis emerge, then admit for acute treatment with a full mood stabiliser and antipsychotic regimen

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment - DBT vs medication
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with a clearly documented diagnosis of borderline personality disorder sees you as her general practitioner under a Mental Health Treatment Plan. Over the past year she has had four brief emergency presentations after superficial cutting following relationship arguments, and she describes chronic emptiness and rapid swings between idealising and devaluing her ex-partner and her sister.

She has completed adequate trials of sertraline and then escitalopram over 14 months with no lasting benefit. Her K-10 today is 28. She has no current major depressive episode by full DSM-5-TR criteria, no psychotic features, is not pregnant, drinks under 3 standard drinks per week, and has stopped occasional cannabis. She asks what treatment specifically targets the pattern of self-harm and relationship instability rather than just her mood.

data_table.Examination: Multiple healed and recent superficial linear scars to bilateral forearms. MSE reactive affect, no perceptual disturbance, no current suicidal intent.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 28. FBC, EUC, LFT, TSH within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management for the core disorder?

options.text: Commence low-dose quetiapine 100 mg nocte for chronic affective instability
Commence lamotrigine titrated to 200 mg daily for affective mood swings
Refer to a structured group-based dialectical behaviour therapy program
Trial a third SSRI at maximum dose over 12 weeks with regular monitoring
Arrange voluntary inpatient admission for six weeks of behavioural work

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic pharmacotherapy - benzodiazepine avoidance
stem:
A 32-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is in an established DBT program in her 4th month. She presents to your general practice for a routine review requesting a script for regular diazepam 5 mg three times daily, saying it is the only thing that stops her cutting when she is very distressed. She has a prior history of two mixed diazepam and alcohol overdoses in her early twenties and a documented previous alprazolam dependence that took 9 months to taper. She has no current comorbid anxiety disorder meeting DSM-5-TR criteria and no current major depressive episode.

She has a written DBT crisis plan she can produce on her phone and lists her DBT therapist and after-hours mental health line as contacts. She tells you that other doctors have prescribed short PRN diazepam courses in the past and that it always helped her in the moment.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, tearful when discussing recent partner conflict, no acute intoxication, no fresh injuries.
data_table.Investigations: Nil today. Prior CBC, EUC, LFTs within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg PRN twice daily for two weeks then review at the practice
Switch to oxazepam 15 mg three times daily as a lower-abuse-potential alternative
Commence low-dose quetiapine 25 mg nocte as ongoing symptomatic anxiolysis nightly
Commence pregabalin 75 mg twice daily as a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic option
Decline regular benzodiazepines and reinforce use of the existing DBT crisis plan

subtopic_detail: BPD vs bipolar II differentiation
stem:
A 24-year-old university student is referred by her general practitioner with a query of bipolar II disorder after her family raised the question. She describes rapid mood shifts every few hours which she can date to specific interactions with her partner and mother, chronic emptiness since her mid-teens, three low-lethality overdoses in the past 18 months following relationship arguments, and superficial cutting since age 14.

On detailed enquiry she has never had a period of persistently elevated or irritable mood lasting four consecutive days with a change in functioning. She has never had a sustained decreased need for sleep independent of her distress, and her energy tracks her interpersonal situation. Family history is negative for bipolar disorder; her father had recurrent depressive episodes. She has not used stimulants and her thyroid function and urine drug screen are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, no pressured speech, no flight of ideas, no grandiosity elicited today. Multiple healed and recent linear forearm scars.
data_table.Investigations: TSH within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative. K-10 30. Mood chart over the last month shows swings occurring within a single day and mapping onto interpersonal events.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly supports borderline personality disorder over bipolar II disorder?

options.text: Recurrent low-lethality self-harm and overdose behaviour since her mid-adolescence years
Mood shifts lasting hours and clearly tied to interpersonal events on a prospective chart
A negative family history for bipolar disorder in her first-degree biological relatives
Chronic subjective feelings of emptiness across the past several years of her life
Onset of the pattern of instability in mid-teens rather than in early adulthood

subtopic_detail: ASPD vs BPD differentiation
stem:
A 28-year-old man is seen in your community mental health clinic after release from a 4-month custodial sentence for aggravated assault. He describes a pattern from age 12 of animal cruelty, truancy, fire-setting and property theft. He has been dismissed from four jobs for stealing, has three prior convictions for assault, and reports no remorse for hospitalising a stranger in his most recent offence, describing the man as an idiot who deserved it. He denies any past self-harm, denies chronic emptiness, and denies fear of abandonment. His relationships have been brief and instrumental; he says he ends them when the woman becomes boring.

He is not currently depressed, drinks 6 standard drinks nightly, uses methamphetamine 2 to 3 times per month, and is not psychotic today. He describes his aggression as goal-directed and premeditated when he feels disrespected, rather than as a distressed response to relationship crises.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, callous affect, no evidence of acute intoxication.
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for amphetamines. FBC, EUC, LFTs within normal limits.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours antisocial rather than borderline personality disorder?

options.text: History of three separate convictions for assault leading to a recent custodial sentence
Comorbid daily heavy alcohol use and intermittent methamphetamine use twice per month
Premeditated instrumental aggression with absent remorse plus a childhood conduct pattern
Brief unstable relationships that he ends when the partner becomes uninteresting to him
Absence of prior mental health service contact or documented psychiatric diagnosis in file

subtopic_detail: Schizotypal vs schizophrenia discrimination
stem:
A 29-year-old man is referred by his general practitioner because his family are concerned that he might have schizophrenia. He describes a longstanding conviction since his late teens that he can sense the intentions of people three floors up in his apartment block, and he interprets flickers in the lights as messages meant specifically for him. He has magical thinking about numbers and superstitions that he has held consistently for a decade. He has very few friends, is anxious in social settings, and speaks in a slightly odd tangential manner.

He has no clear fixed false belief held with conviction against contrary evidence, no true auditory hallucinations, no clear thought disorder on formal examination, and no functional decline over the past decade - he has held the same warehouse job for 9 years. He is not depressed, uses no substances, and has never had a discrete psychotic episode.

data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly guarded, tangential speech but redirectable. No clear delusions or hallucinations. Affect constricted. No cognitive impairment on brief testing.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, EUC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary diagnosis for this presentation?

options.text: Schizophrenia with predominantly negative and disorganised symptoms
Delusional disorder of the referential subtype
Schizotypal personality disorder with ego-syntonic magical beliefs
Schizoid personality disorder with preferred long-term solitude
Attenuated psychosis syndrome under the DSM-5 conditions

subtopic_detail: Avoidant PD vs social anxiety disorder
stem:
A 34-year-old man presents to your general practice reporting that he has never had a romantic partner and has no close friends outside his brother. He tells you he desperately wants closeness but has always felt inferior, socially inept, and unappealing, and he avoids new work opportunities because he expects to be criticised or rejected. His avoidance is not limited to performance or scrutiny situations - he also avoids one-to-one meetings, small dinners, and neighbourly conversations that would not involve any observable performance. He describes the pattern as present since childhood and stable.

He does not have physiological anxiety spikes when he is not in feared situations. He is not currently depressed, does not use alcohol to cope, and has held a back-office data role for 8 years. His self-view of being fundamentally inadequate persists even when he receives clearly positive feedback at work.

data_table.Examination: Alert, guarded, poor eye contact, self-deprecating speech content. No thought disorder. Affect constricted.
data_table.Investigations: Nil today. TSH within normal limits at last review.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary diagnosis in this case?

options.text: Social anxiety disorder of the generalised performance subtype
Persistent depressive disorder with prominent interpersonal features
Schizoid personality disorder with detached interpersonal preference
Avoidant personality disorder of the pervasive interpersonal type
Autism spectrum disorder recognised for the first time in adulthood

subtopic_detail: Vulnerable subtype recognition
stem:
A 41-year-old lawyer is referred by his general practitioner with 6 months of low mood after being passed over for promotion. He is chronically preoccupied with a sense that his talents are not recognised, that his colleagues are inferior yet somehow being favoured, and that he deserves special treatment because of his exceptional intellect. He is exquisitely sensitive to any perceived slight and describes recurrent hypochondriacal worries about his health that have prompted three specialist referrals in the past year.

Unlike an overtly grandiose presentation he is not boastful in the room, appears shy and self-effacing, and complains at length of shame and inadequacy. His relationships are marked by intense envy of successful peers, subtle contempt for those he sees as beneath him, and an inability to sustain the initial idealisation he shows new therapists once they fail to provide the mirroring he expects.

data_table.Examination: Alert, quietly spoken, shy manner, easily wounded by any exploration of his professional setbacks, subtle contempt expressed toward colleagues.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 24. TSH within normal limits. Nil other relevant investigations.

lead_in: Which construct best captures this presentation on further formulation?

options.text: Grandiose subtype of narcissistic personality disorder with overt entitlement in room
Major depressive disorder with atypical features and interpersonal rejection sensitivity
Illness anxiety disorder driven by preoccupation with health across multiple domains
Vulnerable subtype of narcissistic personality disorder with covert grandiosity and shame
Persistent depressive disorder with sustained low mood over the past several years

subtopic_detail: Team recognition and response
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar covering a mixed medical ward. A 25-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is admitted with cellulitis. Over 48 hours the nursing team has become polarised: two nurses describe her as manipulative, demanding, and undeserving of a bed, while one senior nurse and a junior doctor describe her as vulnerable, misunderstood, and mistreated by their colleagues. She has told the sympathetic staff that the other nurses are cruel, and told the critical staff that the sympathetic ones are the only ones who really care.

The medical team ask you to see her because they are worried she is escalating and want your advice about how to manage the ward-level disagreement, not just the patient. She is medically stable, not currently suicidal, and is engaged with her outpatient DBT program. There is no acute risk needing immediate transfer.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, minimises her distress with the critical nurses and amplifies it with the sympathetic staff. No psychotic features.
data_table.Investigations: Nil relevant to the request. Cellulitis parameters improving on IV antibiotics.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intervention for the ward-level dynamic?

options.text: Move her to a single room and restrict her contact to only the sympathetic nurses on each shift
Commence a short course of low-dose olanzapine 5 mg nocte to reduce her interpersonal reactivity
Discharge her home once medically fit and refer for outpatient behavioural therapy follow up
Convene a brief team meeting to name the splitting dynamic and agree a consistent unified response
Ask her outpatient DBT therapist to attend the ward and provide crisis skills coaching each day

subtopic_detail: MBT indication and modality fit
stem:
A 30-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is being considered for structured therapy after a year of unsuccessful supportive counselling. Her main difficulties are misreading other people's intentions, jumping to conclusions that partners and colleagues are contemptuous of her when they are not, and losing her capacity to think clearly about her own mental states when she is upset. She has had two previous suicide attempts by paracetamol overdose 3 and 5 years ago but no episodes in the past year.

She has struggled with the highly structured behavioural skills format of a previous partial DBT trial and dropped out at week 6, saying the skills felt mechanical. She is articulate, insightful when calm, and interested in understanding why she gets into these misreading spirals. She is not psychotic, is not currently misusing substances, and has stable social security housing.

data_table.Examination: Alert, thoughtful when calm, becomes anxious and prematurely certain when discussing recent interpersonal ruptures.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 26. FBC, EUC, LFT within normal limits.

lead_in: Which structured psychotherapy is the best fit for this specific presentation?

options.text: A second full trial of dialectical behaviour therapy in the same group format
Mentalisation-based therapy focused on restoring reflective capacity under arousal
Cognitive behavioural therapy for depression using the standard weekly format
Interpersonal psychotherapy for depression focused on identified role conflicts
Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing for previously identified past trauma

subtopic_detail: Safety planning and brief-contact intervention
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 23-year-old woman with a documented diagnosis of borderline personality disorder self-presents at 02:00 having taken 6 paracetamol tablets after a fight with her partner. Her paracetamol level at 4 hours is below the treatment line, LFTs and INR are normal, and she is medically fit for discharge. She is engaged with an established outpatient DBT program with a dedicated therapist. She has had two similar low-lethality presentations in the past 3 months, both discharged after brief safety planning.

She is now calm, describes the argument as resolved, does not want admission, and is asking to go home to sleep. Her mother is on the way to collect her and she has agreed to attend her regular DBT session in 2 days. There is no acute suicidal intent and no plan disclosed on repeat questioning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/70, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent on air, temperature 36.7.
data_table.Examination: Alert, calm, oriented, reactive affect, no fresh injury, no intoxication.
data_table.Investigations: Serum paracetamol below Rumack-Matthew treatment line at 4 hours. ALT 22, INR 1.0. Ethanol not detected.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition from the emergency department tonight?

options.text: Admit to the acute psychiatric ward for a planned 5-day observation and stabilisation stay
Admit under the state Mental Health Act for involuntary assessment and psychiatric observation
Commence low-dose quetiapine 50 mg PRN from the emergency department to manage her future crises
Refer for a new intake referral to a different DBT program given her presentations keep occurring
Discharge home with a written safety plan and early communication with her established DBT therapist

subtopic_detail: Multidisciplinary planning and attachment
stem:
A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks gestation with a first pregnancy attends your general practice. She has a longstanding diagnosis of borderline personality disorder, is currently 8 months into a DBT program with good engagement and no self-harm in the last 5 months, and lives with a supportive partner. She has stopped an occasional cannabis habit and does not drink alcohol. Her last two K-10 scores were 18 and 16.

She is asking how to plan for the perinatal period. She reports specific anxiety about how she will manage her emotional reactivity around a newborn, and about whether her own experience of a chaotic childhood will affect her ability to attach to the baby. She is not currently taking psychotropic medication. She has a booked antenatal appointment at the local maternity hospital in 2 weeks.

data_table.Examination: Well, appropriate affect, 20 weeks fundus, fetal heart auscultated.
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal bloods within normal limits at booking. K-10 today 17.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional step to arrange at this visit?

options.text: Commence low-dose sertraline 50 mg daily as prophylaxis against a postpartum decompensation episode
Reduce her DBT contact during pregnancy to avoid overburdening her ahead of the birth event
Refer to a perinatal mental health service for coordinated care including infant mental health input
Advise against breastfeeding preemptively given her personality disorder diagnosis and reactivity
Recommend elective caesarean at 39 weeks to reduce anticipated emotional dysregulation during labour

subtopic_detail: RANZCP position on early diagnosis
stem:
A 16-year-old girl is brought to your child and adolescent mental health clinic by her mother after her fourth episode of superficial cutting in 8 months. Her mother reports 18 months of intense unstable relationships with peers, rapid shifts between idealising and devaluing friends, chronic emptiness, angry outbursts, and difficulty being alone. She has had two low-lethality overdoses in the past year following peer rejections. She has completed a full DSM-5-TR assessment which shows 6 of 9 borderline features present with a persistent pattern for more than 12 months and no active manic or psychotic features.

Her mother has read online that personality disorders should not be diagnosed in adolescence and is asking you to defer any diagnosis until she is 18. She wants to know what evidence-based structured therapy is available if her daughter meets criteria now, and whether waiting would be safer.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, multiple superficial healed and recent linear forearm scars.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 32. FBC, EUC, LFT, TSH within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the mother's question today?

options.text: Defer any personality disorder diagnosis until she turns 18 as the mother has explicitly requested today
Explain the diagnosis can be made in adolescence when full criteria are met and refer for adolescent DBT
Commence low-dose fluoxetine 20 mg daily for affective instability while waiting to reassess at age 18 years
Refer to a general community counselling service for supportive listening without any formal diagnosis attached
Diagnose emerging borderline traits only and avoid the formal disorder label until she becomes a legal adult

subtopic: Comorbid personality disorder and eating disorder
subtopic_detail: Treatment sequencing
stem:
A 22-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder and a 4-year history of bulimia nervosa is referred to your community mental health team. She currently has 6 to 8 binge-and-purge episodes per week, weight 58 kg, BMI 20.5, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), and bicarbonate 32 mmol/L (22 to 32). She has recurrent self-harm and two low-lethality overdoses in the past year. She is currently on a DBT waitlist with an expected 3 month wait, and has not yet started any eating disorder specific therapy. She is medically stable today with electrocardiogram showing QTc 440 ms and no U waves.

She is anxious about starting two therapies at once and asks what should be prioritised. She lives alone, has supportive family, and is engaged with her general practitioner. She is not pregnant, is not using illicit substances, and drinks under 2 standard drinks per week.

data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly anxious, weight 58 kg, BMI 20.5, no cardiovascular compromise, no parotid enlargement today.
data_table.Investigations: K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), HCO3 32 mmol/L (22 to 32), Na 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45 to 90), ECG QTc 440 ms, ferritin 45 micrograms/L (30 to 300).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment sequencing plan today?

options.text: Defer all specific therapy until she reaches the top of the DBT waitlist in approximately 3 months
Admit for a planned 6 week inpatient stay to address both comorbidities simultaneously as combined care
Correct hypokalaemia and commence eating disorder focused therapy now while continuing on the DBT waitlist
Commence fluoxetine 60 mg daily as sole monotherapy while she remains on the DBT waitlist as planned
Prioritise a formal MBT program first and address the eating disorder afterwards once she is stable

subtopic: Personality change due to medical condition
subtopic_detail: Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia
stem:
A 58-year-old previously reserved and conscientious accountant is brought to your clinic by his wife, who reports 14 months of progressive change. He has begun making inappropriate sexual comments to strangers, gambled the family savings on impulse, developed a rigid preference for sweet foods and finishes an entire block of chocolate daily, and shows no concern when told his behaviour has cost him his job. He has no history of any personality disorder and premorbid personality was universally described as thoughtful and restrained.

He scores 28 out of 30 on the MMSE and 84 out of 100 on the ACE-III with disproportionate loss on verbal fluency and social cognition subtests, but preserved episodic memory. There is no depression by history, no substance use, no thyroid or B12 deficiency, and no midbrain signs. MRI brain shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy.

data_table.Examination: Disinhibited in the room, laughs at his wife's tears, mild primitive reflexes present (grasp and palmomental). No focal motor deficit.
data_table.Investigations: TSH within normal limits. B12 340 pmol/L. MMSE 28 of 30. ACE-III 84 of 100 with reduced verbal fluency and social cognition subscales. MRI bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary diagnosis for this presentation?

options.text: New-onset antisocial personality disorder emerging in mid-life following stress
Late-onset bipolar disorder presenting with hypomanic disinhibition
Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia meeting consensus criteria
Alzheimer disease presenting atypically with early behavioural symptoms
Persistent depressive disorder producing cognitive and behavioural slowing

subtopic_detail: Declining construct and differential
stem:
A 35-year-old actor is referred by her general practitioner for a personality assessment. Since her early twenties she has been the centre of attention at every social gathering, dresses provocatively, uses dramatic and vague speech, is easily influenced by strong personalities, and considers her professional relationships as far closer than her colleagues do. She feels flat when she is not the focus of attention but does not describe emptiness. She has no history of self-harm, no suicide attempts, no chronic fears of abandonment as a core feature, no rapid shifts between idealising and devaluing individuals, and no impulsive substance use or overdose behaviour.

Her relationships have been shallow but not turbulent; two long-term partners describe her as attention-seeking rather than volatile. She is not currently depressed and is engaged in her acting career. She asks whether her long pattern amounts to a formal diagnosis.

data_table.Examination: Alert, theatrically presented, dramatic gestures, superficial rapport, no thought disorder.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 12. FBC, EUC, LFT within normal limits.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary personality disorder in this presentation?

options.text: Borderline personality disorder with subthreshold self-harm features
Narcissistic personality disorder of the grandiose exhibitionistic subtype
Histrionic personality disorder with sustained attention-seeking presentation
Persistent depressive disorder with associated interpersonal emptiness features
Bipolar II disorder with recurrent past hypomanic episodes and current euthymia

subtopic_detail: OCPD vs OCD discrimination
stem:
A 42-year-old accountant is referred by his general practitioner after his wife complained he is impossible to live with. He describes a lifelong preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism that interferes with completing tax returns because they are never quite good enough, excessive devotion to work at the expense of leisure and family, rigid morality, hoarding of worn-out items, reluctance to delegate at work because others cannot meet his standards, miserliness, and stubbornness. He experiences these traits as consistent with his values and does not want to change them.

He does not have unwanted intrusive thoughts that he tries to resist, and does not perform time-consuming rituals to neutralise anxiety. He is not depressed and does not use substances.

data_table.Examination: Alert, meticulously dressed, precise speech, no obvious rituals in the room.
data_table.Investigations: Nil relevant. K-10 14.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary diagnosis in this presentation?

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder with contamination-related intrusive obsessions
Generalised anxiety disorder with prominent perfectionistic worry across domains
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder with lifelong ego-syntonic perfectionism
Autism spectrum disorder recognised for the first time in adulthood
Hoarding disorder with prominent clutter compromising his living space at home

subtopic_detail: Acute-on-chronic thresholds and dialysis triggers
stem:
A 58-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for bipolar I disorder presents to ED after 48 hours of gastroenteritis. She reports coarse tremor, unsteady gait and confusion. Her GP started ramipril 5 mg daily three weeks ago for hypertension. She has taken her usual lithium dose each morning. The intern has already given 1 L normal saline over one hour. A 12-hour post-dose lithium level returns while you are reviewing her.

She is drowsy but rousable, coarse tremor in both hands, brisk reflexes and bilateral horizontal nystagmus. Speech is dysarthric.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 98% on air, temp 36.8.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, nystagmus, dysarthria.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 3.1 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 78), eGFR 32, sodium 142, potassium 4.4, urea 12.6.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold lithium, continue IV normal saline at 200 mL/h, and repeat a level in six hours before deciding on further escalation
Give a single dose of activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube and admit to a ward bed for six-hourly level and neurological observations
Urgent referral for extracorporeal treatment with haemodialysis, alongside IV fluids and cessation of lithium and ramipril, with HDU monitoring
Commence a forced alkaline diuresis with sodium bicarbonate infusion targeting a urinary pH above 7.5 to accelerate lithium clearance safely
Start intravenous diazepam infusion for the neurological features and admit for observation while awaiting spontaneous renal clearance of lithium

subtopic_detail: NSAID, ACEi and thiazide interactions in general practice
stem:
A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder stable on lithium 500 mg bd (last level 0.7 mmol/L four weeks ago) attends his GP with a two-week history of low back pain after moving house. He asks what over-the-counter or short-course prescription options are safe, given previous good response to ibuprofen. His BP today is 138/86 with normal renal function.

He drinks 1.5 L of water daily, takes no other medications, and has no history of peptic ulcer disease.

data_table.Examination: Paraspinal muscle spasm L4-L5, no red flags, neurologically intact.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 76 micromol/L, eGFR >90, sodium 140, potassium 4.2, lithium 0.7 mmol/L (four weeks ago).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate analgesic plan?

options.text: Recommend regular ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for two weeks with a check lithium level in one week and adjustment of dose thereafter as clinically indicated
Prescribe celecoxib 200 mg daily as a COX-2 selective agent that avoids the lithium interaction seen with non-selective NSAIDs in maintenance therapy
Recommend regular paracetamol with heat, gentle mobilisation and physiotherapy referral; avoid all NSAIDs while on lithium therapy, and review at one week
Add a low-dose thiazide diuretic to reduce lithium excretion and allow a lower lithium dose while treating incidental hypertension at the same visit
Prescribe a short course of oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for five days for anti-inflammatory effect while continuing his usual lithium regimen at home

subtopic_detail: Dose adjustment and monitoring frequency with declining eGFR
stem:
A 66-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium 750 mg nocte for 22 years, with excellent mood stability and no admissions in the past decade. Routine annual bloods show eGFR has fallen from 68 to 42 mL/min/1.73m^2 over 18 months. His last lithium level (four weeks ago) was 0.85 mmol/L. Urinalysis is bland, ACR normal, ultrasound shows no obstruction.

He has type 2 diabetes on metformin and takes perindopril 5 mg for hypertension.

data_table.Examination: No signs of lithium toxicity, no volume overload.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.85 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8 for maintenance), creatinine 148 (baseline 96), eGFR 42, HbA1c 51 mmol/mol, ACR 1.2 mg/mmol.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Continue current dose; recheck lithium level and renal function in 12 months in line with routine outpatient monitoring schedule for this patient
Reduce lithium dose targeting 0.4-0.6 mmol/L, increase to 3-monthly levels and 6-monthly renal function, and involve psychiatry, monitor closely
Cease lithium immediately and commence sodium valproate 500 mg bd as a renally safer mood stabiliser starting this evening as a same-day switch
Refer urgently to nephrology for consideration of renal biopsy before making any change to lithium therapy at this level of function
Switch perindopril to amlodipine on the basis that ACE inhibitors are contributing to falling eGFR and lithium can then be continued unchanged safely

subtopic_detail: ANC thresholds and haematology-directed management
stem:
A 36-year-old man on clozapine 400 mg nocte for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (18 months, stable) has a routine weekly FBC as part of the CPMS/ClopineCentral monitoring program. He is well, denies fever or infection, and has no other medication changes. The FBC returns while he is still in the clinic waiting room and the nurse escalates it to you.

He has no personal or family history of haematological disorders and does not identify as being of a background with a high prevalence of benign ethnic neutropenia.

data_table.Examination: Well, no oral ulcers, no lymphadenopathy, no signs of infection.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 3.1 x10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count (ANC) 1.2 x10^9/L, Hb 142 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L. Previous ANC 2.3 four weeks ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately, admit for reverse isolation and commence broad-spectrum antibiotics with G-CSF while awaiting haematology review
Continue clozapine unchanged and repeat FBC at the routine four-weekly interval since he is asymptomatic and there is no other red flag
Cease clozapine and switch to olanzapine 20 mg nocte as an equivalent-efficacy alternative pending haematology review of the neutropenia today
Continue clozapine, increase FBC monitoring to twice-weekly until ANC returns to green range (>=2.0), and educate the patient on infection red flags
Continue clozapine but reduce the dose to 200 mg nocte on the basis that neutropenia is a dose-dependent adverse effect that reverses with dose reduction

subtopic_detail: First 6-8 week troponin and CRP screening
stem:
A 24-year-old man was commenced on clozapine 21 days ago for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, titrated to 200 mg nocte. He presents with 48 hours of low-grade fever, mild dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain. He is otherwise stable and his mental state has improved on clozapine.

His routine baseline monitoring included ECG, echocardiogram, troponin and CRP, all normal. He has no personal or family history of cardiac disease and no recent viral illness in the household.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/64, RR 22, SpO2 96% on air, temp 37.9.
data_table.Examination: Mildly dyspnoeic, no murmur, no pericardial rub, chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 62 ng/L (upper reference 26), CRP 84 mg/L, ECG sinus tachycardia with non-specific T wave flattening, FBC normal, ANC 3.8.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine, admit for cardiology review including urgent echocardiogram, and do not rechallenge without specialist input, cardiology review
Continue clozapine at current dose, prescribe paracetamol for fever, and recheck troponin and CRP in 48 hours before making a management decision
Continue clozapine and start empirical oral doxycycline 100 mg bd for a presumed atypical respiratory infection given the fever, dyspnoea and tachycardia
Reduce clozapine to 100 mg nocte, continue slow titration schedule at halved rate, and repeat troponin weekly while remaining as an outpatient in community
Continue clozapine and refer for outpatient cardiac MRI within four weeks to confirm myocarditis before making any changes to psychiatric medication

subtopic_detail: Highest-mortality side effect and aperient prophylaxis
stem:
A 48-year-old woman on clozapine 500 mg nocte for eight years presents to ED with three days of increasing abdominal distension, nausea and no bowel motion for six days. She admits to chronic constipation, uses lactulose intermittently but has been non-adherent for two weeks. She has no fever.

She is otherwise medically well, does not use opioids, and has no prior abdominal surgery.

data_table.Examination: Grossly distended, tympanic, minimal bowel sounds, mild diffuse tenderness, no peritonism, empty rectum.
data_table.Investigations: AXR gross faecal loading throughout colon with dilated loops (transverse colon 8 cm), CT confirms severe constipation with early small bowel dilatation, no perforation, lactate 2.1.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue clozapine, prescribe oral macrogol at usual dose and discharge with GP follow-up for further titration of laxative therapy over the next week
Prescribe metoclopramide 10 mg IV three times daily as a prokinetic and monitor for symptomatic improvement over the next 12 hours before considering imaging
Perform a manual disimpaction in the ED and arrange same-day outpatient colonoscopy for evaluation of possible mechanical obstruction contributing to the picture
Admit, keep nil by mouth with IV fluids, involve surgery, cease clozapine and start multi-agent aperients with serial abdominal examination, review after 48 h
Continue clozapine, prescribe a sodium picosulfate bowel preparation regimen and arrange outpatient colonic transit study in the next fortnight for further work up

subtopic_detail: Impact of smoking cessation on plasma levels
stem:
A 40-year-old man on clozapine 450 mg nocte for schizophrenia (5 years, stable) is admitted to a medical ward for cellulitis. He is a smoker of 30 cigarettes/day. On day two of admission he tells you he has been given nicotine patches and has not smoked since arrival. On day four he develops sedation, hypersalivation, mild myoclonus and a resting tremor.

He is afebrile, no infective deterioration, and no new medications have been started other than IV flucloxacillin.

data_table.Examination: Sedated but rousable, hypersalivation, fine tremor, hyperreflexia mild.
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine level 1180 microg/L (pre-admission 620), norclozapine 340, FBC and CRP unchanged from admission, ECG QTc 460 ms.

lead_in: What is the most likely mechanism and best immediate action?

options.text: Clozapine level has risen because of loss of tobacco induction of CYP1A2; reduce clozapine dose and monitor level and clinical response daily, support cessation
Nicotine replacement patches have precipitated clozapine toxicity via a direct pharmacokinetic interaction at the CYP1A2 enzyme system similar to tobacco itself
Flucloxacillin has inhibited hepatic clozapine metabolism producing an acute toxic rise in plasma level that should resolve on completion of the antibiotic course
The clozapine assay is spuriously elevated by sampling outside the recommended trough window and the true steady-state level is unchanged from baseline
Cellulitis-related inflammation reduces hepatic clozapine clearance transiently; recheck level in 48 hours before making any dose change to therapy

subtopic_detail: TGA restrictions and pregnancy prevention program
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is stable on sodium valproate 1 g bd (18 months, no relapses). She attends for review and reports that she has recently started a new relationship and wants to stop contraception in the next 6 months to attempt pregnancy. Previous trials of lithium (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) and lamotrigine (SJS) both failed.

She understands the diagnosis, has capacity, and has read written materials about her medication.

data_table.Examination: Well, no adverse effects on current dose.
data_table.Investigations: LFTs normal, ammonia normal, valproate level 480 micromol/L, contraception: combined oral contraceptive current, no recent pregnancy tests.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate, recommend high-dose folate 5 mg daily and cease contraception in six months as her mood is stable and folate reduces neural tube defect risk sufficiently for planned pregnancy
Enrol her in the valproate pregnancy prevention program, arrange psychiatry review to explore alternatives, and continue contraception during transition, contraception documented
Halve the valproate dose to 500 mg bd immediately and check level at trough; a lower dose reduces teratogenic risk to an acceptable range for planned pregnancy and preserves clinical stability
Cease valproate today, commence quetiapine 300 mg nocte and advise pregnancy attempts can start immediately provided ongoing psychiatric follow up is maintained across the plan
Refer for pre-implantation genetic testing so the couple can screen embryos for valproate-related neural tube defects prior to implantation and continue valproate in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: HLA-B*15:02 screening and SJS/TEN risk
stem:
A 32-year-old woman of Han Chinese background is being considered for carbamazepine as second-line mood stabiliser after inadequate response to lithium (nephrotoxicity concerns) and intolerance of valproate (severe weight gain). She has no personal or family history of skin reactions to medications and is currently on no other drugs.

She has capacity, understands the diagnosis and has agreed to shared decision-making regarding options.

data_table.Examination: Well, no rash, no lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs and UEC normal. Sodium 140, no baseline pharmacogenomic testing yet performed.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before commencing carbamazepine?

options.text: Perform HLA-B*15:02 genotyping and only proceed with carbamazepine if she tests negative for the allele; positive result mandates avoidance of the drug, involve neurology and pharmacy
Commence carbamazepine at standard low starting dose with slow titration and counsel her to present immediately if any rash appears during the first eight weeks of therapy
Substitute oxcarbazepine for carbamazepine as it is chemically similar but does not carry any risk of SJS/TEN or the HLA-B*15:02 pharmacogenomic association in Asian populations
Perform HLA-B*57:01 testing before commencing carbamazepine as this allele confers major hypersensitivity risk to aromatic anticonvulsants across all patient populations in Australia
Proceed with carbamazepine at a slow titration schedule and check LFTs weekly for four weeks as the main serious risk is hepatotoxicity rather than severe cutaneous adverse reaction

subtopic_detail: Titration with valproate co-therapy and COC interaction
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with bipolar II disorder is stabilised on sodium valproate 500 mg bd. Her psychiatrist decides to add lamotrigine for a predominantly depressive relapse pattern. She is also on a combined oral contraceptive pill and has no history of rash.

She is otherwise well and takes no other medications.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: LFTs normal, valproate level 460 micromol/L, FBC normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate lamotrigine starting and titration approach?

options.text: Standard lamotrigine titration starting at 25 mg daily with weekly doubling to 100 mg over four weeks; the COC has no effect on lamotrigine metabolism in this age group
Load lamotrigine at 200 mg on day one to achieve rapid therapeutic effect; this approach is preferred in bipolar depression where symptom burden is high and time to effect matters
Cease valproate before starting lamotrigine and then use standard monotherapy titration since combining the two agents provides no clinical benefit in bipolar spectrum illness overall
Start lamotrigine 25 mg on alternate days for two weeks, then 25 mg daily for two weeks, then increase by 25-50 mg every two weeks under review, review at each dose step
Advise stopping the COC before commencing lamotrigine as they are contraindicated together; use a copper intrauterine device from cycle day one for ongoing contraception plan

subtopic_detail: Switching from MAOI to SSRI with safe washout period
stem:
A 52-year-old woman with treatment-resistant atypical depression has been on phenelzine 45 mg daily for 10 months with partial response. Ongoing symptoms lead her psychiatrist to plan a switch to sertraline. She asks how the transition will be managed and what she needs to do at home.

She has been adherent to a low-tyramine diet and has no significant medical comorbidities.

data_table.Examination: Well, no autonomic instability.
data_table.Investigations: LFTs normal, ECG normal, UEC normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate transition plan?

options.text: Cease phenelzine today, wait 14 days off all MAOI medication (with dietary restrictions continuing during this washout), then commence sertraline at usual starting dose, with handover
Cross-titrate by reducing phenelzine and introducing sertraline in overlapping doses over two weeks to minimise the depressive symptom gap that occurs during a strict washout period
Cease phenelzine and start sertraline after a 5-day washout as this is sufficient given phenelzine's short elimination half-life of approximately 12 hours from the last dose administered
Cease phenelzine and start moclobemide (a reversible MAOI-A) after a 24-hour washout as an interim step, then transition to sertraline after a further two weeks in the sequence
Cease phenelzine and start sertraline after a 48-hour washout given adequate dietary washout and absence of any drug interactions with other medications she is currently taking at home

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing serotonin syndrome, NMS, anticholinergic and linezolid interactions
stem:
A 46-year-old man with major depressive disorder on venlafaxine 225 mg daily is admitted from ED with confusion, agitation, sweating, dilated pupils, tremor and myoclonus. Vitals show HR 128, BP 168/102, RR 24, temperature 39.1. He was commenced on linezolid IV three days ago for MRSA vertebral osteomyelitis. On examination he has hyperreflexia and inducible clonus, particularly in the lower limbs. Mental state is agitated but not rigid.

He has no recent antipsychotic exposure.

data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils, sweating, hyperreflexia, sustained clonus L>R, coarse tremor, agitation.
data_table.Investigations: CK 340 U/L (mildly elevated), UEC and LFTs normal, no leukocytosis.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and best immediate action?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; commence dantrolene, cease all serotonergic agents and support in ICU with cooling and rehydration measures throughout resuscitation
Anticholinergic toxidrome from an occult ingestion; commence physostigmine as reversal agent, admit for cardiac monitoring and psychiatric review after clinical stabilisation is achieved
Serotonin syndrome from venlafaxine-linezolid interaction; cease both serotonergic agents, supportive care with benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine if severe, admit to a monitored bed
Malignant hyperthermia triggered by recent anaesthetic exposure; commence dantrolene infusion, active cooling and admission to high dependency unit for close monitoring of temperature and CK

Sepsis with metabolic encephalopathy from progression of the osteomyelitis; commence broad-spectrum antibiotics escalation, source control review and empirical steroids for suspected relative adrenal insufficiency

subtopic_detail: QRS widening and sodium bicarbonate
stem:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to ED 90 minutes after ingesting an unknown quantity of amitriptyline in a suicide attempt. She is drowsy, confused, warm and flushed. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 128, PR normal, QRS 128 ms, terminal R wave in aVR, QTc 480 ms. BP is 88/50. She has had one brief generalised seizure in triage that self-terminated within 30 seconds.

She is intubated for airway protection and started on IV crystalloid.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 88/50, RR 12 (ventilated), SpO2 98%, temp 37.6.
data_table.Examination: GCS 8 pre-intubation, dilated pupils, dry skin, hyperreflexia.
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 128 ms, terminal R wave aVR, VBG pH 7.28, sodium 138, potassium 3.6, lactate 3.4, paracetamol level pending.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation and improve airway protection before making further decisions about ongoing airway or ventilation management strategy
Administer intravenous lidocaine (lidocaine) infusion as class Ib antiarrhythmic to reverse the ventricular ectopy and QRS prolongation seen on the current bedside ECG tracing
Give IV magnesium sulfate 2 g as initial treatment for the widened QRS and associated risk of torsades de pointes in TCA overdose with concurrent QTc prolongation on presentation ECG
Start intralipid 20% emulsion infusion as first-line treatment for lipophilic TCA toxicity in the setting of QRS prolongation, hypotension and post-seizure state after suicide attempt
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate bolus (1-2 mmol/kg) to narrow the QRS and raise blood pressure, and repeat as needed with electrolyte monitoring, with airway support

subtopic_detail: Paroxetine and venlafaxine discontinuation risk
stem:
A 38-year-old woman on paroxetine 20 mg daily for 18 months attends her GP asking to stop the medication. Her depression has been in full remission for over 12 months and she is well-supported. She reports missing occasional doses when travelling and feeling flu-like and dizzy within 24 hours.

She has no other medications and no significant comorbidities.

data_table.Examination: Well, no depressive symptoms on MSE.
data_table.Investigations: Nil relevant.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discontinuation plan?

options.text: Cease paroxetine today and provide brief education about self-limiting flu-like symptoms that may occur over the first fortnight after stopping the medication in general practice
Switch to a long half-life SSRI such as fluoxetine 20 mg for two weeks and then abruptly stop; this avoids the taper process altogether and eliminates discontinuation symptoms
Continue paroxetine indefinitely because the flu-like symptoms during missed doses indicate that the patient remains dependent on the medication for continued mood stability
Halve to paroxetine 10 mg daily this week and cease completely the following week; a rapid two-week taper minimises total exposure and avoids prolonged withdrawal effects over time
Taper paroxetine over several weeks (halve to 10 mg for 2-4 weeks, then 10 mg alternate days, then cease), monitoring for discontinuation and relapse, with review at each step

subtopic_detail: Switch strategy for symptomatic prolactin elevation
stem:
A 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia stabilised on risperidone 4 mg daily for 12 months presents with amenorrhoea for 6 months, galactorrhoea and loss of libido. Pregnancy is excluded. Prolactin is 2400 mIU/L (upper reference 500). TSH and pituitary MRI are normal.

She is otherwise well, denies mood symptoms, and does not want to become pregnant in the immediate future.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral galactorrhoea, no visual field defect.
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2400 mIU/L, TSH 1.8, MRI pituitary normal, beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Continue risperidone and add cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly to lower prolactin, with monitoring for possible psychiatric destabilisation from dopamine agonist therapy over the following months
Continue risperidone and reassure her that antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia does not cause long-term consequences and menstruation typically returns once psychiatric symptoms fully remit
Cease risperidone abruptly and commence olanzapine 20 mg nocte as it does not cause hyperprolactinaemia; this can be done as a same-day switch without any cross-titration for convenience
Cross-titrate to aripiprazole (a partial dopamine D2 agonist) which lowers prolactin, with a gradual switch over several weeks under psychiatric supervision, and monitor prolactin at 6 weeks
Halve the risperidone dose to 2 mg daily and reassess prolactin at eight weeks; if prolactin remains elevated then consider dopamine agonist addition to further reduce the level over time

subtopic_detail: Oral to long-acting injectable transition with overlap
stem:
A 35-year-old man with schizophrenia stable on oral paliperidone 6 mg daily for 8 months is being switched to paliperidone palmitate long-acting injectable due to recurrent adherence problems. He has tolerated oral paliperidone well and has no cardiac or renal issues. He agrees to depot therapy after shared decision-making.

His current adherence is estimated at 60% and previous relapses have followed medication cessation.

data_table.Examination: Well, no adverse effects on oral paliperidone.
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, FBC normal, ECG normal, no other medications.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initiation regimen for paliperidone palmitate?

options.text: Give paliperidone palmitate 100 mg IM gluteal monthly starting today and continue oral paliperidone 6 mg daily for 4 weeks to ensure adequate therapeutic coverage during the induction phase
Cease oral paliperidone and start haloperidol decanoate 100 mg IM monthly as a cheaper depot alternative; oral haloperidol overlap for 4 weeks needed while depot levels establish gradually
Give a single loading dose of paliperidone palmitate 234 mg IM deltoid today only and cease oral paliperidone; a single loading dose achieves therapeutic levels without any need for the day-8 dose
Start paliperidone palmitate 3-monthly formulation now without prior use of the 1-monthly product; this is convenient given his adherence issues and avoids the need for monthly clinic visits
Give paliperidone palmitate 150 mg IM deltoid on day 1 and 100 mg IM deltoid on day 8; oral paliperidone can be ceased on day 1 without further oral overlap, with medication review at discharge

subtopic_detail: CIWA-Ar severity and benzo choice by hepatic function
stem:
A 54-year-old man on a Melbourne inpatient detoxification ward is 16 hours from his last drink. He describes 20 standard drinks per day for six years. Alcoholic cirrhosis was confirmed on biopsy 18 months ago; today his Child-Pugh score is B (9 points) with INR 1.9, bilirubin 55 micromol/L (5-20), albumin 27 g/L (35-50) and mild ascites. He is tremulous and diaphoretic. Nurse-administered CIWA-Ar is 18. He is oriented, has no asterixis, and has no history of withdrawal seizures.

Routine bloods show sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 5.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, magnesium 0.82 mmol/L (0.7-1.1) and glucose 6.4 mmol/L. Thiamine 300 mg IV has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112, BP 158/94, RR 20, SpO2 97 percent room air, temp 37.3
data_table.Examination: Tremor of outstretched hands, diaphoretic, alert and oriented, no asterixis, mild ascites
data_table.Investigations: INR 1.9, bilirubin 55, albumin 27, Na 136, K 4.1, creatinine 78, Mg 0.82

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate benzodiazepine choice?

options.text: Diazepam 20 mg PO now, then repeat 2-hourly to CIWA-Ar
Chlordiazepoxide 25 mg PO 4-hourly fixed
Oxazepam 30 mg PO 2-hourly titrated to CIWA-Ar
Midazolam 2 mg IV 2-hourly PRN for this presentation
Clonazepam 1 mg PO 6-hourly fixed in this scenario

subtopic_detail: Withdrawal seizure vs delirium tremens vs Wernicke's - timing and priority
stem:
A 47-year-old woman is on the general medical ward day 3 after admission for pancreatitis. She drinks 15 standard drinks daily. Overnight she has become progressively confused, tremulous, and visually hallucinating small animals in the corner of the room. She is now oriented only to person, tugging at her lines. Her CIWA-Ar is 26.

She received a single dose of thiamine 100 mg IM on admission and oral diazepam 5 mg twice daily as scheduled prophylaxis; her actual last drink was 68 hours ago. Sodium is 138 mmol/L, glucose 6.1 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), phosphate normal, ammonia not elevated, and CT brain plain is unremarkable. She has no focal neurology and no ocular palsy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 176/104, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent, temp 38.2
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, diaphoretic, disoriented to time and place, visual hallucinations, no ataxia, no ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Timeline: Last drink 68 hours ago; scheduled diazepam prophylaxis 5 mg BD only
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, glucose 6.1, Mg 0.62, ammonia normal, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase scheduled diazepam to 10 mg QID and reassess in 4 hours in this clinical setting with formal handover documentation
Haloperidol 5 mg IM for the hallucinations in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
Diazepam 20 mg PO now, repeat 1-2 hourly to CIWA-Ar under 10, plus thiamine 500 mg IV TDS and IV magnesium replacement
Lumbar puncture and empirical IV ceftriaxone for encephalitis in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
Phenytoin loading 15 mg/kg IV to prevent progression to seizure in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician

subtopic_detail: Wernicke's encephalopathy - thiamine dose and route
stem:
A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after being found confused in a park. He is known to drink one to two litres of cask wine per day and lives in supported accommodation. On arrival he is disoriented to time and place, has horizontal nystagmus and a broad-based unsteady gait. He does not smell of recent alcohol. He has not eaten for at least two days.

Capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L. Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7-1.1). CT brain is unremarkable. Ammonia is not elevated. He has no focal weakness and no signs of head trauma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 128/78, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Horizontal nystagmus, broad-based ataxia, disoriented to time and place, no focal weakness
data_table.Investigations: BSL 3.9, Na 138, K 3.7, Mg 0.68, ammonia normal, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Thiamine 100 mg IM daily for 3 days then oral 100 mg daily in this clinical setting
Thiamine 500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days, then reassess for step-down to 300 mg IV daily
IV 50 percent dextrose 50 mL first, then oral thiamine 100 mg for this presentation
Oral thiamine 300 mg daily with folate and B12 co-administration under a supervising clinician
Diazepam 10 mg IV for suspected complex partial seizure in this clinical setting

subtopic_detail: MATOD selection: methadone vs buprenorphine vs buprenorphine-naloxone
stem:
A 34-year-old man attends a public opioid treatment program (OTP) clinic in Sydney requesting to start medication-assisted treatment. He injects heroin daily (approximately 0.5 g), has never been on maintenance treatment before, and has a two-year history of injecting via femoral access. He works full-time in construction, drives 45 minutes to work each morning, and lives with his partner and two young children. He wants a regimen that allows unsupervised take-away doses at the earliest safe opportunity to minimise clinic attendance.

He has no cardiac history and a recent ECG shows QTc 420 ms. LFTs are within normal limits. Urine drug screen is positive for morphine and codeine and negative for benzodiazepines, methamphetamine and cocaine. He is not on any other CNS depressants and reports no alcohol use.

data_table.History: Daily IV heroin 0.5 g, 2 years IVDU, no prior MATOD, working full-time
data_table.Family: Lives with partner and two children aged 3 and 5
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 420 ms, LFTs normal, UDS heroin metabolites positive, benzos/meth/cocaine negative
data_table.Preferences: Wants earliest safe take-away doses to reduce clinic attendance

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line MATOD choice?

options.text: Methadone syrup 30 mg PO daily supervised in this clinical setting
Buprenorphine mono-product 4 mg SL day 1 titrated in this scenario
Buprenorphine-naloxone 4 mg/1 mg SL day 1, titrate up
Naltrexone 50 mg PO daily after supervised opioid detox
Long-acting injectable buprenorphine (Buvidal) 8 mg SC weekly loading

subtopic_detail: Buprenorphine micro-induction to avoid precipitated withdrawal
stem:
A 41-year-old woman on long-term methadone 80 mg daily for chronic pain from a spinal injury asks to transition to buprenorphine-naloxone because she is planning international travel and finds methadone dispensing arrangements impractical. She has been on methadone for 6 years. She takes it every morning under supervision and reports no illicit opioid use. Her most recent dose was 8 hours ago.

She has no other substance use, is not pregnant, has normal LFTs, no QT prolongation, and has read written information about the risks of switching. She strongly prefers not to experience any period of significant opioid withdrawal because she is the sole carer for her elderly father. Standard induction would require her to reach COWS >=12 before the first buprenorphine dose.

data_table.History: Methadone 80 mg daily x 6 years, no illicit use, no other substances
data_table.Reason for switch: Travel logistics, no illicit use, prefers no significant withdrawal window
data_table.Investigations: LFTs normal, QTc 410 ms, not pregnant
data_table.Preferences: Cannot tolerate a withdrawal window due to sole-carer responsibilities

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate induction approach?

options.text: Stop methadone, wait for COWS >=12 (typically 72 h), then buprenorphine 4 mg SL in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
Halve methadone to 40 mg for 3 days, then start buprenorphine 8 mg in this clinical setting as the primary intervention for this presentation under a supervising clinician
Give naloxone 0.4 mg IM before the first buprenorphine dose to shorten washout in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
Switch directly to depot buprenorphine (Buvidal) at 24 mg SC without SL bridging in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
Micro-induction: buprenorphine 0.5 mg SL day 1 while continuing methadone, doubling approximately every 1-2 days, stop methadone once buprenorphine reaches ~12 mg

subtopic_detail: Naltrexone vs acamprosate vs disulfiram - mechanism-based selection
stem:
A 46-year-old accountant attends her general practice in Perth requesting help to reduce her drinking. She currently drinks 6-8 standard drinks per evening, most days per week, describing the first drink as "the one I really look forward to". She has completed a supervised outpatient detoxification 4 weeks ago and has been abstinent since. Her goal is now sustained abstinence rather than controlled drinking.

She has no liver disease (LFTs and INR normal), is not on opioids for any indication, has never had opioid use disorder, has no seizure disorder, and is not planning pregnancy. She works in a client-facing role and is anxious about a medication that would make her acutely unwell if she "slipped" at a work function.

data_table.History: Detox 4 weeks ago, currently abstinent, wants sustained abstinence
data_table.Craving: Reports strong reward-response cravings, especially first drink of the evening
data_table.Investigations: LFTs and INR normal, U&E normal, not pregnant
data_table.Preferences: Prefers to avoid a drug that causes acute illness if she drinks

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Acamprosate 666 mg TDS orally in this scenario
Disulfiram 200 mg orally daily under supervision
Baclofen 10 mg TDS orally titrated in this scenario
Naltrexone 50 mg orally daily in this scenario
Topiramate 25 mg BD titrated in this scenario

subtopic_detail: IM sedation of acute methamphetamine intoxication
stem:
A 27-year-old man is brought into an outer-suburban Brisbane emergency department by paramedics after smashing furniture at a friend's house. He is dishevelled, sweating profusely, agitated, and shouting that people are watching him through the walls. He has confirmed methamphetamine use in the previous 12 hours. He refuses oral medication, cannot cooperate with venous access, and has been placed in a resuscitation cubicle with security in attendance.

He is 92 kg, has no known medical history, no known medications, and no known allergies. There is no evidence of trauma. Point-of-care glucose is 5.6 mmol/L. He is not sedated on inhaled agents. ECG is not yet feasible. Restraint is required for staff safety.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 168/98, RR 22, SpO2 97 percent, temp 38.4
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, agitated, paranoid, no focal neurology, no head injury
data_table.Access: No IV access; oral route refused
data_table.History: Confirmed methamphetamine use in prior 12 h; no other substances known

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first sedating agent?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg IM in this clinical setting
Midazolam 5 mg IM in this clinical setting
Haloperidol 5 mg IM plus promethazine 25 mg IM
Droperidol 10 mg IM in this clinical setting
Ketamine 4 mg/kg IM in this clinical setting

subtopic_detail: Meth-induced psychosis vs primary schizophrenia - course and antipsychotic pathway
stem:
A 24-year-old man is reviewed on the mental health unit after admission a week ago with paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations. On admission urine drug screen was positive for methamphetamine and cannabis. He has been abstinent from all substances since admission (supervised, urine drug screens repeatedly negative). Over the last seven days his positive symptoms have improved substantially: he now denies paranoid content, sleeps normally, and is engaging in ward activities.

He has no family history of psychotic illness. He first used methamphetamine 3 years ago and has had two prior brief presentations with paranoid symptoms, each resolving within 1-2 weeks of abstinence. He is not on any regular medication. He was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nocte on admission with good response.

data_table.History: Meth use 3 years, 2 prior brief paranoid episodes each resolved <2 weeks abstinence
data_table.Course this admission: Symptoms substantially resolved by day 7 abstinence on olanzapine 10 mg nocte
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative from day 2 onward; MSE now euthymic non-psychotic

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step for antipsychotic management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine 10 mg nocte lifelong and add a mood stabiliser in this clinical setting
Stop olanzapine tomorrow now symptoms have resolved in this clinical setting in accordance with department protocol
