Continue olanzapine for 3-6 months with staged taper, and refer to AOD service for relapse prevention
Switch to clozapine as evolving treatment-resistant schizophrenia in this clinical setting
Commence a long-acting injectable antipsychotic for improved adherence in this clinical setting

subtopic_detail: GHB overdose - supportive monitoring, no reversal agent
stem:
A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at a Sydney nightclub. Her friend reports she took two capfuls of "G" approximately 45 minutes earlier and had a small amount of vodka. On arrival she is unresponsive to voice, groans to painful stimulus, and localises briefly. Her respiratory rate is 8 with normal SpO2 on 4 L nasal prongs and a preserved gag reflex. She is otherwise haemodynamically stable.

Capillary glucose is 4.8 mmol/L. Point-of-care venous blood gas: pH 7.32, pCO2 55 mmHg, bicarbonate 26 mmol/L. Urine drug screen for opioids and benzodiazepines is negative. There is no evidence of trauma. Paramedics have not given any medication.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62, BP 108/68, RR 8, SpO2 98 percent on 4 L NP, temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Preserved gag reflex, no head injury, no needle marks
data_table.Investigations: BSL 4.8, VBG pH 7.32 pCO2 55 HCO3 26, UDS opioid and benzo negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Supportive care in a monitored bed with continuous SpO2, capnography, and airway attendance until GCS returns to baseline
Naloxone 400 mcg IV bolus in this clinical setting as the primary intervention for this presentation
Flumazenil 200 mcg IV bolus in this clinical setting as the primary intervention for this presentation under a supervising clinician
Rapid sequence intubation for airway protection in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
Activated charcoal 50 g NG immediately in this clinical setting as the primary intervention and arrange next-day review

subtopic_detail: MDMA hyponatraemia vs serotonin syndrome differentiation
stem:
A 19-year-old woman is brought to an emergency department in Adelaide by friends after collapsing with a generalised seizure at a music festival. She took MDMA approximately 6 hours ago. Her friends report she has been drinking large volumes of water throughout the day to "stay safe". On arrival she is post-ictal, confused, and has vomited once. There is no hyperreflexia, no ankle clonus, no ocular clonus, no muscle rigidity, and no severe hyperthermia.

Sodium is 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L, urea 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L. Urine osmolality is high relative to plasma osmolality. CK is 320 U/L. Serum tryptase, if it mattered, is not indicated. There is no other drug co-ingestion by history.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 122/78, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, temp 37.6
data_table.Neuro: Post-ictal, no clonus, no rigidity, no hyperreflexia, no ocular clonus
data_table.Investigations: Na 118, K 3.6, urea 3.2, creatinine 62, glucose 5.4, CK 320

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Hypertonic (3 percent) saline 150 mL IV over 10 min, repeat once if seizure or persistent severe hyponatraemia
Cyproheptadine 12 mg PO for serotonin syndrome in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
Isotonic (0.9 percent) saline 1 L IV over 1 hour in this clinical setting as the primary intervention under a supervising clinician
Fluid restriction to 800 mL/24 h with 6-hourly sodium recheck in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
Dantrolene 2 mg/kg IV for suspected NMS variant in this clinical setting as the primary intervention

subtopic_detail: Cannabis use disorder - first-line management
stem:
A 26-year-old plumber attends his general practice in regional Victoria asking for help to reduce his cannabis use. He has been smoking daily for 8 years, currently 3-5 cones each evening, and describes low motivation, disturbed sleep on the days he tries to abstain, and a growing worry about the impact on his work and relationship. He has no history of psychotic illness, no other substance use, no medical comorbidities, and no current suicidal ideation.

He has not tried any structured program before. His partner is supportive and he wants to stop entirely.

data_table.History: Daily cannabis 8 years, 3-5 cones/evening, wants to stop entirely

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg PO daily in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg BD PO in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
Prescribed dronabinol as a substitution therapy for this presentation under a supervising clinician
Diazepam 5 mg PO nocte for 4 weeks for sleep and withdrawal under a supervising clinician
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy and motivational interviewing under a supervising clinician

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine deprescribing via diazepam substitution taper
stem:
A 68-year-old woman has been on temazepam 20 mg nocte for insomnia for the last 12 years, initially started after her husband's death. She now wishes to stop because a family member had a fall after starting a similar medication. She has hypertension controlled on perindopril, no cognitive impairment on MoCA (28/30), no depression on PHQ-9, and no other sedative use. She lives independently, drives, and has no falls or fractures to date.

Renal function and LFTs are within normal limits. She has been counselled about withdrawal symptoms and the timeframe involved and is committed to a deliberate taper.

data_table.Medications: Temazepam 20 mg nocte x 12 years, perindopril, no other sedatives
data_table.Investigations: U&E and LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate deprescribing approach?

options.text: Stop temazepam abruptly this week in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
Switch to zopiclone 7.5 mg nocte then taper over 4 weeks under a supervising clinician
Add flumazenil 0.2 mg IV weekly to speed receptor down-regulation under a supervising clinician
Add pregabalin 75 mg BD to cover withdrawal in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
Convert to equivalent diazepam and reduce by 5-10 percent every 2 weeks in this scenario

subtopic_detail: Screening for gambling disorder
stem:
A 39-year-old man attends his general practice in Perth requesting a mental health care plan for "anxiety". On further discussion he tells you he has been staying up late at night placing bets on international sport, is now taking cash advances from his credit card to keep betting, and hides his gambling from his partner. He denies any substance use, has never attempted suicide, and has no other psychiatric history. He is asking for help.

He is otherwise well, on no medications, and has never been assessed for gambling before. You want to briefly screen for gambling disorder in the consultation before proceeding to a more detailed assessment.

data_table.History: Escalating sports betting, credit-card cash advances, concealing from partner
data_table.Prior assessment: Never screened or assessed for gambling

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate brief screening tool?

options.text: PHQ-9 depression screen in this scenario
Lie/Bet screen (two questions)
AUDIT-C alcohol screen in this scenario
K10 psychological distress screen
GAD-7 anxiety screen in this scenario

subtopic_detail: Polysubstance detoxification sequencing
stem:
A 33-year-old man presents to a public drug and alcohol inpatient unit in Melbourne requesting supervised withdrawal. He drinks 18 standard drinks daily, uses diazepam 40 mg daily (obtained from multiple prescribers), and uses methamphetamine intranasally 3-4 times per week. He has no cardiac history and has previously had one alcohol withdrawal seizure. He is committed to abstinence and has arranged accommodation and residential rehabilitation for after detox.

He has no active infection, LFTs are mildly elevated (ALT 65, AST 55), INR 1.1, and no signs of hepatic encephalopathy. Renal function and electrolytes are within normal limits. He is not currently intoxicated on arrival.

data_table.Substances: Alcohol 18 SD/day, diazepam 40 mg/day, meth 3-4x/week intranasal
data_table.History: Prior alcohol withdrawal seizure, wants abstinence, rehab arranged
data_table.Investigations: ALT 65, AST 55, INR 1.1, UEC within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate detoxification sequencing plan?

options.text: Complete meth detox first, then alcohol, then benzodiazepine in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
Alcohol first with diazepam, discharge, and re-admit for benzodiazepine detox in 3 months in this clinical setting
Detox benzodiazepine over 6 months as outpatient before admission for alcohol detox in this clinical setting
Detox alcohol and benzodiazepine simultaneously with symptom-triggered diazepam CIWA-guided, then meth psychosocial support
Refuse admission until meth is stopped for 4 weeks in this clinical setting as the primary intervention

subtopic_detail: Opioid maintenance in pregnancy
stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation attends a specialist drug and alcohol clinic in Sydney for review of her opioid use. She has been on methadone 60 mg daily for two years and is stable, working part-time, and engaged with antenatal care. She has read online that methadone crosses the placenta and asks whether she should stop it now, taper it, or switch to buprenorphine or buprenorphine-naloxone for the rest of the pregnancy.

She has no other substance use (urine drug screens negative for other opioids, benzodiazepines, meth), no infection, and LFTs are normal. She is not on any other CNS depressants. She has no history of opioid diversion, has children in the home from a previous relationship, and asks specifically about the safest option for her baby.

data_table.History: Methadone 60 mg daily x 2 years, stable, working, engaged in antenatal care
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative for other substances, LFTs normal, no infection
data_table.Home: Children from prior relationship in the home

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate opioid-use management plan for this pregnancy?

options.text: Continue methadone at current stable dose; monitor for dose adjustments as pregnancy progresses
Taper methadone off during the second trimester in this clinical setting
Switch to buprenorphine-naloxone 8 mg/2 mg daily this trimester in this clinical setting
Cease methadone at 36 weeks to avoid neonatal abstinence syndrome in this clinical setting
Start naltrexone after supervised detox for the third trimester in this clinical setting

subtopic_detail: AU alcohol guidelines quantification
stem: A 44-year-old woman attends her general practice for a routine review. She reports drinking approximately 5 standard drinks on a Friday and 5 standard drinks on a Saturday, with no drinking on other days. She has no medical comorbidities, is not pregnant, is not on any medication, and has no personal or family history of substance use disorder. She asks whether her current drinking pattern is within the recommended Australian guidelines.

data_table.History: 10 SD/week, split as 5 Friday + 5 Saturday; no other drinking days

lead_in: What is the single most accurate answer per the NHMRC 2020 Australian alcohol guidelines?

options.text: Both weekly and per-session amounts breach the guideline
Her weekly total is within the guideline but per-session amount exceeds it
Both weekly and per-session amounts are within the guideline
Weekly amount breaches guideline, per-session amount is within
The guideline uses total weekly ethanol grams, not standard drinks

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose sodium bicarbonate
stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to your ED by ambulance one hour after taking her partner's amitriptyline in a suicide attempt. She reports taking about 30 tablets of 25 mg each. She was found drowsy but rousable at home.

On arrival she is drowsy with GCS 12, has warm dry skin, and dilated poorly reactive pupils. Her bladder is distended and there are no bowel sounds. ECG shows a broad QRS with a terminal R wave in aVR.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 sinus tachycardia, BP 96/58, RR 16, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5); pupils dilated 6 mm and poorly reactive; skin warm dry; bladder distended
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L; potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); paracetamol level negative
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia, QRS 148 ms, terminal R wave in aVR height 4 mm, QTc 512 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g nasogastric with airway protection with cardiac monitoring throughout
Intravenous physostigmine 2 mg over 5 minutes for reversal of anticholinergic toxicity
Sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 100 mL intravenous bolus with cardiac monitoring throughout
Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV titrated to arousal and repeat as clinically indicated
Amiodarone 300 mg IV infusion for the broad complex tachycardia with cardiac monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation first-line
stem:
A 52-year-old man with stable schizophrenia on olanzapine 15 mg nocte for the past 4 years attends your general practice wanting to stop smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day and has smoked for 30 years. He has tried to quit unassisted twice, each time relapsing within 2 weeks. He has no history of severe depression, no active suicidal ideation, and his last psychiatric review documented stable mood.

He has hypertension well controlled on perindopril, no history of seizures, and no cardiovascular events. His Fagerstrom Test for Nicotine Dependence score is 7 of 10 (high).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 132/78, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 39 mmol/mol (<42); LDL 3.6 mmol/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg nocte; perindopril 5 mg mane; no other regular medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrating to 1 mg twice daily with cardiac monitoring throughout
Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily with cardiac monitoring throughout
Nicotine replacement patch 21 mg daily monotherapy without oral NRT top up with cardiac monitoring throughout
Nicotine vaping product first-line before other pharmacotherapy with cardiac monitoring throughout
Behavioural counselling only with no pharmacotherapy given his psychiatric history with cardiac monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: FBT adolescent anorexia
stem:
You are a psychiatry registrar reviewing a 15-year-old girl brought by her parents to a specialist eating disorders clinic. She has lost 12 kg over 6 months to a BMI of 15.4. Blood pressure is 88/56 supine and drops to 68/44 on standing; heart rate is 44 bpm at rest. She meets DSM-5 criteria for anorexia nervosa, restrictive subtype.

Her parents are supportive but exhausted. She lives with both parents and a 12-year-old brother. Her physical status is medically stable enough for outpatient management by the eating disorder physician who is co-managing her. She has no comorbid depression or suicidality that requires acute admission.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 44 sinus bradycardia, BP 88/56 supine (68/44 standing), RR 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temp 36.1 C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); phosphate 0.8 mmol/L (0.8-1.5); LFTs mildly elevated; ECG QTc 452 ms
data_table.History: Bradycardia and orthostasis but medically manageable outpatient with weekly medical review; no comorbid depression; family intact and engaged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line psychological intervention?

options.text: Family Based Therapy (FBT / Maudsley) with parents taking initial control of refeeding
Individual cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders (CBT-E) as first-line for this age
Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) as first-line with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
Fluoxetine 20 mg daily as first-line to treat the underlying anxiety and improve intake
Olanzapine 2.5 mg nocte for weight gain and reduction of anorexic cognitions with cardiac monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: MDMA acute presentation
stem:
A 22-year-old man is brought in by friends after taking a tablet at a music festival 3 hours ago. He has been sweating profusely, has drunk 3 to 4 litres of water in the last 90 minutes, and now looks confused. His last regular medication is escitalopram 10 mg daily for anxiety.

On examination he is agitated, has hyperreflexia and inducible clonus at both ankles, and pupils are dilated. His skin is diaphoretic and warm. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. There is no focal neurology. He is oriented to person only.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 158/98, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 39.6 C
data_table.Examination: Agitated, confused; hyperreflexia lower more than upper limbs; inducible clonus both ankles; pupils dilated; diaphoretic; hyperactive bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); CK 4200 U/L (<200); glucose 5.8 mmol/L; venous ammonia not indicated

lead_in: Which single treatment addresses the most urgent life threat first?

options.text: Hypertonic 3 percent sodium chloride 150 mL over 15 minutes with cardiac monitoring throughout
Cyproheptadine 12 mg oral single dose for serotonin syndrome with cardiac monitoring throughout
Dantrolene 2.5 mg per kg IV for hyperthermia with cardiac monitoring throughout
Activated charcoal 50 g nasogastric with airway protection with cardiac monitoring throughout
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced vs primary psychosis
stem:
A 20-year-old university student is brought to your community mental health service by his parents after 5 weeks of paranoid delusions that a lecturer is broadcasting his thoughts, and third person auditory hallucinations. He has been smoking high-potency cannabis daily for 3 months at increasing dose.

He has one prior week-long episode of similar symptoms 6 months ago that self-resolved within 5 days of stopping cannabis. Family history is negative for psychotic illness. He has no depression, no mania, and is medically well. His urine drug screen is positive for cannabis and negative for methamphetamine.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for THC, negative for methamphetamine, amphetamines, MDMA, cocaine; TFTs normal; CT head normal; syphilis serology negative
data_table.History: Daily high-potency cannabis for 3 months; prior 1 week self-limiting episode 6 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic formulation and management?

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder; commence aripiprazole and re-evaluate at 6 months
First-episode schizophrenia; commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte with cardiac monitoring throughout
Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder; short course of oral risperidone 1 to 2 mg daily
Brief psychotic disorder; observe without medication for 4 weeks with cardiac monitoring throughout
Delusional disorder; commence pimozide and cognitive therapy with cardiac monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: Persistent psychosis after two adequate antipsychotic trials
stem: A 38-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder still has daily persecutory delusions and hostile voices after eight weeks of risperidone and then ten weeks of quetiapine, both at adequate doses with adherence confirmed by depot-free dispensing records and by her carer. Her mood has been stable on lithium.

data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L, neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L, TSH 2.0 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change quetiapine to clozapine
Change quetiapine to olanzapine
Add a second antipsychotic agent
Increase the quetiapine dose further
Add an antidepressant to the lithium

subtopic_detail: GHB overdose recognition
stem:
A 27-year-old man is brought in by ambulance from a nightclub at 3 am after being found unresponsive on the dance floor. Friends report he had a small dose of a clear liquid drink from a friend about 40 minutes ago and appeared normal until sudden collapse. He has no known medical history and is not on regular medication.

On arrival he responds to painful stimulus only. Airway is patent and self-maintained. Pupils are 3 mm and reactive. There is no track marks. Ambulance report saline 500 mL infused en route. His symptoms are already improving within 20 minutes of ED arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 52, BP 108/64, RR 14, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.4 C
data_table.Examination: GCS 8 (E2 V2 M4) on arrival, improving to E3 V4 M5 within 20 minutes; pupils 3 mm and reactive; no track marks
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.36, HCO3 24 mmol/L; ethanol level 0.02 percent (0.020 g per 100 mL); paracetamol negative; salicylate negative

lead_in: What is the most likely toxin and appropriate management?

options.text: Ethanol toxicity - fluids, thiamine, and monitor for withdrawal with cardiac monitoring throughout
Opioid overdose - naloxone 0.4 mg IV titrated to respiratory rate over 12 with cardiac monitoring throughout
Benzodiazepine overdose - flumazenil 0.2 mg IV titrated to arousal with cardiac monitoring throughout
Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) toxicity - supportive care with airway protection with cardiac monitoring throughout
Ketamine toxicity - benzodiazepines for agitation on emergence, no specific antidote with cardiac monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: Clozapine myocarditis in initiation phase
stem:
A 26-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine for 18 days, titrated up to a current dose of 300 mg daily. He presents to your consultation-liaison psychiatry service with 2 days of fever, tachycardia, and generalised fatigue. He denies chest pain but reports mild shortness of breath on climbing stairs, which is new. There is no cough or productive sputum.

On examination he looks systemically unwell. There is a soft third heart sound on auscultation with no murmur, no peripheral oedema, and mild bibasal crackles. Chest is otherwise clear. Neutrophil count is within normal limits. His clozapine level is 400 micrograms per litre.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/68, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; fatigued; soft third heart sound; no murmur; no peripheral oedema; mild bibasal crackles; chest otherwise clear; no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.4 x10^9/L neutrophils 5.6; CRP 82 mg/L; troponin I 480 ng/L (upper limit 26); NT-pro-BNP 3400 pg/mL; ECG shows sinus tachycardia with widespread T wave inversion; chest X-ray shows mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette without pulmonary oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop clozapine immediately and arrange urgent transthoracic echocardiogram plus cardiology review with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging if echocardiogram is abnormal
Continue clozapine at current dose and start empirical intravenous ceftriaxone plus vancomycin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia or infective endocarditis
Halve the clozapine dose to 150 milligrams and repeat troponin and echocardiogram in 72 hours before deciding on definitive cessation of therapy
Continue clozapine and add oral aspirin 100 milligrams and oral atorvastatin 40 milligrams for presumed acute coronary syndrome in a young smoker
Withhold clozapine for 48 hours and restart at the same dose if the patient defervesces and the troponin trends downward on repeat testing

subtopic_detail: Lithium toxicity threshold for dialysis
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium 900 mg daily for 15 years presents to your emergency department with 4 days of nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and confusion after a gastroenteritis illness. Her partner reports she has been more unsteady on her feet over the last 48 hours. She recently started perindopril 4 mg daily for hypertension.

On examination she is confused with coarse tremor, fasciculations at the shoulders and thighs, and marked ataxia. Reflexes are hyperactive with sustained clonus at the ankles bilaterally. There is no focal neurology and pupils are equal. Serum lithium level, taken 8 hours after her last dose, is 3.6 mmol/L. Creatinine is 180 micromol/L (baseline 82). She has been catheterised with urine output of 20 mL over 2 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 108/68, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Confused (GCS 14); coarse tremor with fasciculations; marked ataxia; hyperreflexia with sustained clonus; pupils equal and reactive; no focal weakness; skin turgor reduced
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 3.6 mmol/L (target 0.4-1.0 mmol/L); sodium 148 potassium 4.2 urea 14 creatinine 180 (baseline 82); venous gas pH 7.42 lactate 2.1 mmol/L; TSH 5.2 mIU/L; ECG sinus rhythm with prolonged QT 480 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lithium, commence intravenous normal saline at 200 millilitres per hour, and admit for observation without initiating haemodialysis at this stage
Cease lithium, cease perindopril, commence intravenous normal saline resuscitation, arrange urgent intermittent haemodialysis, and consult toxicology and renal
Continue lithium at a reduced dose of 450 milligrams daily, give intravenous 5 percent dextrose 2 litres over 12 hours, and repeat lithium level in 24 hours
Administer activated charcoal 50 grams orally and observe with fluid resuscitation and antiemetics before deciding on further management at 6 hours
Administer intravenous sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 grams and rectal enema 60 grams to enhance lithium elimination via the gastrointestinal tract

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
A 34-year-old woman is admitted overnight to your consultation-liaison psychiatry service. She has depression on venlafaxine 225 mg daily and has recently been started on tramadol 100 mg four times daily by her general practitioner for lower back pain 3 days ago. Over 6 hours she has become confused, agitated, diaphoretic, and febrile.

On examination she is agitated and restless with dilated pupils. There is marked lower limb hyperreflexia with 5 beats of clonus at the ankles bilaterally. Muscle tone is greater in the lower than upper limbs. She has not received any antipsychotics or antiemetics. There is no rash. She is on IV crystalloid at 125 mL/hr and has had one dose of oral diazepam 10 mg 30 minutes ago without effect.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 168/104, RR 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 39.4 C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and restless; dilated pupils; diaphoretic; lower limb tone increased; hyperreflexia with 5 beats of clonus at ankles bilaterally; upper limbs less affected; no cog-wheel rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 480 U/L; sodium 138 potassium 4.4 creatinine 92; venous gas pH 7.36 lactate 2.4 mmol/L; TSH 2.1 mIU/L; ECG sinus tachycardia; drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue current medications and give intravenous paracetamol 1 gram plus rapid external cooling with iced peritoneal lavage for immediate temperature control
Give intravenous bromocriptine 2.5 milligrams four times daily and intravenous dantrolene 2 milligrams per kilogram every 6 hours for presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Cease venlafaxine and tramadol, give intravenous benzodiazepines titrated to sedation, and give oral cyproheptadine 12 milligrams then 2 milligrams hourly up to 32 milligrams daily
Give intravenous haloperidol 5 milligrams for the agitation and add intravenous ceftriaxone 2 grams plus vancomycin for presumed sepsis with meningitis
Give intravenous naloxone 0.4 milligrams and IV physostigmine 0.5 milligrams for presumed opioid toxidrome with anticholinergic delirium from the tramadol

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD pharmacotherapy with cardiac history
stem:
A 38-year-old man is referred to your general adult psychiatry outpatient clinic for management of newly diagnosed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (combined presentation). He has trialled cognitive behavioural strategies and workplace accommodations over 6 months without adequate response. He now requests pharmacotherapy to help with worsening occupational functioning as a lawyer.

His medical history includes an unprovoked pulmonary embolism 3 years ago (currently off anticoagulation) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy diagnosed after a syncopal episode 5 years ago with a septal thickness of 22 mm. He has an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator and is under regular cardiology follow-up. Baseline resting blood pressure is 138/86 and heart rate 82.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 138/86, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no dysmorphism; ICD scar in place; JVP not raised; no ankle oedema; apex beat displaced with a soft ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG shows LV hypertrophy and left axis deviation; recent echocardiogram septal thickness 22 mm and preserved LVEF at 60 percent; TSH 1.8 mIU/L; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Methylphenidate immediate release starting at 5 milligrams twice daily titrating to 20 milligrams three times daily with 4 weekly ECG and blood pressure review
Dexamfetamine 5 milligrams twice daily titrating to 15 milligrams three times daily with weekly cardiology liaison and 4 weekly ECG monitoring throughout titration
Atomoxetine starting at 40 milligrams daily and titrating to 80 milligrams daily after 7 days with 4 weekly review of blood pressure, heart rate, and mood
Bupropion 150 milligrams sustained release daily titrating to 300 milligrams as first-line non-stimulant with cardiology and neurologist input on seizure and cardiac risk
Modafinil 100 milligrams daily titrating to 200 milligrams daily as off-label first-line non-stimulant with regular blood pressure monitoring and cardiology input

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and lorazepam challenge
stem:
A 30-year-old man with a first episode of psychosis is admitted to your inpatient psychiatry unit. Over 48 hours he has become progressively withdrawn with reduced oral intake. On the morning of day 3 he is found lying on his bed, eyes open but unresponsive to verbal commands. He has not been on any regular medication. There is no history of head trauma or fever.

On examination he is mute, staring, and shows waxy flexibility (his arm remains in whatever position it is placed). He has echopraxia (mimicking the examiner's arm movements when tested) and marked negativism (resisting attempts at passive movement). Vital signs are within normal limits. There is no rigidity, no tremor, no autonomic instability, and no localising neurology. CT head is normal. Urinalysis is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Mute; staring; waxy flexibility; echopraxia; negativism; no rigidity; no tremor; no autonomic instability; no focal neurology; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.2 x10^9/L; CRP 4 mg/L; creatine kinase 92 U/L; sodium 140 potassium 4.0 creatinine 76; TSH 2.0 mIU/L; venous gas within normal limits; urinalysis clear; urine drug screen negative; CT head normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral bromocriptine 2.5 milligrams three times daily as a dopamine agonist with concurrent intravenous dantrolene to reverse muscular rigidity
Administer intramuscular olanzapine 10 milligrams to treat the underlying psychotic disorder and reassess catatonic features over the next 4 to 6 hours
Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 milligrams per kilogram three times daily empirically for possible herpes simplex encephalitis while awaiting cerebrospinal fluid PCR
Refer for immediate bilateral electroconvulsive therapy as first-line treatment for suspected catatonia given the risk of malignant catatonia developing acutely
Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 milligrams as a challenge and observe over 20 to 30 minutes for improvement in mutism, negativism, and posturing

subtopic_detail: PTSD first-line pharmacotherapy
stem: A 34-year-old male veteran presents to your general practice with 8 months of intrusive memories of combat, hypervigilance, sleep disturbance and avoidance of crowds after his return from deployment. He meets criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder and has completed 8 sessions of trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy with partial response. He is not currently suicidal. He has no history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or substance dependence. He has agreed to add pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, mood low, no thought disorder, no suicidal ideation, no substance intoxication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Oral quetiapine 25 mg at night, titrated up to 300 mg daily total for management of hyperarousal, sleep disturbance and residual anxiety symptoms during the day
Oral sertraline 50 mg daily, titrated up to 100 to 200 mg daily based on response and tolerability over 4 to 6 weeks with symptom and side effect monitoring
Oral benzodiazepine diazepam 5 mg three times daily to manage hyperarousal and improve sleep in the short term while awaiting response to psychological therapies
Oral prazosin 1 mg at night titrated up to 5 mg for nightmares as first-line pharmacotherapy addressing the full spectrum of post-traumatic symptoms he is experiencing
Oral mirtazapine 15 mg at night as first-line pharmacotherapy given its sedative properties and appetite stimulation useful in patients with PTSD and comorbid insomnia now

subtopic_detail: Borderline PD self-harm ED management
stem: A 26-year-old woman with known borderline personality disorder presents to your emergency department after superficial cutting to her forearm following an argument with her partner. She has been drinking wine but is coherent. She reports fleeting suicidal thoughts but no current intent or plan. She has attended the emergency department 12 times in the past 6 months for similar presentations. She is currently engaged with a dialectical behaviour therapy program.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Superficial linear lacerations left forearm, no active bleeding, no tendon or nerve involvement, coherent conversation, no gross intoxication
data_table.Investigations: Alcohol breath test 0.06; paracetamol undetectable; ECG normal sinus rhythm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit her as an involuntary patient to a general psychiatric ward under the Mental Health Act for 7 days of containment and to allow safety planning to occur
Administer intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg for behavioural containment and admit for 24 hours of observation to prevent escalation of her presenting complaint tonight
Wound care and dressing, collaborative safety planning, contact her DBT therapist, then discharge with clear crisis contacts and a written safety plan for home
Commence oral fluoxetine 20 mg daily for chronic suicidality and prescribe a 3 month supply on discharge from the emergency department tonight without further review
Refer her to a general medical ward under the medical registrar for observation and then transfer to a psychiatry inpatient bed on the morning ward round tomorrow

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia switch
stem: A 28-year-old woman with first-episode psychosis has been stable on risperidone 4 mg daily for 8 months. She presents to your clinic complaining of secondary amenorrhoea for 5 months, galactorrhoea and reduced libido. Her serum prolactin is 2800 mIU/L (normal under 500). Pituitary MRI is normal. Beta-hCG is negative. She is otherwise well and has no history of seizures, cardiovascular disease or diabetes. She wants to preserve her current mental state.

data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, mood euthymic, no thought disorder, galactorrhoea on breast expression, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2800 mIU/L, MRI pituitary normal, beta-hCG negative, TSH 1.8, LFTs normal, U&E normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add oral cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly to lower the prolactin level over time while continuing her current dose of risperidone 4 mg daily unchanged during this period
Reduce risperidone to 2 mg daily and repeat the prolactin level in 4 weeks to determine whether the level normalises with a lower dose of the current antipsychotic
Cease risperidone entirely and commence oral haloperidol 5 mg daily as a first-generation alternative antipsychotic in order to reduce elevated serum prolactin level to normal
Switch antipsychotic to aripiprazole 10 mg daily using a cross-titration schedule over 4 weeks, monitoring closely for relapse of any psychotic symptoms during the switch period
Refer her to endocrinology and continue risperidone at 4 mg daily unchanged while awaiting specialist input over the next 3 to 6 months for further formal assessment

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in pregnancy
stem: A 30-year-old woman in her first trimester (10 weeks) presents to your general practice with a 6 week history of persistent low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and thoughts of worthlessness. She has a history of major depressive disorder and has been off medication since planning pregnancy 4 months ago. She has no suicidal intent. She has moderate depression on PHQ-9 (score 16) and has already been referred for perinatal psychology. She wants to consider pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Examination: Alert, tearful at times, cooperative, no psychotic features, no suicidal intent, PHQ-9 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antidepressant?

options.text: Oral paroxetine 20 mg daily titrated based on response, then continued throughout pregnancy and into the lactation period with obstetric and mental health team follow-up
Oral fluoxetine 20 mg daily titrated based on response, then continued throughout the pregnancy and lactation period with regular obstetric and mental health team monitoring reviews
Oral venlafaxine 75 mg daily titrated based on response, then continued throughout the pregnancy and lactation period with regular obstetric and mental health team monitoring for tolerability
Oral mirtazapine 30 mg at night titrated based on response, then continued throughout pregnancy and lactation with regular obstetric and mental health monitoring at each visit
Oral sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to therapeutic dose, with obstetric and mental health follow-up throughout pregnancy and continuation planned into the postnatal period

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus NMS differentiation and treatment
stem: A 42-year-old woman on sertraline 200 mg daily was started on tramadol 50 mg four times daily for back pain 6 hours ago. She now presents to your emergency department with tremor, agitation, diaphoresis and diarrhoea. On examination she has lower limb hyperreflexia and inducible clonus at the ankles, sustained on the right. Muscle tone is normal in the upper limbs. Temperature is 38.9 C. There is no rigidity of the neck or trunk.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 158/95, RR 24, SpO2 97 percent, temp 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, agitated, dilated pupils, hyperreflexia lower limbs, inducible ankle clonus (sustained right), no lead-pipe rigidity, no dyskinesia
data_table.Investigations: CK 340 U/L, WCC 12, glucose 6.2, U&E normal, ECG sinus tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease serotonergic agents (sertraline and tramadol), give IV benzodiazepines (diazepam 5 to 10 mg titrated), active external cooling if temperature above 38.5 C, add cyproheptadine 12 mg PO
IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg push, then cool to 37 C, cease serotonergic agents and admit for benzodiazepine sedation and monitoring in the intensive care unit overnight for stability
IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg via nasogastric tube every 8 hours, cease tramadol only, continue sertraline and admit for observation with paracetamol for fever and IV rehydration overnight
IV haloperidol 5 mg to control agitation, IV normal saline 2 L bolus, continue serotonergic agents to avoid rebound depression and admit for cardiac monitoring and observation overnight
IV midazolam 5 mg then intubation with propofol and rocuronium, admit for 48 hours of therapeutic hypothermia to 33 C on the intensive care unit for neuroprotection during recovery

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal seizure prevention with thiamine dosing
stem: A 48-year-old man is admitted to your surgical ward pre-operatively for elective cholecystectomy tomorrow. He reports drinking 15 standard drinks daily for 20 years. His last drink was 12 hours ago. He is now tremulous, mildly anxious and diaphoretic. He has a CIWA-Ar score of 14. He has no history of seizures. His full blood count and electrolytes are normal but he has a mildly elevated GGT.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 152/95, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly anxious, tremulous, sweaty, no focal neurology, no ataxia or ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Investigations: CIWA-Ar 14, glucose 5.4, U&E normal, LFTs GGT 180 (5 to 55), MCV 102

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial regimen?

options.text: Oral thiamine 100 mg daily plus oral diazepam 5 mg every 6 hours PRN for CIWA-Ar score above 8, and reassess him in the morning ward round before the operating list starts
IV thiamine 300 mg three times daily for at least 3 days before any glucose, oral diazepam symptom-triggered per CIWA-Ar (10 to 20 mg if score above 10), and admit for close monitoring
IV glucose 10 percent at 100 mL per hour, oral diazepam 10 mg every 6 hours fixed dose regimen, IM thiamine 100 mg once daily for 3 days total and observation overnight
Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every 6 hours as fixed-dose reducing regimen without thiamine, and standard nil by mouth from midnight for the elective operation planned tomorrow morning
IM haloperidol 5 mg for agitation, oral thiamine 100 mg daily, and reduce diazepam to 2 mg every 8 hours PRN in view of the anaesthetic and surgery scheduled for tomorrow morning

subtopic_detail: Delirium versus dementia in acute presentation
stem: An 82-year-old woman with mild dementia is brought to your emergency department by her daughter with 2 days of increased confusion, agitation and visual hallucinations of small animals. She has a background of hypertension and a urinary tract infection was treated 3 weeks ago. Cognitive scores have been stable at MMSE 22 for 12 months. On examination her attention is inconsistent, she is disorientated, and she is intermittently drowsy. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 138/84, RR 20, SpO2 96 percent, temp 37.4 C
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating attention (positive months-backwards error), disorientation, drowsy at times, no focal neurology, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: leucocytes and nitrites positive; U&E, glucose, calcium normal; CXR clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral risperidone 2 mg twice daily as a maintenance antipsychotic to control the hallucinations and agitation for at least 4 weeks with a review appointment planned
Refer her for CT head and lumbar puncture to exclude an intracranial cause and CNS infection before starting any treatment for the acute confusional presentation observed today
Admit for a delirium care package: identify and treat the infection, empirical oral antibiotics, ensure hydration, avoid physical restraints, use environmental de-escalation and family presence
Cease all her regular antihypertensive medications plus her cholinesterase inhibitor and start IV dexamethasone 8 mg for the acute confusional presentation with agitation observed today
Discharge her home with her daughter with education about sundowning and follow up with her general practitioner in one week to reassess her cognitive status and current medications

subtopic_detail: Metabolic monitoring intervals on olanzapine
stem: A 27-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg orally at night 3 months ago in your community mental health team clinic. He reports improved auditory hallucinations and returning to part-time work. He has gained 6 kg. Baseline weight 78 kg, waist 92 cm, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4 percent, total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, LDL 2.6 mmol/L, HDL 1.2 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L, BP 118/72. Today weight 84 kg, waist 100 cm, BP 130/82.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 130/82, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: BMI 27 kg/m2 (from 25 kg/m2); waist circumference now 100 cm (from 92 cm); no acanthosis; euthymic mood; no EPS
data_table.Investigations: Not yet repeated since baseline; family history of type 2 diabetes in mother

lead_in: What is the most appropriate monitoring plan today?

options.text: Continue current antipsychotic without repeat blood investigations, review in 6 months as per routine annual metabolic panel and provide brief general lifestyle advice on diet and exercise
Cease olanzapine immediately, start clozapine 12.5 mg orally at night with weekly FBC and BP monitoring in the community over the next 4 weeks and defer any metabolic testing until then
Add metformin 500 mg orally twice daily empirically without repeat blood work, based on the weight gain alone and family history of type 2 diabetes, and review in 6 weeks for tolerance
Focus solely on lifestyle counselling with dietitian referral, defer any monitoring bloods until the annual review as symptomatic control is currently very good on the present antipsychotic dose
Repeat fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid panel today with the follow-up appointment in 4 weeks to review results and consider metformin or antipsychotic switch to a lower metabolic-risk agent

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose ECG changes and management
stem: A 26-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department 90 minutes after an impulsive ingestion of approximately 30 tablets of amitriptyline 50 mg following an argument with her partner. She is drowsy but rousable. On assessment she is briefly confused but denies suicidal intent now. Bedside cardiac monitoring shows a broad complex regular rhythm at 118. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QRS 138 ms and rightward terminal axis. She has no history of cardiac disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/58, RR 20, SpO2 97 percent, temp 36.5 C, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dilated pupils reactive, dry mucous membranes, warm dry skin, urinary retention on bladder scan; no localising neurology; no seizure witnessed
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 138 ms with right axis of terminal 40 ms; VBG pH 7.28, HCO3 18 mmol/L (22 to 26), lactate 2.6 mmol/L (<2), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), paracetamol level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: IV flumazenil 200 microgram bolus and 30 g activated charcoal orally, IV normal saline 500 mL bolus and continuous cardiac monitoring while awaiting further tricyclic drug level results to guide next step
IV amiodarone 300 mg loading dose over 20 minutes for the broad complex rhythm and IV magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus to prevent torsades, then arrange ICU admission for observation
IV sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 100 mL bolus with continuous ECG monitoring, intubation for airway protection, IV potassium replacement and Poisons Information consultation for further boluses
Oral activated charcoal 50 g single dose, IV normal saline maintenance and observation on the emergency short-stay unit for 6 hours before deciding on medical or psychiatric admission
IV physostigmine 1 mg bolus for anticholinergic delirium and dilated pupils, oral magnesium hydroxide for gut decontamination and continuous cardiac monitoring for the next 4 hours

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome recognition and management
stem: A 42-year-old man presents to your emergency department 6 hours after his GP started tramadol 100 mg three times daily for back pain. He has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for 3 years for depression. On arrival he is agitated, sweating and tremulous. Examination shows a rigid trunk but rhythmic lower limb clonus that is more prominent than upper. His temperature is 38.9 C and he is tachycardic. Pupils are widely dilated with brisk hyperreflexia in the lower limbs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 168/98, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent, temp 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Agitated, sweaty, tremulous; dilated pupils; lower limb rhythmic clonus > upper; hyperreflexia lower limbs; rigid trunk but not lead-pipe; alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: CK 250 U/L (<200), Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, VBG pH 7.35

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease sertraline and tramadol, IV fluid resuscitation, IV diazepam 5 to 10 mg titrated for agitation and hyperthermia, active cooling and admit for observation with a target temperature under 38 C
IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally 8 hourly plus IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg loading dose treating neuroleptic malignant syndrome then transfer to intensive care for continuous cardiac monitoring
Continue current medications, start IV paracetamol 1 g and IV metoclopramide 10 mg to control fever and nausea, observation for 6 hours to see if the symptoms settle spontaneously today
IV haloperidol 5 mg for agitation and IV droperidol 10 mg for hyperthermia while continuing tramadol for analgesia and sertraline for underlying depressed mood over the acute presentation window
IV physostigmine 1 mg to reverse anticholinergic delirium and IV lorazepam 2 mg for the tremor while awaiting return of the initial drug screen results to guide further management this evening

subtopic_detail: BPD in ED - self-harm assessment
stem: A 24-year-old woman with a documented diagnosis of borderline personality disorder is brought to your emergency department by her mother at 2 am after cutting her forearms superficially with a broken glass. This is her 8th presentation in 6 months. Her mother reports she was upset after a fight with her boyfriend. On arrival she is tearful but co-operative and denies suicidal intent. Wounds are shallow, non-bleeding and require 3 stitches. She has no acute medical concerns.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Multiple superficial linear lacerations left forearm, shallow bleeding stopped; older well-healed scars right forearm; calm engagement, tearful, orientated; no acute intoxication signs
data_table.Investigations: Not otherwise indicated; BAC 0.02 percent; UDS negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Admit for a minimum 72 hour psychiatric observation on the acute unit for containment given repeat presentations, prescribe olanzapine 5 mg orally at night and defer any outpatient follow-up planning until after discharge
Refer to the on-call psychiatric registrar for consideration of involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act for ongoing suicide risk given the recurrent nature of these episodic presentations

Discharge with paracetamol advice and no formal psychiatric follow-up as she has an established BPD diagnosis and outpatient team, provide a brief written summary to her general practitioner in the morning

Attend to the wounds, calmly discuss the trigger with a validating approach, agree a short crisis plan with her outpatient team including safety planning and dialectical behaviour therapy, arrange follow-up within 48 hours

Prescribe short course quetiapine 25 mg orally three times daily for 2 weeks to manage emotional dysregulation, provide GP letter and discharge without psychiatric team review while she is asymptomatic

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and lorazepam challenge
stem: A 37-year-old woman with bipolar disorder is admitted to your acute psychiatry unit after 5 days of increasing withdrawal, mutism and refusal to eat or drink. On examination she sits motionless on the edge of the bed, mute, staring, does not respond to verbal command but resists passive movement of her limbs. She holds her right arm in the air after you place it there. She has no fever. Recent medications include lithium and olanzapine 20 mg. Bloods including CK, TFT and calcium are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 68, BP 110/72, RR 12, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, gaze fixed; waxy flexibility on limb positioning; posturing sustained 60 seconds; negativism resisting passive movement; grimacing; no lead-pipe rigidity; no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: CK 180 U/L (<200), Na 138 mmol/L, TSH 2.4 mIU/L, calcium 2.35 mmol/L; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and initial management step?

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly for control of the acute agitation and psychotic symptoms and IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg loading dose for the accompanying rigidity while transferring to intensive care
IV lorazepam 2 mg bolus with observation of catatonia scale response over 15 minutes, aiming for at least 50 percent Bush-Francis reduction, and repeat dosing 6-hourly if partial response
Commence sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily and IV normal saline 1000 mL over 4 hours for supportive dehydration management pending psychiatric team review in the morning ward round
Continue olanzapine, add sertraline 50 mg orally daily for underlying mood, IV normal saline 1000 mL over 4 hours and observe for 48 hours in the acute unit for spontaneous response
Refer for ECT the following morning without a lorazepam challenge as ECT is the definitive treatment for catatonia and delaying with a benzodiazepine trial adds no additional diagnostic information

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis and driving obligations
stem: A 30-year-old primary school teacher attends your GP clinic asking for assessment for possible attention deficit hyperactivity disorder after her nephew was diagnosed. She reports lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, chronic time blindness, poor sleep because her mind races, and multiple career changes. Her school reports at age 8 mention she is bright but does not finish her work. She drives daily including for work, has no seizures, no substance use and is otherwise well. She scores 17/24 on the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaging, mild psychomotor restlessness; euthymic; no cognitive deficit at bedside; no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, iron studies within normal limits, FBC and UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence dexamfetamine 5 mg orally twice daily as a therapeutic trial and review clinical response in 4 weeks in general practice before deciding on formal specialist referral for the ADHD assessment

Reassure that the ASRS is only a screening tool with limited specificity, provide sleep hygiene advice and refer for CBT for adult inattention symptoms while deferring any formal diagnostic assessment for 6 months
Advise her to stop driving immediately pending diagnostic assessment and treatment initiation as untreated adult ADHD is deemed to preclude a safe class C car licence under Austroads standards

Order neuropsychological testing including Wisconsin Card Sort and Trail Making tests in general practice to formally diagnose ADHD before making any specialist referral or considering any treatment options

Refer to a psychiatrist or specialist paediatric-adult ADHD service for structured diagnostic assessment including collateral childhood history, comorbidity screen and consideration of stimulant treatment

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder discrimination
stem: A 52-year-old woman is referred to your community mental health team by her GP because for 18 months she has been convinced her neighbour is releasing carbon monoxide gas through her bedroom wall to poison her. She has had the vents boarded up and installed multiple detectors that consistently read zero. She works full-time as a bookkeeper without difficulty, maintains social contact with three long-term friends, and reports no hallucinations. Her mood is euthymic. On mental state she is well-groomed, articulate and no formal thought disorder. Cognitive screen is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well-groomed, articulate; euthymic; no formal thought disorder; single persistent non-bizarre delusion regarding neighbour poisoning; no hallucinations; insight absent regarding delusion, preserved regarding functioning; MMSE 30/30
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.4 mIU/L, B12 320 pmol/L, folate within normal limits, CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and initial pharmacological approach?

options.text: Schizophrenia paranoid subtype; olanzapine 10 mg orally at night with community mental health team weekly follow-up, weight and metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks and 3 months
Late-onset psychosis secondary to dementia; commence donepezil 5 mg orally daily and refer to memory clinic for MRI, formal neuropsychology and progressive cognitive care planning for the household
Delusional disorder (persecutory type); slow low-dose risperidone 0.5 mg orally at night titrated over 6 weeks with regular RANZCP outcome measure review and engagement in trust-building therapy
Brief psychotic disorder; monitor without antipsychotic for 4 weeks awaiting spontaneous resolution, review in 4 weeks with the community mental health team before any pharmacological intervention
Major depressive disorder with psychotic features; sertraline 100 mg orally daily plus low-dose olanzapine 5 mg orally at night as combination pharmacotherapy for mood-congruent psychotic symptoms

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant sequencing
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman in outpatient clinic. She was diagnosed with a first episode of moderate major depressive disorder 14 weeks ago. She commenced sertraline titrated over 6 weeks to 150 mg daily, which she has taken consistently for 8 weeks at the current dose with clear improvement in initiation and appetite but persistent hopelessness, anhedonia and suicidal ideation without plan. PHQ-9 has moved from 20 to 14. Sleep initiation is poor. She tolerates sertraline without side effects, has no active substance use, and completes weekly individual CBT with fidelity. There is no bipolar family history and no manic features. Baseline blood pressure is 118/76.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 42 mcg/L (30-300), vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (>200)
data_table.History: Sertraline 150 mg daily for 8 weeks at target dose, weekly CBT with a psychologist, PHQ-9 20 -> 14 with persistent hopelessness and suicidal ideation, no bipolarity, no substances, no thyroid or cardiac disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose to 200 mg daily and review response at four weeks in clinic
Cross-taper sertraline to venlafaxine extended-release and titrate to 225 mg daily over three weeks
Add fluoxetine 20 mg daily to the current sertraline regimen as combination antidepressant therapy
Add tranylcypromine 10 mg daily on top of the current sertraline for augmentation of antidepressant effect
Cease sertraline abruptly and start amitriptyline 25 mg nightly the next day for treatment-resistant depression

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal management
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 48-year-old man for elective alcohol detoxification. He has been drinking 20 standard drinks per day for 8 years. His last drink was 14 hours ago. He has a history of tonic-clonic seizure during a prior unassisted withdrawal 3 years ago but no delirium tremens. He is medically stable, taking no other substances, and has no benzodiazepine tolerance issues. On admission examination he is tremulous with mild diaphoresis, orientated to person, place and time, and following commands. His CIWA-Ar score is currently 12 and rising over the last 2 hours. He weighs 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.75-1.5), LFTs mildly deranged with AST 92 U/L (<35), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), thiamine and B12 not yet measured
data_table.History: Prior tonic-clonic seizure during unassisted withdrawal, no prior DTs, no other substances, no allergies, weight 82 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Give oral haloperidol 5 mg now and repeat every 4 hours as required for withdrawal-associated agitation
Commence phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous loading dose to prevent further alcohol-withdrawal seizures
Give parenteral thiamine 300 mg then symptom-triggered diazepam by CIWA-Ar with a scheduled loading dose
Prescribe fixed-dose oral diazepam 5 mg every 6 hours regardless of the current CIWA-Ar score
Commence oral naltrexone 50 mg daily now and continue CIWA-Ar assessment every 4 hours through withdrawal

subtopic_detail: Clozapine dosing when a patient stops smoking
stem: A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for four years and smokes 30 cigarettes daily. He is admitted to a smoke-free ward, stops smoking abruptly and accepts nicotine patches.

data_table.Observations: BP 104/68 lying, HR 104, afebrile, full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reduce the clozapine dose and take a clozapine plasma level today
Withhold clozapine for 48 hours and repeat the full blood count
Continue the current dose and add benztropine for the hypersalivation
Remove the nicotine patch, since it raises the clozapine level
Increase the clozapine dose to cover the stress of admission

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar called by the postnatal ward at 02:00. A 32-year-old primipara is 9 days postnatal after a normal vaginal delivery. Over the last 48 hours she has been increasingly agitated, sleeping less than 2 hours per night, speaking pressured and rapidly about needing to protect the baby from spiritual harm, and today insisted the baby is possessed and requires cleansing rituals. She has personal history of bipolar I disorder untreated in pregnancy following her decision to stop lithium 3 years ago when planning conception. Her mother had a psychiatric admission after her own second child was born. On assessment tonight she is disorientated to date, has fluctuating attention, and told the midwife earlier that she saw shadows moving around the baby's cot. Baby is currently with her partner in the ward.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 112, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH 1.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, urinalysis clear, no illicit substance use, CT head deferred pending medical review
data_table.History: 9 days postpartum, prior bipolar I stopped lithium 3 years ago, maternal aunt puerperal admission, agitation with delusional beliefs about baby, hallucinations reported, sleep <2 h nightly for 48 h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Discharge overnight with the partner as informal supervision and outpatient perinatal team follow-up in 48 hours
Prescribe oral zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly to normalise sleep and review the ward assessment during daytime rounds
Remove the baby from the ward tonight and commence sertraline 50 mg for postpartum depression with psychotic features
Admit to a mother-baby psychiatric unit under mental health legislation and start olanzapine with perinatal plan
Give intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg and physical restraint pending transfer to a general adult psychiatric unit

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced vs primary psychosis
stem: You are the mental health registrar reviewing a 20-year-old male university student in a community psychiatric emergency clinic. Over the past 6 weeks he has developed persecutory delusions about being tracked by a coordinated group, auditory hallucinations of two voices commenting on his behaviour, and social withdrawal. Onset was gradual over 4 weeks; the last 2 weeks his function has collapsed. He commenced daily high-potency cannabis (~1.5 g/day of a THC-dominant product) 12 months ago and stopped completely 3 weeks ago on family insistence. There is no other substance use, no alcohol above two standard drinks per week, no synthetic cannabinoid use, no prescribed medications, no head injury, no seizure history. There is a family history of schizophrenia in a maternal uncle. Mental state examination confirms first-rank symptoms with preserved orientation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, LFTs normal, urine drug screen positive for cannabinoids (from prior use, up to 30 days), negative for methamphetamine and cocaine, CT head normal
data_table.History: 6 weeks psychotic symptoms, cannabis daily 12 months then stopped 3 weeks ago, no other substances, family history schizophrenia (maternal uncle), function collapsed over 2 weeks

lead_in: How would you formulate this presentation and what is the most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Diagnose cannabis-induced psychotic disorder likely to resolve within 24 hours and observe without any antipsychotic
Commence lorazepam 1 mg twice daily as required and defer antipsychotic while awaiting spontaneous resolution over weeks
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as first-line therapy for likely major depression with psychotic features
Commence quetiapine 100 mg titrated to 400 mg over 4 weeks as first-line therapy for likely bipolar depression
Commence risperidone titrated to 2 to 4 mg, refer to early psychosis intervention, and provide cannabis relapse plan

subtopic_detail: Autism spectrum disorder in adult women
stem: You are the general practice registrar in an adult clinic. A 28-year-old professional woman presents with 12 months of severe fatigue and burnout following a workplace restructure. She reports lifelong difficulty with sustained group social interaction, exhaustion after work social events, intense special interests (medieval history, and prior periods of hyper-focused folklore research), sensory sensitivities to fluorescent light and clothing labels, and a longstanding sense of masking to fit in socially. She has previously been diagnosed with anxiety and depression at ages 16 and 22 with only partial response to sertraline and CBT. She has close but limited friendships with women who share her special interests. Her general practitioner is considering a formal neurodevelopmental assessment. She is not autistic-identifying at this time. She has no psychotic features, no substance use, and no mood elevation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 62 mcg/L (30-300), vitamin D 68 nmol/L (>50), TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and glucose within normal limits, PHQ-9 12 (mild-moderate), GAD-7 14 (moderate), AUDIT 3, PDSS-SR 6
data_table.History: 12 months burnout, lifelong social difficulty, intense special interests, sensory sensitivities, masking; prior anxiety and depression diagnoses partially responsive to sertraline and CBT; no psychosis, no substances, no mood elevation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in your assessment plan?

options.text: Refer for structured autism assessment with ADOS-2 and ADI-R and continue psychological therapy for anxiety in parallel
Reassure her this is generalised anxiety disorder and increase sertraline to the maximum dose of 200 mg daily
Perform brief AQ-10 screening and, if score under 6, discharge from any further adult neurodevelopmental workup
Commence a trial of methylphenidate 10 mg daily for suspected adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder empirically
Refer for inpatient adult psychiatric admission today for stabilisation of burnout and multi-system fatigue symptoms

subtopic_detail: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to see a 22-year-old woman on the medical ward. She was admitted 3 days ago via emergency after 2 weeks of subacute onset of behavioural change (odd laughter, agitation), paranoid delusions, and orofacial dyskinesias. During today's ward round she had a 90 second focal aware seizure with right facial twitching and afterwards was mute for 20 minutes. Vital signs earlier showed transient tachycardia to 138 and blood pressure fluctuation between 92/58 and 168/98 within 30 minutes. The bedside neurological examination is inconsistent. She has no prior psychiatric or seizure history. She does not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit substances. Screening MRI brain has been reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118 with fluctuation, blood pressure fluctuating 92/58 to 168/98, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: full blood count within normal limits, urea 5.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 68 micromol/L (60-110), C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (<5), TSH within normal limits, HIV and syphilis serology negative, urine drug screen negative, MRI brain normal, EEG shows generalised slowing with extreme delta brush pattern intermittently, CSF pleocytosis 42 white cells/microL with lymphocyte predominance and elevated CSF protein 0.68 g/L (<0.45), CSF glucose within normal limits, oligoclonal bands positive
data_table.History: 2 weeks subacute behavioural change, dyskinesias, focal seizure today, autonomic instability, no substances, no prior psychiatric or neurological history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally daily for suspected first-episode psychosis and defer further neurological workup
Send CSF and serum for anti-NMDA antibody, image pelvis for teratoma, and start empirical first-line immunotherapy
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for likely conversion disorder and refer to outpatient psychiatry follow-up
Load with sodium valproate 20 mg/kg intravenously and monitor for further seizures without further diagnostic workup
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy given the presence of catatonic features and prominent orofacial dyskinesias

subtopic_detail: Treatment-refractory schizophrenia after clozapine myocarditis
stem: You are the senior psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man with schizophrenia. He has failed adequate trials (>=6 weeks at target dose) of risperidone 6 mg, olanzapine 20 mg and paliperidone 12 mg. Two years ago clozapine was commenced but ceased at week 3 for probable clozapine-induced myocarditis (troponin rise to 220 ng/L, CRP 82 mg/L, echocardiogram showed globally reduced LV function with EF 42%, no other cause identified). He was rehospitalised. Over the past 2 years he has been on aripiprazole 30 mg plus lurasidone 120 mg with persistent auditory hallucinations, negative symptoms and social withdrawal. Most recent echocardiogram (this week) shows LV EF 60% with no wall motion abnormality. He has been abstinent from all recreational substances for 12 months. Cardiology has been consulted.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count with neutrophils 4.8 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), troponin 6 ng/L (<15), NT-proBNP 62 pg/mL (<125), echocardiogram LV EF 60% with no wall motion abnormality and no diastolic dysfunction, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 420 ms
data_table.History: Schizophrenia with failure of 3 adequate atypical trials, clozapine ceased for myocarditis 2 years ago, current medications aripiprazole + lurasidone with persistent positive and negative symptoms, cardiology reviewed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for symptom control?

options.text: Refer for maintenance bilateral electroconvulsive therapy three times weekly indefinitely as ongoing symptom control
Add high-dose quetiapine 800 mg nightly to the current aripiprazole plus lurasidone regimen and continue indefinitely
Undertake supervised clozapine re-challenge with slower titration and structured cardiac surveillance with cardiology
Discontinue all antipsychotic medication and manage with high-dose lorazepam 4 mg four times daily for symptom control
Add long-acting paliperidone 150 mg intramuscular injection monthly to the current oral aripiprazole and lurasidone

subtopic_detail: Lithium initiation baseline workup
stem: You are the community psychiatry registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman with confirmed bipolar I disorder, currently euthymic 4 weeks after a hypomanic episode. She has had two clear manic episodes and one depressive episode in the past 3 years. The consultant recommends starting lithium for maintenance. She has no significant medical history, is not pregnant (LMP 1 week ago, using condoms consistently), is a non-smoker, and drinks 4 standard drinks weekly. She takes no regular medications and has no known allergies. She wants to complete her studies and eventually plan a pregnancy in 2 to 3 years.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.History: Bipolar I, 2 manic + 1 depressive episodes over 3 years, currently euthymic, LMP 1 week ago, no meds, no comorbidities

lead_in: Which baseline investigation set is most appropriate before starting lithium?

options.text: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, HbA1c, and vitamin B12 only; no imaging or ECG required before initiation
Urea, creatinine, electrolytes, thyroid function, calcium, ECG, pregnancy test, and weight recorded today
MRI brain and EEG to rule out structural or epileptic conditions before beginning any mood stabiliser treatment
24-hour urine collection for creatinine clearance and iothalamate GFR before every mood stabiliser starts today
Fasting lipids, iron studies, HbA1c, and echocardiogram are all required baseline tests before starting lithium

subtopic_detail: Initial organic screen
stem: You are the ED registrar assessing a 19-year-old university student brought in by parents with a 3 week history of paranoid delusions (belief he is being tracked), auditory hallucinations, and social withdrawal. He denies substance use but parents suspect cannabis. He has no fever, no headache, no neurological symptoms, no seizures, and no recent travel. He is on no medications and has no personal or family history of psychiatric illness. He appears clinically well hydrated and oriented. Physical and neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.MSE: Thought-disordered, paranoid delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, blunted affect, cognition intact
data_table.Neuro: GCS 15, cranial nerves intact, no focal deficits, no meningism, no movement abnormalities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation set?

options.text: MRI brain with contrast and lumbar puncture for CSF anti-NMDA antibodies on every first episode of psychosis case
24-hour urinary catecholamines and metanephrines to rule out phaeochromocytoma-related psychiatric manifestations
FBC, UEC, LFTs, CRP, TFTs, B12/folate, urine drug screen, hCG if appropriate, and CT brain if focal signs
PET scan of the brain to characterise dopamine receptor availability before commencing any antipsychotic therapy
Full lupus autoantibody panel including ANA, dsDNA, ENA, complement, ANCA at the first ED assessment routinely

subtopic_detail: Acute mania first-line pharmacotherapy
stem: You are the psychiatric registrar admitting a 28-year-old man with 6 days of florid mania: elevated mood, grandiose delusions of being a business magnate, 2 hours sleep per night, pressured speech, and disinhibited spending. He has a 2 year history of bipolar I with 3 prior admissions. He is not on any current mood stabiliser (stopped lithium 6 months ago due to weight gain). He has no medical comorbidities, no substance use, and is not planning fatherhood. He is willing to take oral medication.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 98, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.MSE: Elevated mood, grandiose delusions, pressured speech, flight of ideas, no active psychotic threat
data_table.Bloods: UEC, LFTs, TSH, calcium all normal; beta hCG not applicable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrated to therapeutic dose plus zolpidem 10 mg nocte for sleep for two weeks
Carbamazepine 200 mg oral BD titrated with therapeutic drug monitoring plus prazosin 1 mg for sleep at night
Diazepam 10 mg TDS as monotherapy for 2 weeks until behavioural containment allows further treatment consideration
Olanzapine 10 mg oral daily, titrating up over 3 days, with lorazepam 1 to 2 mg TDS for acute agitation and sleep
Electroconvulsive therapy this week as first-line treatment before any trial of pharmacological options is undertaken

subtopic_detail: PTSD first-line management
stem: You are the GP seeing a 34-year-old man 4 months after a serious motor vehicle accident. He describes intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of driving, hypervigilance and irritability. Symptoms are causing occupational impairment. He has no current mood disorder criteria met, no active substance misuse, and no suicidal ideation. He has no significant past psychiatric history and no current medications. He asks how to get better without medication if possible.

data_table.History: MVA 4 months ago, meets DSM-5-TR PTSD criteria, occupational impairment, no comorbid MDD or SUD
