data_table.MSE: Anxious mood, congruent affect, no psychotic features, cognition intact, no self-harm
data_table.Function: Off work 3 months, avoiding driving, sleep 4 hours per night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrated to 100 mg after 2 weeks and continued for at least 12 months as monotherapy
Prazosin 1 mg orally nocte, titrated for nightmares, as sole intervention without psychotherapy or SSRI cover
Diazepam 5 mg TDS for 6 weeks to reduce hyperarousal symptoms and improve sleep architecture during recovery period
Quetiapine 50 mg nocte for insomnia and low-dose paroxetine for daytime symptoms with weekly follow up review
Trauma-focused CBT (or EMDR) with weekly sessions over 8 to 12 weeks as first-line evidence-based psychotherapy

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine dependence taper
stem: You are the GP seeing a 48-year-old woman on alprazolam 1 mg three times daily for 6 years, initially started for panic disorder. She wants to reduce and eventually stop. She has no current alcohol misuse, no seizure history, and no current mood disorder criteria met. She has partner support and is committed to a slow taper. She has no active plans to conceive and has no other benzodiazepines or z-drugs prescribed. She is otherwise well and on no other regular medications.

data_table.History: Alprazolam 1 mg TDS for 6 years, wants to stop, no alcohol misuse, no seizures, no MDD, supportive partner
data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 122/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.MSE: Anxious but not depressed, no psychosis, no active self-harm, cognition intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?

options.text: Convert to equivalent diazepam and reduce by 10 percent of the current dose every 2 to 4 weeks with monitoring
Stop alprazolam abruptly today and prescribe zopiclone 7.5 mg nocte for sleep for 4 weeks then review the taper
Add mirtazapine 30 mg nocte and continue current alprazolam dose indefinitely because it is providing symptomatic relief
Refer for inpatient detoxification and admission for rapid clonidine-assisted withdrawal over a 7 to 10 day period
Prescribe flumazenil infusion in a monitored day-stay unit to accelerate receptor recovery over a 4 to 7 day admission

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and initial management
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman with a 12-year history of bipolar I disorder on lithium and quetiapine, admitted to the medical ward 3 days ago after her family found her mute in bed. She has stopped eating and drinking, is refusing medication, and has been withdrawn from the community mental health service for two months.

On examination she is awake with eyes open, staring past you, not responsive to questioning. When you raise her right arm above her head it remains suspended for over 60 seconds. She exhibits echopraxia when you touch your nose. When you attempt to move her limb she resists with equal counter-force in both directions. She has been afebrile, saturations normal, blood pressure 128/78, pulse 92. Bloods including CK, TFTs, calcium, and infection screen are normal. Head CT is unremarkable. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 18.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: CK 148 U/L (<170), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), infection screen negative, head CT unremarkable
data_table.Exam: mute, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, gegenhalten, BFCRS 18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Give IM haloperidol 5 mg to sedate her and enable enteral feeding via nasogastric tube for adequate hydration
Continue current quetiapine and start olanzapine 10 mg for suspected relapse of bipolar affective disorder with psychosis
Commence electroconvulsive therapy immediately without first trialling any benzodiazepine treatment for this presentation
Give IV lorazepam 2 mg as a challenge and observe for symptomatic response over 5 to 10 minutes
Start amantadine 100 mg 12-hourly for NMDA-glutamate modulation as first-line therapy for treatment-refractory catatonia today

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome in anorexia nervosa admission
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman referred from the eating disorders clinic. She has a 4-year history of anorexia nervosa (restrictive subtype) and has lost 8 kg over 2 months. Current BMI is 12.8 (weight 34 kg, height 163 cm). She is bradycardic at 42, blood pressure 88/54 lying and 74/48 standing, temperature 35.4, ECG shows sinus bradycardia with corrected QT of 460 ms and prominent U waves.

Admission bloods: sodium 138, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, albumin 34 g/L, creatinine 42 umol/L, calcium 2.20 mmol/L, LFTs mildly deranged with ALT 68 U/L.

The medical team has been asked to plan refeeding. She has been eating minimal food for two weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 42, blood pressure 88/54 lying and 74/48 standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 35.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, ALT 68 U/L
data_table.ECG: sinus bradycardia 42, QTc 460 ms, prominent U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate refeeding plan?

options.text: Withhold all nutrition for 48 hours to allow gradual electrolyte normalisation then start at 15 kcal/kg/day with oral supplements once stable
Commence a standard maintenance diet at 30 kcal/kg/day today with oral supplementation and correct electrolytes only if levels fall further
Insert a nasogastric tube and deliver 100 percent of estimated caloric needs immediately by continuous feed to accelerate weight restoration
Give a rapid IV glucose bolus of 200 mL 10 percent dextrose to correct hypoglycaemia, then start standard diet at full maintenance today
Start oral thiamine 200 mg daily, correct electrolyte deficits first, then commence energy at 20 kcal/kg/day and increase over 5 to 7 days

subtopic_detail: Acute-on-chronic lithium toxicity with renal impairment
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 62-year-old woman with a 25-year history of bipolar I on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for maintenance. She started ramipril 10 mg for hypertension 3 weeks ago and had a gastroenteritis 4 days ago. Her family brought her in because she has been increasingly confused, tremulous, and unsteady over 48 hours. On examination she is drowsy (GCS 12), coarse tremor of both hands, hyperreflexia, myoclonic jerks, ataxia. She is not febrile.

Bloods: lithium level 3.4 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6 to 1.0), sodium 148 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 216 umol/L (baseline 78 six months ago), eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. TFTs normal. Anion gap normal. ECG shows sinus rhythm at 92 with T-wave flattening and one PVC per 10 beats.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: lithium 3.4 mmol/L (0.6-1.0 therapeutic), sodium 148 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 216 umol/L (baseline 78), eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2
data_table.Neuro: GCS 12, coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, ataxia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold lithium, commence IV 0.9 percent saline at maintenance plus 5 percent deficit, and refer to renal for urgent haemodialysis
Give IV activated charcoal 50 g nasogastrically to reduce further lithium absorption before further specific management
Commence forced alkaline diuresis with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to accelerate renal lithium clearance
Continue lithium at a reduced dose of 250 mg nocte and add oral quetiapine 50 mg for symptomatic control while awaiting stabilisation
Give intravenous physostigmine 2 mg to reverse the anticholinergic effects contributing to her acute confusional state

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on-call reviewing a 42-year-old man admitted 48 hours ago after presenting acutely psychotic and agitated. He was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg BD and lorazepam 2 mg TDS. He has a background of major depressive disorder for which he takes citalopram 40 mg, and his GP added tramadol 100 mg TDS two weeks ago for back pain. Overnight he became increasingly restless, developed generalised tremor, and vomited twice.

On examination: temperature 38.6, pulse 128, blood pressure 168/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96 percent on room air. He is alert and oriented but confused. Pupils are 6 mm, reactive. Marked lower-limb hyperreflexia with inducible ankle clonus (6 beats) and spontaneous myoclonic jerks. Increased tone in the legs more than the arms. Bowel sounds hyperactive. Diaphoretic. CK 220 U/L (below 170).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 168/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: CK 220 U/L (<170), WCC 10.4 x10^9/L, creatinine 84 umol/L, lithium not applicable
data_table.Neuro: 6 mm reactive pupils, lower limb hyperreflexia > upper, inducible ankle clonus 6 beats, myoclonic jerks, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; stop olanzapine, commence dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV and bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally
Serotonin syndrome; cease citalopram and tramadol, provide supportive care with IV fluids and benzodiazepines, add cyproheptadine 12 mg orally if severe
Anticholinergic toxidrome; give physostigmine 2 mg IV and monitor cardiac rhythm continuously until symptoms resolve
Sympathomimetic toxidrome from illicit stimulant use; administer IV benzodiazepines only and observe for clinical improvement
Malignant hyperthermia; give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV every 5 minutes and active surface cooling with ice packs and fanning

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder in crisis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on-call in ED reviewing a 27-year-old woman brought by ambulance after making superficial parallel cuts to her left forearm. She has known borderline personality disorder, is engaged with a public mental health service where she attends weekly DBT skills group and monthly psychiatrist review. She has 14 prior admissions for self-harm and one prior serious attempt with paracetamol overdose 3 years ago. Tonight she cut after an argument with her partner. She has not consumed alcohol or drugs.

On assessment she is calm, engaged, and future-oriented. She apologises for coming in and says she used all her DBT skills first, only cut after they failed. She wants to go home. She has no active plan, has removed the razor blades from her flat, has agreed to phone her case manager tomorrow morning, and will attend group later this week. Her partner is present, supportive, and can stay with her overnight. Wounds do not require sutures.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Assessment: calm, engaged, apologetic, future-oriented, denies active plan, DBT-engaged, safety plan in place, partner supportive
data_table.Wound: 3 superficial parallel forearm cuts, no bleeding, dressed, no suture needed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act to a psychiatric ward for observation given the pattern of repeated self-harm
Refer for a 6 to 8 week course of ECT to reduce her recurrent affective dysregulation and self-harm behaviours
Admit voluntarily to a psychiatric ward for a 3 to 5 day break and commence olanzapine 5 mg for affective instability during admission
Discharge with a joint written safety plan, contact her case manager tomorrow, and arrange next scheduled DBT session as planned this week
Prescribe short-course diazepam 5 mg TDS for 2 weeks and increase her SSRI dose empirically to reduce chronic self-harm behaviour

subtopic_detail: Bipolar I depressive episode pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder (diagnosed at 22, 3 prior manic episodes, 4 prior depressive episodes) currently in a 5-week depressive episode. She has low mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia (sleeping 12 to 14 hours), psychomotor slowing, guilt, poor concentration, and passive suicidal thoughts without plan. She stopped lithium 4 months ago because she disliked hand tremor and lost weight. She has never taken an antidepressant.

Her weight is 68 kg, BMI 24. Thyroid function normal, U&Es normal (eGFR over 90), creatinine 62 umol/L. Her most recent manic episode was 3 years ago on lithium monotherapy at level 0.6 mmol/L; she was hospitalised for two weeks. She and her husband are planning a pregnancy in the next 12 to 18 months.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: TSH 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 62 umol/L, eGFR >90, calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), pregnancy test negative
data_table.History: bipolar I, 3 manic and 4 depressive episodes, off lithium 4 months, planning pregnancy 12-18 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for this depressive episode?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte plus fluoxetine 20 mg daily (OFC combination) as first-line for the current bipolar depressive episode
Commence sertraline 50 mg alone with no mood stabiliser cover because the priority is treating the acute depressive episode symptomatically
Commence sodium valproate 500 mg BD as monotherapy for both mood stabilisation and treatment of the depressive episode she now has
Commence carbamazepine 200 mg BD as first-line mood stabiliser and add fluoxetine 20 mg for the current depressive symptomatology
Restart lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte alone, target level 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L, and involve reproductive psychiatry for pregnancy planning

subtopic_detail: Postnatal depression identified at 6-week check
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 32-year-old primiparous woman at her routine 6-week postnatal check. Her baby is thriving and exclusively breastfed. She scored 15 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) today (positive 13 or above), scoring 1 on item 10 (thought of harming self). She reports 4 weeks of persistent low mood, tearfulness most days, sleep disruption beyond baby's feeds, feeling overwhelmed, and reduced enjoyment of her baby. She denies thoughts of harming the baby. There is no personal history of psychiatric illness. Her mother had postnatal depression.

She has no active suicidal plan or intent, no psychotic features, no acute safety concerns. Her partner is supportive and present. Social support is intact. Physical examination and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), FBC and iron studies unremarkable
data_table.Assessment: EPDS 15, item 10 score 1 (occasional thoughts, no active plan), no psychosis, partner supportive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Advise her to stop breastfeeding immediately so that safe pharmacotherapy can be commenced without concern for infant exposure
Commence sertraline 25 mg titrated to 50 mg daily monotherapy alone for depression without any psychological therapy referral in first-line management
Refer for structured psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT) with GP review in 2 weeks and safety plan for any escalation
Admit to a mother-baby unit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act for immediate psychiatric assessment and stabilisation
Reassure her that this is baby blues and will resolve spontaneously in the next 2 weeks; follow up if not improving

subtopic_detail: 17 year old cannabis user with 3 months of delusions and functional decline
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 17-year-old boy referred by his GP with 3 months of persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, and withdrawal from school. He has been using cannabis 4 times a week since age 15. His mother describes him as flat, suspicious, and staying awake at night. There is no substance intoxication currently and no acute suicidality or violence. He has no medical comorbidity. Physical examination and bloods are normal. He is engaged with his mother and willing to try treatment.

He is being seen in the Early Intervention Service outpatient clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 68 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT normal, urine drug screen positive cannabis only, HbA1c 33 mmol/mol, prolactin 320 mIU/L (males under 350)
data_table.Imaging: MRI brain unremarkable, ECG QTc 400 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: SSRI sertraline 50 mg orally daily as first line because cannabis-induced anxiety underlies the presentation
Olanzapine 20 mg orally at night at full target dose from day one to control positive symptoms rapidly
Haloperidol 10 mg orally daily and lithium 800 mg orally at night for mood stabilisation as first therapy
Clozapine 12.5 mg orally at night and titrate over 2 weeks alongside weekly full blood count monitoring
Risperidone 1 mg orally at night with slow titration to 2 to 4 mg daily, plus psychosocial support in EIS

subtopic_detail: CIWA 22 with tremor and tachycardia at day 2
stem:
You are the psychiatry consultation liaison registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man 36 hours after admission to a medical ward for pancreatitis. He drinks 200 g alcohol daily. He is tremulous, sweating, agitated, and disoriented to time. Heart rate is 128 and blood pressure 168/98. He has had a single 5 mg IV diazepam so far. CIWA-Ar score is now 22. Blood alcohol is zero. He has no seizure yet. Magnesium is 0.62, potassium 3.4. He is nil by mouth for pancreatitis.

The medical team asks about withdrawal management.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 168/98, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.5 degrees Celsius, weight 82 kg
data_table.Bloods: sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), glucose 6.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), lipase 780 U/L (10-60), CK 240 U/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV diazepam 10 mg boluses every 15 minutes until CIWA under 10, plus IV thiamine 300 mg daily and magnesium replacement
Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg 6 hourly fixed schedule for 5 days and oral thiamine 100 mg once daily
IV haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg IM to sedate the agitation without further benzodiazepine
IV dextrose 50 percent 50 mL bolus first for hypoglycaemia risk then thiamine 100 mg IV over 2 hours after
IV clonidine 150 mcg boluses only to lower blood pressure and pulse, without benzodiazepine or thiamine therapy

subtopic_detail: Generalised tonic clonic seizure at day 3 of withdrawal on the ward
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to a 60-year-old man on day 3 of an admission for alcohol withdrawal. He has just had a witnessed 90 second generalised tonic clonic seizure. He is now post-ictal and confused with GCS 12. He was on oral diazepam 10 mg 6 hourly as needed. He is diaphoretic, tremulous, and tachycardic. He has had no vomiting and airway is patent. Point-of-care glucose is 4.6 and sodium is 132. Magnesium is 0.55. He has no head injury. He is being nursed in a general medical bay.

The consultant is on their way. You must act now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 172/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius, GCS 12 post-ictal
data_table.Bloods: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.55 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), ethanol 0 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: CT brain arranged non-urgently after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV phenytoin 20 mg per kg loading dose infused over 30 minutes and continue oral diazepam as previously prescribed
IV lorazepam 4 mg bolus now with airway support, IV thiamine 300 mg, IV magnesium 10 mmol over 1 hour, transfer to HDU
IV levetiracetam 60 mg per kg loading dose alone and no additional benzodiazepine for the withdrawal seizure now
IV thiopental 3 mg per kg for immediate seizure abortion and paralysis with rocuronium for tracheal intubation
IV haloperidol 5 mg and lorazepam 1 mg IM to manage agitation, and defer thiamine until confirmed nutritional status

subtopic_detail: Persistent orofacial dyskinesia after 5 years of antipsychotic therapy
stem:
You are the community psychiatrist reviewing a 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia stable on risperidone 4 mg daily for 5 years. She has developed persistent tongue protrusion, lip smacking, and choreoathetoid movements of her fingers over the past 6 months. The Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score is 12. She has not had recent dose changes. She is not depressed and functioning well socially. Reducing or switching antipsychotic in the past has caused relapse. She is on no other movement affecting medication.

She finds the movements distressing.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 76 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, calcium and copper normal, HbA1c 41 mmol/mol, prolactin 620 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Add propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily and continue current antipsychotic without switching agent
Add oral benzatropine 2 mg orally twice daily as anticholinergic therapy for the involuntary movements now
Add valbenazine 40 mg orally once daily, uptitrate to 80 mg after 1 week if tolerated and monitor for sedation
Increase risperidone dose to 6 mg orally daily to suppress the movements and manage residual psychotic symptoms
Switch to clozapine 12.5 mg orally at night with weekly full blood count first line as best option for TD control

subtopic_detail: Severe depression with psychosis and food refusal, prior medication failure
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman admitted involuntarily for severe depression with mood congruent psychotic delusions of decay and 4 weeks of food and fluid refusal. She has lost 12 kg. She has failed adequate trials of sertraline and mirtazapine over 6 months. She is now dehydrated, bradycardic, and mute. Blood tests show mild AKI. She has capacity assessed as impaired for treatment decisions. Her adult daughter is her formally appointed medical treatment decision maker and consents to ECT. There are no contraindications.

An anaesthetist has assessed her and approves ECT under general anaesthetic.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 56, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, weight 52 kg (was 64 kg)
data_table.Bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 128 umol/L (45-90), ECG sinus bradycardia QTc 420 ms
data_table.Imaging: CT brain no acute pathology or mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: IV ketamine 0.5 mg per kg over 40 minutes weekly in outpatient clinic as first line therapy after medication failure
Trial venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily uptitrating over 4 weeks before considering electroconvulsive therapy referral
Add lithium 400 mg orally at night augmentation of current SSRI as first step before any ECT is considered
Start twice weekly bitemporal ECT with 6 to 12 sessions expected, rehydrate first, prescribe pre-ECT metoclopramide and monitor cognition
IV clomipramine 25 mg daily infusion titrated up over 10 days as intravenous antidepressant instead of ECT

subtopic_detail: Chronic post traumatic stress with dissociation after childhood abuse
stem:
You are the psychiatry consultant reviewing a 34-year-old woman with 10 years of intrusive memories, dissociative episodes, chronic nightmares, hyperarousal, and unstable relationships since childhood sexual abuse. She has tried sertraline for 6 months at 200 mg with partial response. She is stable psychosocially with supportive partner and no active substance use. She has no current suicidal intent but self-harmed 6 months ago. She wants to reduce dissociation and nightmares. She has read about EMDR and asks whether it might help her.

She is engaged and prefers a structured psychological approach.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 68 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT normal, HbA1c 34 mmol/mol, no substance use on urine screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her care?

options.text: Refer for supportive counselling only and continue current sertraline without additional pharmacological or psychological therapy
Switch sertraline to venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily and add quetiapine 100 mg at night for dissociation control
Start clonazepam 0.5 mg at night for hyperarousal and defer psychological therapy until symptoms are controlled first
Add mirtazapine 30 mg at night for sleep and continue sertraline without any psychological intervention referral
Refer for trauma-focused psychological therapy (either EMDR or trauma-focused CBT), and add prazosin 1 mg at night for nightmares

subtopic_detail: Treatment intensity selection when psychosis is mood-congruent
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team reviewing a 52-year-old man referred by his general practitioner after 6 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking, 4 kg weight loss, and psychomotor retardation. In the last week he has developed the belief that his liver is rotting and that he does not deserve to eat. He denies command hallucinations and current suicidal plan but describes passive death wishes. He is a lawyer with previously good function. He has no prior mental health history and is not on any medications.

His wife has taken time off work to stay with him and is present with him today.

data_table.MSE: flat affect, thought content includes nihilistic delusion (rotting liver), passive death wish, no perceptual disturbance elicited
data_table.Bloods: urea, electrolytes, LFTs, TSH, B12, folate within normal limits
data_table.Weight: 4 kg loss over 6 weeks, currently 68 kg
data_table.Suicide risk: no plan, no means, passive death wish, wife providing support

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily as monotherapy with follow up in 2 weeks in the community mental health team clinic setting
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone with medication review deferred until 6 sessions have been completed
Combined sertraline 50 mg with olanzapine 5 mg nocte, admission for observation and safety planning with the wife
Commence olanzapine 10 mg monotherapy nocte for the psychotic symptoms with weekly community follow up appointments
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily for sleep and anxiety while awaiting outpatient psychiatry review appointment

subtopic_detail: Switching to diazepam equivalent for stepwise reduction
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 46-year-old woman who has been taking oxazepam 15 mg three times daily for 4 years for generalised anxiety, initially prescribed by a previous doctor. She wants to reduce and stop and has read about withdrawal risks. She has no history of substance use. She works as an accountant and manages her business commitments. She has no current suicidal ideation and her mood is generally good. She has already commenced cognitive behavioural therapy sessions for anxiety.

Her BMI, blood pressure and screening bloods are within normal limits.

data_table.Medication history: oxazepam 15 mg TDS for 4 years, no other psychotropics
data_table.Comorbidity: no substance use, mood generally euthymic, function preserved
data_table.Support: engaged in CBT with clinical psychologist, husband supportive
data_table.Bloods: LFTs, UEC, TFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological approach?

options.text: Continue oxazepam TDS and reduce the dose by 15 mg every fortnight over 6 weeks in a monitored stepwise approach
Add pregabalin 75 mg twice daily indefinitely to cover withdrawal symptoms without a taper of the benzodiazepine
Ceasing oxazepam abruptly and providing propranolol 40 mg twice daily for autonomic symptoms of withdrawal
Switch to alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily and taper over 6 to 8 weeks with monthly medical review appointments
Switch to diazepam 15 mg daily equivalent and reduce by 10 percent of the daily dose every 2 to 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: First-line agent selection when antidepressants have destabilised
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder in the crisis assessment team clinic. She was diagnosed 4 years ago after a manic episode and stabilised on lithium. Three months ago her general practitioner added sertraline for a low mood episode. Today she presents with 2 weeks of low mood, tearfulness, and hopelessness combined with pressured speech, marked irritability, racing thoughts, and reduced sleep. Suicide ideation is present without plan. She has full insight and no psychosis. Lithium level 2 days ago was 0.8 mmol/L.

Her partner has driven her to the review after concerns her mood swings have escalated.

data_table.MSE: labile affect, tearful with pressured speech, thought racing, no psychosis, insight preserved, suicidal ideation without plan
data_table.Bloods: lithium 0.8 mmol/L (0.6-1.0), TSH within normal limits, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR >90
data_table.Medications: lithium carbonate 800 mg nocte, sertraline 100 mg mane (started 3 months ago)
data_table.Sleep: reduced from 8 to 4 hours per night in last 10 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her medication regimen?

options.text: Cease sertraline and add quetiapine 300 mg nocte for the mixed features, continuing lithium at the current dose regimen
Increase lithium to 1000 mg nocte to target a level above 0.8 mmol/L for enhanced mixed features stabilisation
Switch sertraline to venlafaxine XR 150 mg daily to improve the depressive symptoms with more potent SNRI activity
Add lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated to 100 mg over 6 weeks with continuation of both lithium and current sertraline
Continue sertraline and add diazepam 5 mg twice daily as short term symptomatic management for the current agitation

subtopic_detail: Trauma-focused therapy timing versus early pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old woman 4 months after a serious motor vehicle collision in which she was the driver and a friend passenger died. She describes nightmares 4 to 5 nights per week, avoiding driving past the site, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, and intrusive memories. Sleep is 4 hours per night. Her mood is low but she has no suicidal ideation. She is functioning at reduced capacity in her work as a teacher. She has no prior mental health history and is not on any medications.

She asks what is likely to help her recover.

data_table.MSE: anxious, tearful describing the collision, no psychosis, sleep 4 hours, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Substance use: no alcohol, no illicit substances, no benzodiazepine use
data_table.Comorbidity: no diagnosed depression or anxiety, no prior trauma disclosed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg twice daily for anxiety and insomnia with plan to review at monthly intervals for symptom improvement
Sertraline 50 mg daily first-line with review at 4 weeks and titration up to 200 mg for full antidepressant effect
Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing over 8 to 12 sessions
Prazosin 1 mg nocte titrated to 6 mg for nightmares with no other psychological or pharmacological therapy started
Debriefing single session with a trauma counsellor within the next week to prevent chronic PTSD development in future

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic selection when cannabis co-morbidity is dominant
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the early psychosis service reviewing a 20-year-old university student with 3 weeks of increasingly disorganised speech, persecutory delusions that his housemates are recording him, and third-person auditory hallucinations. He has been smoking around 3 g of high-potency cannabis daily for 18 months, with insight lost 4 weeks ago. He is otherwise physically well. There is a paternal uncle with schizophrenia. He has no prior psychiatric contact. He is currently residing with his mother who has agreed to support him at home during any pharmacotherapy trial.

He accepts oral treatment and refuses depot injection at this stage.

data_table.MSE: disorganised speech, persecutory delusions, third-person AH, no suicidal ideation, insight impaired
data_table.Bloods: urea, electrolytes, LFTs, TSH, glucose, lipids, prolactin within normal limits
data_table.Urine drug screen: positive THC, negative amphetamines, cocaine, opioids
data_table.Weight: 78 kg, BMI 24, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HDL 1.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oral antipsychotic choice?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg nocte titrated to 20 mg as first-line therapy given its rapid effect and reliable response
Chlorpromazine 100 mg three times daily as a broad spectrum first line agent with mild sedative benefit for sleep
Clozapine 12.5 mg twice daily titrated to 300 mg to address treatment-resistant cannabis-related psychosis quickly
Risperidone 1 mg twice daily titrated to 2 to 4 mg over 1 week with monitoring for extrapyramidal side effects
Quetiapine 300 mg nocte titrated to 600 mg as first line agent to improve sleep and reduce paranoid ideation

subtopic_detail: SSRI selection when breastfeeding an exclusively breastfed newborn
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatrist reviewing a 32-year-old G1P1 who is 6 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding a term male infant. She reports 4 weeks of pervasive low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia, guilt about not enjoying her baby, and early morning waking. EPDS score today is 18. She has passive suicidal ideation without plan and no thoughts of harming her baby. She has good social support with her partner and her mother visiting daily. Sleep is fragmented but the baby is feeding and gaining weight well. She has no personal history of depression prior to this pregnancy.

She would prefer to continue breastfeeding if safe to do so and asks about medication options today.

data_table.MSE: flat affect, tearful, thought content of guilt and hopelessness, no psychosis, passive SI no plan, insight intact
data_table.Infant: 6-week-old term male, exclusively breastfed, gaining weight along 50th centile
data_table.Bloods: TSH, iron studies, ferritin, B12 within normal limits, no anaemia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line SSRI to prescribe?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily as the first line SSRI in breastfeeding with review at 2 weeks for response and tolerability
Fluoxetine 20 mg daily as first line agent, with reduction to alternate day dosing if the infant develops symptoms
Escitalopram 10 mg daily as it has a favourable side effect profile and gentle onset for postnatal use in mothers
Venlafaxine XR 75 mg daily as an SNRI to address concurrent anxiety symptoms with the depressed mood presenting
St John's wort standardised extract 300 mg three times daily as a natural alternative for mild to moderate depression

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic clarification when cognitive complaints coexist
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 74-year-old retired teacher accompanied by his wife with 6 months of progressive loss of interest, low energy, appetite loss with 5 kg weight loss, and complaints of poor memory and concentration. His wife reports he says he is a burden. He denies suicidal plans. On testing he scores poorly on serial 7s citing lack of effort, but recall is intact with cueing. His Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination is 82 out of 100 with a global reduction (not domain-specific). CT brain 6 months ago was unremarkable for atrophy or vascular changes.

He has hypertension controlled with perindopril and no other medications.

data_table.MSE: flat affect, psychomotor slowing, thought content of guilt and worthlessness, no psychosis, passive suicidal ideation no plan
data_table.Cognitive: ACE 82/100 with global reduction, recall improves with semantic cueing, no focal deficits
data_table.Bloods: TSH, B12, folate, calcium, urea, electrolytes, LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Refer for donepezil trial as a therapeutic diagnostic step for early Alzheimer's disease with treatment response
Refer for immediate lumbar puncture and CSF amyloid biomarkers before any medication trial to establish diagnosis clearly
Commence sertraline 25 mg daily titrated to 50 mg with cognitive reassessment at 8 to 12 weeks after remission achieved
Order MRI brain with hippocampal volumes prior to any treatment intervention to define underlying neurodegeneration presence
Start memantine 5 mg daily titrated to 20 mg for suspected moderate Alzheimer's disease as a therapeutic diagnostic step

subtopic_detail: Escalation pathway when non-pharmacological measures have failed
stem:
You are the child and adolescent psychiatry registrar reviewing a 15-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder (level 3, minimally verbal) and moderate intellectual disability. His mother reports 3 months of escalating head-banging producing scalp abrasions, biting his hand producing skin breaks, and hitting his siblings when transitions occur. A structured behavioural plan with visual schedules, sensory environment modification, and functional communication training has been implemented by his ABA team for 3 months with limited response. Sleep is 4 hours per night. Medical review has excluded pain (dental, constipation, otitis).

He has never been on psychotropic medication.

data_table.Diagnostic: ASD level 3, minimally verbal, moderate ID (WISC-V IQ 45)
data_table.Behaviour: SIB (head banging, self biting) plus aggression at transitions
data_table.Medical workup: no dental caries, no otitis media, no constipation, urinalysis clear
data_table.Non-pharmacological: 3 months structured ABA and visual schedule with limited response

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Melatonin 3 mg nocte only, targeting sleep with the hope this reduces daytime irritability and self injurious behaviour
Clonidine 25 micrograms nocte for arousal reduction and hyperactivity as an alternative to antipsychotic exposure
Diazepam 5 mg twice daily as first line to reduce agitation and self injurious behaviour at difficult transition periods
Fluoxetine 10 mg daily as first line for rigid repetitive behaviours with plan to add antipsychotic only if it fails
Risperidone 0.25 mg nocte, titrating slowly to 0.5 mg BD, with metabolic monitoring baseline and every 3 months planned

subtopic_detail: IV sodium bicarbonate threshold for QRS widening
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 25-year-old woman brought in by her flatmate 90 minutes after finding empty amitriptyline packets and a suicide note. She had been prescribed amitriptyline 25 mg tablets for chronic migraine. She estimates 40 tablets ingested. She is drowsy but rousable and has vomited once en route.

Her flatmate confirms she has been increasingly withdrawn over recent weeks after relationship breakdown and university stress.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.ECG: sinus tachycardia rate 128, QRS 132 ms (upper limit 100 ms), terminal R wave in aVR 5 mm, no arrhythmia
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.28, pCO2 34 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (<2.0), potassium 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer 100 mmol (100 mL of 8.4 percent) IV sodium bicarbonate as a rapid push and repeat targeting QRS below 100 ms and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55
Administer IV flumazenil 200 micrograms in 15 second increments to reverse sedation and reassess neurological status once alert
Give IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes to prevent progression to malignant ventricular arrhythmia in the context of QRS prolongation
Empirical activated charcoal 50 g orally now to reduce further absorption of the ingested tablets in the current clinical setting
IV hypertonic 3 percent saline 100 mL over 30 minutes to correct the sodium status and stabilise cardiac membranes

subtopic_detail: TGA pregnancy prevention program obligations before initiation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder in your outpatient clinic. She is currently euthymic on lithium 750 mg nocte with a therapeutic level, but she describes intolerable weight gain and tremor. She and her consultant have discussed switching to sodium valproate. She is sexually active with a male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. She reports no current wish for pregnancy.

She asks whether she can start valproate today.

data_table.Contraception: condoms only, inconsistent use, no LARC
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): urea and electrolytes normal, TSH normal, lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0), pregnancy test negative today
data_table.Bipolar history: diagnosed age 20, one mixed episode, one manic episode, three depressive episodes; last episode 18 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily today given the current negative pregnancy test and plan to review in two weeks with an incremental dose escalation
Commence sodium valproate at a low dose of 200 mg twice daily and prescribe oral folic acid 5 mg daily to mitigate neural tube defect risk in event of unplanned pregnancy

Defer valproate initiation, refer for contraceptive counselling with a view to LARC (implant or intrauterine device) or documented dual method, complete a signed pregnancy prevention program acknowledgment
Add sodium valproate to her existing lithium as combination therapy to reduce individual dose exposure while allowing a broader mood stabiliser effect in the current clinical setting
Prescribe valproate but delay the first dose until she confirms she is menstruating this cycle to minimise the risk of exposure during a very early pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Recognising myocarditis in the first weeks of clozapine titration
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia now on day 18 of clozapine titration, currently at 250 mg nocte. He was admitted this morning after his community mental health nurse noticed him looking pale and unwell. He describes three days of malaise, low grade fever, and mild shortness of breath on exertion. His neutrophil count from yesterday was within the accepted range.

He denies chest pain but says his heart is racing all the time.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 122, blood pressure 110/70, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 38.1
data_table.Cardiovascular: no murmurs, JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.ECG: sinus tachycardia rate 122, no ST changes, no PR prolongation
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): troponin I 128 ng/L (<15), CRP 88 mg/L (<5), white cells 8.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 4.6 x10^9/L, eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (0-0.5)
data_table.Chest X-ray: no consolidation, cardiothoracic ratio at upper limit of normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Cease clozapine and commence intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily empirically for immune myocarditis without waiting for echocardiogram results
Continue clozapine at current dose, attribute the fever to intercurrent viral illness, and prescribe paracetamol 1 g four-hourly with review in 48 hours
Reduce clozapine dose by 50 percent, arrange full blood count and daily observations, and defer any structural cardiac assessment unless clinical deterioration occurs
Cease clozapine immediately, arrange urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review for suspected clozapine-induced myocarditis, and admit for cardiac monitoring
Interpret this as clozapine-induced fever benign syndrome (constitutional response to titration) and continue drug with symptomatic management

subtopic_detail: Bush-Francis features, lorazepam challenge, and ECT escalation
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 40-year-old woman admitted three days ago with dehydration and poor oral intake. She is well known to psychiatric services with bipolar I disorder and has had two previous manic episodes on lithium prophylaxis. The medical team say she is lying immobile and unable to answer questions today. On examination she holds an odd position when the examiner moves her arm and echoes fragments of what you say.

She passively resists any attempt to move her limbs and does not respond to commands.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Bush-Francis features observed: mutism, stupor, waxy flexibility, echolalia, negativism, staring, immobility
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 8.9 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, creatine kinase 480 U/L (<200), TSH 2.4 mIU/L, ammonia normal
data_table.Recent medications: lithium 750 mg nocte (level 0.72 mmol/L), no antipsychotics, no recent dopamine antagonists

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Administer IV lorazepam 2 mg and reassess Bush-Francis score at 15 minutes, with escalation to a repeat dose if partial response and ECT if refractory
Commence intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg for underlying manic state given prior bipolar I diagnosis and immediately observed odd behaviour
Immediate empirical intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g for possible autoimmune encephalitis and defer psychiatric intervention until autoantibody panel returns
Perform urgent lumbar puncture and start empirical intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg eight-hourly for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis
Increase lithium to 1000 mg nocte to treat presumed underlying bipolar episode and observe for improvement over 72 hours before re-evaluating

subtopic: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
subtopic_detail: Discriminating features and immediate management divergence
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 46-year-old man brought in by his housemate with three hours of agitation and shaking. He has depression on sertraline 200 mg daily and started tramadol 50 mg four-hourly three days ago after a work back injury. His housemate reports he has been taking St John's wort for chronic pain and just started olanzapine yesterday for anxiety, prescribed by another GP.

On examination he is tremulous, sweating profusely and unable to keep still.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 168/108, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Neurological: sustained lower limb clonus, hyperreflexia (patellar 4+, ankle 4+), inducible clonus in upper limbs, tremor
data_table.Mental state: agitated, restless, confused, mydriasis 5 mm bilaterally
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): creatine kinase 640 U/L (<200), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, urea 6.4 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, white cells 11 x10^9/L
data_table.Onset: over hours after new drug additions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg via nasogastric tube every 8 hours to reverse presumed dopamine blockade underlying the neuroleptic malignant syndrome features
Continue sertraline and olanzapine, add IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg for muscle rigidity, and admit for cardiac monitoring under general medicine
Cease all serotonergic drugs, administer IV midazolam 5 mg titrated for agitation, cool actively, and start IV crystalloid; consider cyproheptadine 12 mg orally if severe features persist
Give IV benzatropine 2 mg for suspected acute dystonic reaction from newly commenced olanzapine and observe over the next hour for resolution
Empirically commence intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and aciclovir 10 mg/kg for suspected meningoencephalitis before further diagnostics in the current clinical setting

subtopic_detail: Electrolyte monitoring and phosphate replacement in refeeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman transferred from a specialist eating disorders unit for medical refeeding. She has anorexia nervosa restricting subtype for 3 years with recent rapid deterioration. Her weight today is 34 kg (BMI 12.4) with 16 percent weight loss over the last 6 weeks. She has been taking around 400 kcal a day for the past 4 weeks. She is medically compliant but ambivalent about weight restoration.

Her parents have accompanied her and she has provided informed consent to the medical management plan.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 42, blood pressure 82/54 (drop of 20 mmHg systolic on standing), respiratory rate 12, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 35.6
data_table.ECG: sinus bradycardia rate 42, QTc 490 ms, no ST changes
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.65 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), glucose 3.4 mmol/L, urea 5.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L
data_table.Nutritional intake last week: ~400 kcal per day of restricted intake

lead_in: What is the most appropriate refeeding plan for the first 72 hours?

options.text: Begin refeeding at 30 kcal/kg/day with rapid escalation to full requirement within 48 hours to achieve early weight gain given severity of malnutrition
Commence total parenteral nutrition at 25 kcal/kg/day to bypass the gastrointestinal tract entirely and secure nutritional delivery
Withhold all feeding for 48 hours until electrolytes fully normalise, then start slow feeding once biochemistry is corrected to reduce the refeeding risk
Insert nasogastric tube and commence continuous feeding at 40 mL/hour of standard 1 kcal/mL feed with once-weekly electrolyte checks throughout the admission
Start refeeding at 10 to 20 kcal/kg/day with immediate IV thiamine 300 mg daily, prophylactic phosphate and multivitamin supplementation, daily bloods (K, PO4, Mg, glucose)

subtopic: Borderline personality disorder in emergency care
subtopic_detail: Structured discharge planning after intentional self-injury
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder who presented with multiple superficial lacerations to her forearms after an argument with her partner. Her wounds have been cleaned and steristripped by the nurses. She is well known to community mental health with regular dialectical behaviour therapy sessions. She denies current suicidal intent and says she wants to go home.

Her usual mental health case manager has just responded that she can offer a review tomorrow morning.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: distressed but engaging, no psychosis, no acute suicidal ideation or plan, chronic passive suicidal ideation only
data_table.Wounds: multiple superficial parallel lacerations bilateral forearms, all closed, no need for further intervention
data_table.Substance use: no acute intoxication, urinary drug screen negative
data_table.Risk factors: high previous self-harm frequency, one past overdose 2 years ago, in DBT program with good engagement
data_table.Social: partner supportive, lives with partner, community mental health case manager available tomorrow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with a written safety plan co-produced with her, confirmed community mental health follow-up within 24 hours, and information about crisis lines
Admit under psychiatry involuntarily under the state Mental Health Act for at least 72 hours of intensive risk assessment and containment
Prescribe olanzapine 10 mg IM in the ED to sedate her acute distress and reduce the immediate risk of further self-harm before disposition
Refer to inpatient dialectical behaviour therapy as day-only intensive intervention for one week to intensify treatment for recurrent self-injury
Discharge home with a prescription for lorazepam 1 mg orally three times daily as required for the next week to manage distress-related self-injury urges
